Brand as a promise, and the ledger it is kept in

Two proposals that improve next year's margin and quietly re-price a promise no balance sheet records.

1. Two decisions, six days apart

On 14 September 2026 Mrudula Bhogaraju opened a note from her procurement head, Girish Hampannavar. Qudrat Air Systems, where she is VP Product, sells air purifiers out of Jodhpur and replacement filters to the people who bought them. The note offered an alternative filter medium: identical bench performance, ₹180 cheaper a pack, certified life eight months rather than twelve. The carton says, in the largest type after the brand name, One filter. One year.

Qudrat ended FY26 with 4,00,000 active devices, 96,000 units sold at an average realisation of ₹11,000, and a filter subscription that 2,32,000 of those 4,00,000 households — 58.0 per cent — renewed at ₹2,500 a pack. The memo was dangerous because it did not look bad: eight-month life means one and a half packs a year, so the CFO, Lalitha Peddireddy, had the swap adding ₹13.28 crore of filter margin in FY27 even after assuming renewals fall. The number arguing against it did not yet exist.

Six days later Manohar Vemuri faced the mirror image. Qaayda Pharmacy Cloud, in Bhubaneswar, runs the billing counter for 6,500 pharmacy outlets at ₹4,200 an outlet a month — ₹32.76 crore of ARR, 20.0 per cent above the ₹3,500 its nearest competitor quotes. Qaayda wins on one sentence: the counter never stops, and it never bills the wrong thing. A pilot of an AI substitution suggester produced 12,600 suggestions at 93.0 per cent clinical appropriateness. Manohar's instinct: 93 per cent is fine for a feature and catastrophic for that sentence.

2. The idea, and its history

A brand, stated precisely, is the set of expectations a buyer has learned to hold about what a product will do — learned because those expectations were met, or violated, before. Brand equity is the differential response: the gap between what she will do for this product and for a physically identical one with no history, visible in what she pays without inspecting, how fast she forgives and how readily she vouches. Logo and campaign state the promise; they are not it.

Two lineages met only recently. The managerial line runs from Neil McElroy's 1931 memo at Procter & Gamble, which invented the brand manager as someone accountable for one product's whole promise, through Gardner and Levy's 1955 Harvard Business Review argument that a brand is a public image with character rather than a list of attributes. It became measurable with Aaker's Managing Brand Equity (1991) and Keller's customer-based model (1993), which put the asset inside the buyer's memory.

The economic line is colder. Nelson's 1970 distinction between search goods, checkable before purchase, and experience goods, knowable only by consuming, explains why brands exist. Klein and Leffler's 1981 model made it explicit — a brand is a bond, future profits forfeited by cheating, which is why paying a premium is rational. Both answer a persistent accounting hole: under Ind AS 38, as under IAS 38, an internally generated brand is not recognised as an asset, so Qudrat's largest asset is invisible to the committee most able to spend it. Nobody hands you the carrying value of a promise; you compute it.

Three schools then disagree. The meaning school (Aaker, Keller) would sign that a distinctive, well-kept claim earns a durable price premium. The availability school (Ehrenberg and Sharp) holds that buyers are light, inattentive and disloyal and that brands are chosen in proportion to how easily they come to mind and can be bought; it would sign that distinctiveness matters and differentiation is largely fiction. The signalling school would sign that equity is the present value of premiums forfeitable by cheating. None will sign what every deck asserts: that a brand is what a company says about itself.

3. Mechanics, in depth

Five steps; the second and the fifth are usually left implicit, and are where the damage happens.

One: write the promise as falsifiable claims with tolerances. A promise a buyer cannot test is a slogan. Mrudula's register held three: twelve months of filter life in Indian dust, with under 5 per cent of units flagged early; an app reporting the true indoor reading; a visit within 48 hours. A tolerance turns a value into an engineering requirement.

Two: map each claim to the decisions that can break it, and name an owner. Against the twelve-month claim Mrudula listed filter-medium sourcing, firmware fan-speed defaults, the sensor's replacement threshold and the app notification's wording; two of the four sat outside product. A promise with no owner is spent by people who never knew they were spending it.

Three: measure on three independent instruments — a tracker for the funnel from awareness to repeat, a price-premium study for per-unit worth, and a preference test for first choice at equal price.

Four: price the promise per unit by decomposing the premium. A premium is everything a buyer pays extra for, only some of it trust. Qudrat sells at ₹11,000 against ₹7,400 for a spec-matched private-label unit — a gross premium of ₹3,600, or 48.6 per cent, which a conjoint exercise split.

The residual, ₹1,400 a device, is the honest brand number: on 96,000 FY26 units, ₹13.44 crore of revenue that exists only because the promise has been kept. That is what a promise-breaking decision risks.

Five: convert per-unit value into an asset, and state what the conversion assumes. Relief from royalty asks what the firm would pay to license this brand if it did not own it. On FY26 revenue of ₹163.60 crore (₹105.60 crore of devices plus ₹58.00 crore of filters) and a 2.5 per cent royalty benchmark, the notional royalty is ₹4.09 crore a year; capitalised in perpetuity at 12 per cent with 4 per cent growth, ₹4.09 crore ÷ 0.08 = ₹51.12 crore, pre-tax — soft, but the right order of magnitude beside a ₹4-crore saving.

4. When it applies, and when it misleads

Five conditions, each testable first. Repeat purchase or renewal exists, so a kept promise compounds — true of Qudrat's filter line, definitional for Qaayda. Quality is not verifiable before purchase: nobody tests a twelve-month claim in a shop, nor offline billing in a demo. The claim is eventually falsifiable, sharply so for dispensing. The buyer can switch: true for Qudrat, partly false for Qaayda, where migration costs delay the break to renewal. The experience is attributed to you — the condition that fails most often, since a third-party technician's botched installation is attributed to Qudrat.

It misleads in a commodity with no repeat and a visible spec; in distress purchases, where availability beats association; before product-market fit; and where the channel owns the relationship.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product. Once one name carries several products each inherits the promise and can spend it for the others: Qudrat's planned car-cabin purifier would be judged against One filter. One year. whether or not the claim was made for it. Mature firms tier — a masterbrand promise true of everything, product claims below. What they say they do is maintain a brand architecture; what they do is argue at launch and settle by seniority.

Two-sided markets. A marketplace keeps two promises in separate ledgers and can spend one to fund the other. Qasba Mandi Network, an agri-produce exchange in Siliguri, promises buyers grade-accurate lots and farmers payment within 24 hours; tightening rejection protects the first and breaks the second, and a tracker sampling only buyers reports health while supply leaves.

Regulated products. Regulation sets a floor, not the promise: Qaayda can be fully compliant with Schedule H record-keeping and still break its promise, because compliance asks whether the record is correct and the promise asks whether the patient got the right medicine.

Hardware plus software. Software can revoke a promise hardware made: one over-the-air change to the filter-life algorithm turns a twelve-month claim into a nine-month experience. The mutable half therefore needs the stricter change control — the reverse of most release processes.

AI-native products. A probabilistic system cannot promise determinism, which is why 93.0 per cent is Manohar's crux. The move is to re-specify the promise so it is keepable — not "the suggestion is right" but "nothing reaches a patient without the pharmacist's confirmation, and every suggestion is logged and reversible."

6. Nine expert distinctions

1A promise has a tolerance; a claim does not. The tell is that nobody can say what would count as a break. An unspecified promise is not stronger, merely unenforceable internally.

2Equity is differential response, not affection. Trackers measuring warmth but never willingness to pay produce rising scores during erosion. The tell: a brand-health deck with no price question.

3Most of a premium is not brand. Quoting Qudrat's gross ₹3,600 as brand value overstates the asset 2.6 times against the ₹1,400 residual, and an inflated number loses its next argument with finance permanently.

4Breaks are priced by the installed base, not the complainant. Disappointed buyers go quiet and skip a renewal, so the tell is a calm support queue while cohort renewal drifts down two points a quarter.

5Consistency beats intensity, and losses are asymmetric. Binet and Field have brand effects accumulating slowly and activation decaying fast. A promise kept 39 times and broken once is not 97.5 per cent kept: the break teaches the buyer the 39 were luck.

6Distinctiveness and differentiation are different assets. Recognisability is cheap, durable and load-bearing; being meaningfully different is expensive and often imaginary. The tell is a rebrand that improves taste and destroys recognition.

7A strong brand makes a weak product fail faster, because the promise raises the bar the experience is measured against. The tell: strong first-week trial, collapsing week-four retention, blamed on messaging.

8The promise you never stated still binds you. Defaults become promises: a brand that quietly accepted returns for two years promised something it never printed. The tell is "we never promised that" while reviews say otherwise.

9Nobody owns the promise unless someone is named. Rights over Mrudula's claim sat with four teams (Fig. 3). Experts ask not for authority but for a standing right to be consulted; the tell is a brand book with an author and no signatory.

7. By product type and stage

In consumer products the promise attaches to an attribute felt at each use, one person decides, and the break shows up at the next purchase, which makes filter renewal a real-time brand instrument. In B2B it is a reliability commitment judged by a committee who mostly never use the product, so it must survive paraphrase by a champion, and breaks surface two or three quarters late, first as a longer sales cycle. On marketplaces the promise is plural and the ledgers separate. In hardware the pack is the contract. In AI products the promise must be restated as a distribution plus a recovery path.

By stage: before product-market fit the promise is provisional and codifying it early is a mistake. While scaling, where both protagonists sit, it must become explicit because decisions now sit with people who never heard the founder say it. At large scale the failure inverts — documented beautifully, ignored structurally, because procurement and pricing scorecards carry no promise column. Plainly, where there is no difference: the mechanics, the lag and the asymmetry of a break are identical in all of them.

8. Three worked examples

8.1 Qudrat: the profitable promise break

Scenario B takes the cheaper medium at ₹1,270 — margin ₹1,230 — but eight-month life means 1.5 packs a renewing household a year, with renewal falling to 51.0 per cent.

8.3 Qaraar Sleep Works: the failure, and recovery

Qaraar Sleep Works, a mattress brand in Udaipur founded by Kiran Nemmani, grew on an unprinted promise: a hundred nights, return it if you do not like it, we collect it. In FY25 it sold 34,000 mattresses at ₹24,500 — ₹83.30 crore — at a 7.2 per cent return rate: 2,448 returns at ₹9,800 each, or ₹2.40 crore. In April 2025 the operations committee required original packaging and a ₹1,500 pickup fee, unannounced. Returns fell to 3.1 per cent of 31,000 FY26 units and the return line to ₹0.80 crore.

9. Failure modes and diagnostics

Filing brand under communications. Early sign: a refresh lands in the quarter procurement changes a specification a claim depends on. Diagnostic: of the last ten sourcing decisions, which claim did each touch, and who signed? Late cost: when the tracker finally moves, the supplier contract is a year old.

Measuring awareness and calling it equity. Early sign: awareness up, preference at equal price flat. Diagnostic: plot both on one timeline for eight quarters. Late cost: a year of spend showing more people a promise fewer believe.

Arguing the promise on the line where the saving sits. Early sign: the debate lives inside one P&L line, as in Table 3. Diagnostic: which line pays for this promise, and is it in this model? Late cost: approval on a true but irrelevant number.

Withdrawing a default that had become a promise. Early sign: "we never promised that" in a thread. Diagnostic: what do the last hundred reviews say we promise? Late cost: Qaraar's ₹5.43 crore of extra acquisition cost.

Promising accuracy for a probabilistic system. Early sign: a launch document quoting one accuracy figure with nothing about the residual. Diagnostic: what is the recovery path for a wrong answer, and is that what we promise instead? Late cost: roughly 6,735 counter-level errors a year.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

One: the promise is the asset. Kept claims build memory structures that produce a measurable premium, and Qudrat's ₹1,400 residual is real. The evidence is decades of conjoint studies and the price collapses that follow public promise failures. It would be wrong if the residual were an artefact of distribution, vanishing once availability were held constant.

Two: availability is the asset and the promise is decoration. Ehrenberg-Bass's replicated findings — double jeopardy, duplication of purchase, the dominance of light buyers — support a view in which brands grow by being easy to recall and easy to buy, and most claimed differentiation is invisible to the buyers who drive volume. On this view Mrudula is mostly wrong and the twelve-month claim matters only as a distinctive asset. It would be wrong if promise breaks destroyed value where availability was constant — close to what Qaraar's year shows.

Three: equity is a bond, to be valued as one. The signalling school computes the present value of forfeitable premiums — ₹51.12 crore for Qudrat — and treats the rest as narrative. It would be wrong if firms with nothing yet to forfeit sustained premiums anyway, which is arguably what strong new entrants do for years.

The three imply different decisions here, and honest practice names the disagreement rather than dissolving it. The unsettled question is whether equity is separable from distribution — whether, stripped of shelf and search rank, a promise retains value. Nobody has run that experiment cleanly.

11. Mastery

Four visible behaviours. They arrive at the trade-off meeting with the promise already decomposed and priced, so the conversation is arithmetic rather than values. They volunteer the pass that goes against them, as Mrudula did with the 44 per cent case, because a brand argument survives only if finance believes the arguer is not motivated. They spend more time on the promise register than the brand book. And they re-state, print and price a claim they cannot hold rather than quietly breaking it.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Mrudula took Table 4 to the 9 October board beside the one-year model, and recommended keeping the twelve-month medium. The board agreed and asked for the ₹4.18 crore elsewhere; Girish Hampannavar found about half in pack logistics and a renegotiated carton spec, neither touching a claim. Manohar shipped the suggester in February 2027 as a confirmation-required suggestion with a reversible trail, gated on a held-out error rate below 1.5 per cent — and did what sales liked least: the stand said what the model gets wrong.

One: had the medium become genuinely unavailable, what would an honest re-statement of One filter. One year. have cost, and would that beat ₹9.36 crore? Two: Qaayda's exposure assumes the premium halves at renewal — what evidence would justify that, and what would falsify it? Three: Qaraar's promise was never printed. Whose job was it to notice that it existed?

13. Going deeper

Messaging hierarchy — which claim leads; brand is that hierarchy held for years. Brand and emotional design in consumer products — a promise felt through form. Brand management — owning a promise across a portfolio. Brand tracking studies — building Table 1 without leading the respondent. Writing a positioning statement — choosing which promise to make. Naming products and features — attaching the masterbrand to something that cannot keep its word is the cheapest way to spend equity. Category design — when the promise is a category. Sales enablement — surviving repetition by someone on quota. Launch communications and PR, and packaging — where the promise becomes public, and where Qudrat's was printed.

Brand fundamentals for PMs

What promise does the brand make, and are today's product decisions keeping it or spending it?

1. A nine-rupee email

On the fourth Monday of September 2026, Sarath Panicker read an email twice: "Formulation change — margin opportunity," from Wishwaas Foods' longtime ingredient vendor, offering to swap the natural preservation process behind its pickles and curries for a synthetic stabiliser, nine rupees cheaper a jar. Sarath, who had built brand and product-marketing at Wishwaas Foods into a team of six, knew exactly what the offer asked him to decide. Every jar carried, as large as the brand name: "No preservatives. Real ghee. My grandmother's recipe." R&D was confident the stabiliser was safe and undetectable in taste — but the label would have to change.

Wishwaas Foods, headquartered in Warangal, had built a ₹42-crore FY26 business on clean-label pickles sold through quick commerce and modern trade, priced at ₹185 a jar against a category average near ₹110 for a mass-market brand on the same shelf — a premium of roughly 68 per cent, paid, the company assumed, for what the label promised and kept. The CFO wanted a recommendation before the board met on 3 October; quick-commerce commissions had climbed from 18 to 22 per cent that year. Nobody could yet say, with more than an opinion, how much of that ₹42 crore rode on the words now in play.

2. The idea

Stripped of its usual metaphors, a brand is the set of expectations a customer has learned to hold about what a product will deliver — learned because those expectations were met, or violated, before — and that expectation decides how much they pay without asking twice, how quickly they forgive a lapse, and how confidently they recommend it onward. A brand is not a logo, a name or a campaign; those state a promise. The brand itself is whether the promise has actually been kept, purchase after purchase.

The idea was formalised as "brand equity" through the late 1980s and 1990s: without a shared way to measure it, brand was treated as marketing's aesthetic project, disconnected from the sourcing, pricing and service decisions actually keeping or breaking the promise. David Aaker's Managing Brand Equity (1991) gave that trust a measurable structure — awareness, quality, associations, loyalty. Kevin Lane Keller's Customer-Based Brand Equity model (1993) reframed it from the customer's memory outward: which associations does a person carry, and did the last experience strengthen or weaken them. Together, management gained a way to ask, before any decision, not "does this look right" but "which promise does this touch, and does it strengthen or spend it."

The sentence Sarath could say in the board meeting without sounding glib: "Brand is the premium we get paid because our last hundred promises came true — and this decision is promise number hundred and one."

3. How it actually works

Keeping a brand promise runs through five steps, and the fifth is the one most teams skip. First, identify the promise pillars — the specific, falsifiable claims customers rely on, not everything in the brand guidelines. Wishwaas Foods' own research had surfaced three: no preservatives and real ingredients; an authentic, grandmother's-recipe taste; and availability, the jar in stock at reorder. A pillar must be falsifiable: a customer must eventually tell, from experience, whether it held.

Second, almost every product decision is an implicit vote on a pillar — what goes into the jar, how it is priced, what a support agent may say about a delayed order. Few of these decisions are made by anyone who has read the guidelines; that gap is where promises get spent unnoticed.

Third, and the step most practitioners leave implicit, is tagging a decision by which pillar it touches before the trade-off is discussed, not after a customer notices. A sourcing scorecard rarely carries a "promise pillar" column; someone has to add one, so the ingredient conversation happens beside the label conversation, not in two rooms that never compare notes.

Fourth, customers keep a private ledger: each kept promise adds a small confirmation, and each broken one subtracts considerably more, because a violation also teaches the customer the promise was never fully reliable. That ledger decides whether the premium gets paid again.

Fifth, a tracker converts that invisible ledger into a number a team can act on before deciding, not after churn shows up quarters later — the step Sarath set out to run before the board met.

4. A worked example

In June 2026, Sarath commissioned a survey of 1,000 repeat buyers — customers who had bought Wishwaas twice in the preceding six months — asking one question: why do you choose Wishwaas over a mass-market pickle costing less than half as much?

5. Nuances a learner must sit with

Promise versus personality

A promise is a functional commitment — what will be true of the product; personality is how that commitment is said. Product decisions spend or build the former; a campaign mostly touches the latter. Teams that confuse the two believe a smarter tagline fixed something a supply-chain memo broke.

Equity versus awareness

Awareness answers "do they know us"; equity answers "do they trust us enough to pay, forgive and recommend without more evidence." A widely known but distrusted brand carries negative equity; visibility spend while equity erodes only shows more people a promise fewer believe.

The lag between decision and damage

A promise-touching decision shows up in the tracker months later, because let-down customers mostly reduce quietly — skipping the next reorder rather than complaining. Revenue can look healthy while the ledger underneath is already turning.

Not every stated claim is load-bearing

A deck can list a dozen claims, but only attribution data like Table 1 shows which one revenue rests on. Founder conviction is not evidence; treating every claim as sacred means the trade-off that matters never happens on the pillar actually paying rent.

Brand cannot rescue a weak product

A sincere promise on a product that under-delivers accelerates disappointment, because the expectation raises the bar the experience is measured against. The framework prices how expensively a promise breaks; it says nothing about whether the product can support the promise.

Confused with positioning, and its own limits

Positioning is choosing which promise to make and to whom; equity is what accumulates from keeping that promise, decision after decision. A reposition changes the target, not the balance already spent — and even a well-run tracker cannot say which promise was worth making, or adjudicate between two true promises now in conflict, such as always in stock against staying small-batch.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace — and scale

In a consumer product like Wishwaas, the promise attaches to an attribute felt directly, renewed or spent meal by meal; one person decides, so individual surveys like Table 1 work cleanly. In B2B, the promise is less an attribute and more a reliability commitment carried across a relationship — uptime, SLA adherence, an account manager's behaviour under pressure — and it breaks at renewal, not in a week's tracker, because the "customer" is a committee trusting a promise repeated second-hand.

In a marketplace, the promise is two-sided and can be spent on one side invisibly to the other: a buyer promise ("genuine, fast, refundable") and a seller promise ("real demand, fair payout") are separate ledgers, and protecting one — aggressive refunds, say — can quietly break the other. A tracker sampling only buyers reports a healthy brand while supply is leaving.

Scale changes where the promise lives. Early on it resides, undocumented, in the founder's word, and works because everyone can check with the founder directly. Growth forces the pillars explicit, since decisions are now made by people who never met the founder; a large company's opposite failure is a polished brand book the sourcing team never opens when it matters.

7. Common mistakes

Mistake 1Treating brand as the logo-and-campaign layer. Symptom: a "refresh" lands the same quarter sourcing quietly changes something a pillar depends on. Misunderstanding: brand is filed under communications, not decisions. Diagnostic: list the last ten sourcing decisions and ask which pillar each touched.

Mistake 2Trusting the founder's gut over the customer's ledger. Symptom: recurring debate about "what we stand for," settled by seniority. Misunderstanding: conviction stands in for a verified promise. Diagnostic: run an attribution survey like Table 1 before the next trade-off meeting.

Mistake 3Reading awareness as if it were affection. Symptom: awareness climbing while repeat-purchase for that cohort is flat. Misunderstanding: visibility spend is assumed to protect equity, a different asset. Diagnostic: plot awareness against cohort repeat-rate on one timeline.

Mistake 4Assuming equity absorbs one bad quarter. Symptom: leadership approves a promise-touching cut, assuming "we'll explain it if anyone notices." Misunderstanding: defection near a trust threshold is usually silent — fewer reorders, not complaints. Diagnostic: track cohort repeat-rate for two quarters after the change.

8. What good looks like

A team that handles this well does not avoid the trade-off; it makes it visible before deciding. Before any promise-touching proposal reaches a board, someone runs the attribution survey, or draws on a tracker already running, and converts the result into a rupee number using the arithmetic above. That number sits on the same slide as the saving the proposal chases, in the same currency — not an unresolved values debate about "authenticity." When the two numbers come out close, the team names it a judgement call openly, rather than letting whoever is most persuasive settle it.

9. What Sarath decided

Sarath took the ₹9.58-crore exposure figure, alongside the ₹1.51-crore saving, to the CFO and R&D a week before the board met — as the number the swap needed to beat. It did not: even discounting stated intentions by half, exposure was still ₹4.79 crore against a ₹1.51 crore saving. Wishwaas Foods kept its preservation method and found margin elsewhere — a smaller jar size, renegotiated quick-commerce fees — decisions that did not touch a load-bearing pillar.

What to learn next: brand tracking studies, on designing such a survey without leading the respondent; and brand and emotional design, on how a promise is expressed at the shelf, not only claimed on a label.

Two questions worth sitting with: which of your product's claims have you verified are load-bearing, versus assumed because they read well in a deck? And the next cost-saving proposal on your desk — what would it cost you if the customer noticed?

Upaja Trace Systems: One Seal, Two Meanings

A Case for Discussion · Go-to-Market, Growth & Monetisation · Brand Fundamentals for Product Managers

1. Sunday night, Berhampur

At twenty past eleven on the night of Sunday, 4 October 2026, Damayanti Panigrahi was still at the long table in Upaja Trace Systems' office above a tyre showroom on Gandhi Nagar Main Road, Berhampur, because the printout in front of her would not stop meaning two things at once.

It was one page, forwarded that afternoon by the head of sales: a bar reading 81% verified coverage above the name of Quellmark Spice Trading B.V., the Rotterdam importer whose June quality notice had made Upaja indispensable to every exporter in the district. The slide went to Quellmark on 21 July and to the board four days later.

Beside it lay a second page, circulated on Friday, 18 September by Devashish Bhoi, Upaja's only data scientist, in Toronto, who had spent five weeks reconciling the company's records against the laboratories that supposedly produced them. On his definition the number lay between 37.0 and 68.3 per cent.

Neither page was wrong. That was the difficulty. At half past eight on Monday she would sit with the product council; at seven that evening she would join a board call with the CEO, the CFO and the partner from the fund that led Upaja's Series A. On Friday, 9 October, four people from Quellmark's quality team would arrive to pull forty passports at random. She did not know which course she would recommend, and no longer believed the four on her whiteboard were the list.

2. How Upaja got here

Upaja Trace Systems was incorporated on Monday, 13 June 2016 by Rabindra Mangaraj and two classmates, working from the back of his father's commission-agent firm in the Berhampur mandi. The proposition was narrow: buyers abroad wanted to know which fields a lot of dry chilli or turmeric came from, how it had been dried and graded, and what a laboratory had found when it looked for pesticide residue and moisture. Every exporter did it the same way, in a folder of scans assembled the week before the container sailed.

Upaja replaced the folder with a lot passport: a record opened when produce was weighed at a collection yard, carrying the plot reference, drying batch, grading line, test results and container number, and closing as a set the buyer could interrogate. The promise was one line on the induction slide, which Rabindra still says in this form: every claim on an Upaja passport can be walked back to a field and to a laboratory record that exists.

On Monday, 12 August 2019 the promise became an asset. Quellmark agreed to accept an Upaja passport in place of its own incoming test on two of four residue analytes, saving the exporter eleven days of port-side delay and giving Upaja what no competitor had: a buyer abroad specifying its name.

On Monday, 15 March 2021, under pressure to grow faster than laboratories could be integrated, Upaja added a second tier — the decision that constrains everything today. In the Verified tier Upaja pulls the residue report directly from an accredited laboratory's system; in the Declared tier the exporter uploads a scan, and Upaja records that it was uploaded. Volume went from 40 lots a day to over 600 within a year, and Upaja now passports 78,000 lots a year, covering ₹2,051 crore of declared export value for ₹8.44 crore of fees — ₹1,082 a lot (Exhibit 1). Both tiers carry the same seal — same mark, same colours, same position — distinguished only by a small letter V or D in its lower right corner.

3. The industry

India is the world's largest producer and exporter of spices, and the trade is documentary as much as agricultural. Exporters register with the Spices Board of India, consignments move under FSSAI rules and the Export Inspection Council's arrangements abroad, and laboratories are accredited by NABL for particular analytes. The binding force is the importing regime: European maximum residue limits have tightened repeatedly, and one border rejection notified through the EU's rapid alert system can make every buyer in that market demand lot-level evidence from every Indian supplier, not only the one at fault.

Berhampur sits in a belt that grows teja and sannam chilli and, north-west of it, the turmeric carrying the Kandhamal geographical indication. Its exporters are mid-sized, selling into Rotterdam, Hamburg and Dubai and into the domestic branded trade as Tata Consumer, ITC and Reliance Retail push traceability to lot level. Upaja has two competitors: Qandeel Trace Networks in Sambalpur, with laboratory integration only at twice the price per lot, and Qadam Agri Assurance in Rourkela, a document generator at a tenth of the price that makes no assurance claim at all.

Fourteen laboratories serve Upaja's customers; three expose results through an interface it can query. Its overseas staff is small — customer success in Singapore, data science in Toronto, sales in Edison, New Jersey — but the buyers who give the seal its value are all abroad, and none pay a rupee for it.

4. What happened, and what has turned out to be wrong

On Tuesday, 9 June 2026, Quellmark's group quality function circulated a notice to its Indian suppliers. After a border alert on a chilli-powder consignment from an exporter outside the district, it required from 31 October 2026 lot-level residue records "verified by an independent third party", and named Upaja passports as acceptable evidence. It did not distinguish the tiers; nobody at Quellmark knew there were two.

Kishore Bisoyi, head of sales, treated it as the event Upaja had waited nine years for, and within six weeks had signed three exporters and put the coverage slide before Quellmark on 21 July. The 81 per cent came from Upaja's dashboard, which counts a lot as covered if any test record is attached by either route. On that definition the figure is exactly right (Exhibit 2).

The first crack appeared on Friday, 7 August. Kalpana Bariha, the compliance lead and once a chemist at a Berhampur laboratory, was preparing Ushas Oleoresins for an audit and checked nine Declared-tier reports by hand against the issuing laboratory. Two did not exist in its register; a third's number also appeared on a different lot. She wrote to Rabindra and Damayanti that evening; the reply, which she did not argue with, was that nine reports were not a finding.

Devashish began on Friday, 4 September and circulated his reconciliation on Friday, 18 September (Exhibit 3). His result was not that Upaja's customers were cheating; most discrepancies were dull — a clerk reusing last season's scan, a laboratory that restarts its report numbers each April. What his work established was narrower and worse: for most of Upaja's volume nobody — not Upaja, not the exporter, not Quellmark — could say whether the document behind the seal existed (Exhibit 4). In the audited subset, 1,554 of 15,300 Declared-tier lots, or 10.2 per cent, matched nothing at all, against 42 of 18,900 Verified lots.

On Friday, 25 September Quellmark announced the 9 October audit, and Joost Brinkman, its category buyer, told Roshni Nayak his team would sample forty passports at random and trace each to source. Forty drawn from a population in which 52 per cent of lots sit in the Declared tier is not a sample designed to find anything. It is a sample almost certain to.

5. The people

Damayanti Panigrahi — Head of Product, Berhampur. Position: the tier distinction must become visible to buyers. Incentive: her promotion case rests on this quarter. Not saying: she read Kalpana's 7 August note the night it arrived and sat on it six weeks.
Rabindra Mangaraj — Co-founder and CEO, Berhampur. Position: the promise is the company. Incentive: a bridge round is being negotiated on the strength of the June notice. Not saying: the Declared tier was his 2021 decision, over his co-founders' objection, and never called a compromise in public.
Kishore Bisoyi — Head of Sales, Edison, New Jersey. Position: disclosure turns a tailwind into a scandal; tighten quietly. Incentive: variable pay is 45 per cent of package, keyed to new logos. Not saying: he tells prospects Upaja passports are "accepted by Quellmark" — true of the seal, not the tier.
Dibakar Patro — Engineering Lead, Sambalpur centre. Position: integrate the eleven remaining laboratories and the problem dissolves. Incentive: next year's headcount rests on that programme. Not saying: six of his fourteen engineers are locked to peak-season work, and two laboratories have no register.
Kalpana Bariha — Quality and Compliance Lead, Berhampur. Position: the Declared seal should never have looked identical to the Verified one. Incentive: none obvious. Not saying: Qandeel Trace Networks has approached her and she has not declined.
Roshni Nayak — Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Position: Quellmark will forgive a disclosed error and never a discovered one. Incentive: she carries renewals for the two most exposed accounts. Not saying: Brinkman asked her in August whether all passports were laboratory-linked, and she never answered.
Devashish Bhoi — Data Scientist, Toronto. Position: refuses a single coverage figure; the honest answer is a range. Incentive: none. Not saying: his three-laboratory subset is not random — the integrated laboratories are the better-run ones.
Ronit Sethi — Chief Financial Officer, Berhampur. Position: no single move may risk more than a quarter of fee revenue (Exhibit 5). Incentive: a diligence question on assurance quality would kill the bridge round. Not saying: the Udbhav liability cap is the only reason he is sleeping.

7. Voices

"Nobody outside this building has ever asked about tiers. Not one buyer, in five years. If the market wanted the distinction it would have asked."Kishore Bisoyi, product council, 22 September
"That is the argument for the tiers, Kishore, and also against them. Nobody asked because the seal told them they did not have to."Damayanti Panigrahi, same meeting
"Option A on Monday and I lose Udbhav by Friday. Seventy-one per cent of their lots are Declared. They will take the paperwork in-house and buy Qadam for a lakh a year."Ronit Sethi, internal chat, 30 September
"Then we will find out what Upaja is worth when it is only telling the truth."Rabindra Mangaraj, same thread, nine minutes later
"Damayanti, help me understand one thing before Friday. When my team accepts your passport instead of running our own test, what exactly have you checked?"Joost Brinkman, Quellmark Spice Trading B.V., email, 2 October

8. The options as Damayanti sees them

A. One tier, one seal

Retire Declared; a lot gets the seal only when the report comes from an integrated laboratory. Clean, and defensible before Brinkman on Friday. The ₹406 lakh it risks is 48.1 per cent of income (Exhibit 6), against ₹9.6 crore of cash and ₹58 lakh a month of burn.

B. Two marks, said out loud

Split the seal into visibly different marks and write to every buyer explaining which lots carried which, going back. Preserves most revenue, but tells Quellmark in writing that some of what it accepted for five years was weaker than it believed, and starts a clock on its supplier code, which requires disclosure of known material inaccuracy within fifteen working days of discovery — and whether discovery was 7 August or 18 September, Upaja's lawyer cannot say.

C. Tighten quietly

Leave the seal alone; raise Declared requirements over two quarters, integrate laboratories as capacity allows, say nothing retroactively. Cheapest and least disruptive — and it means walking Brinkman through forty passports on Friday knowing what Devashish knows.

D. Stop making the claim

Reposition Upaja as a documentation workflow tool — faster folders, fewer clerical errors — and let buyers verify for themselves. Honest and cheap, and it hands the ground on which Quellmark specifies Upaja by name to Qandeel, which never built a Declared tier.

Damayanti has drawn the four on a whiteboard three times this week and each time something has felt mis-drawn. All four treat the seal as the object of the decision. But Upaja's paying customer is the exporter, whose interest is a container that clears, while the party whose trust makes the seal worth anything is the buyer abroad, who pays nothing and holds no contract. None of the four asks which of the two the promise was made to — or contains what Kalpana keeps saying: that the tiers are not the problem, the identical mark is.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Quellmark's supplier deadline is Saturday, 31 October 2026; the audit is Friday, 9 October; the board call is Monday evening. Peak season begins in December, when daily volume triples and no product change ships.

Money: ₹9.6 crore of cash against ₹58 lakh a month of burn — about sixteen and a half months of runway before the bridge. Ronit's ceiling of a quarter of fee revenue at risk admits B and C and excludes A and D. People: fourteen engineers, six locked to peak-season work; two unintegrated laboratories cannot be integrated at any price this year.

Contracts: the master agreement with Udbhav Spice Exports caps liability at fees paid in the preceding twelve months — ₹214 lakh — and requires ninety days' notice of any material change to the service, putting Option A out of reach until January for the customer it would hit hardest. Quellmark has no contract with Upaja, and no obligation to be reasonable.

Regulation: nothing Upaja has done breaches the Spices Board's requirements, FSSAI or any importing regime, and no rule obliges a private assurance mark to disclose its own tiers. Consent for farmer plot geo-coordinates was rebuilt for the DPDP Act in November 2023. The absence of a regulator to blame or hide behind is, Damayanti has come to think, the shape of the problem.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. State the promise Upaja's seal has made since 2019 as a buyer in Rotterdam would state it, then as Udbhav's export manager would. Are they the same promise?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 describe the same year and differ by forty-four points. Which figure belongs in Monday's board deck, and what does choosing it commit Upaja to?
  3. Devashish says his three laboratories are the best-run in the district. What does that do to the 68.3 per cent ceiling in Figure 1, and how should Exhibit 4 be used rather than discarded?
  4. The 2021 decision bought five years of growth. Was it a mistake, a reasonable bet badly labelled, or a correct bet whose bill has now arrived?
  5. Whose trust is Upaja's real asset: the exporter who pays it, or the importer who does not? What does each course do to the other party's trust, and can any improve both?
  6. It is 8.30 a.m. on Monday, 5 October. What does Damayanti tell the product council, what does she put before the board that evening, and what does she say on Friday when the fourteenth passport of forty is Declared and from an unintegrated laboratory?

11. Sunday night, continued

The generator downstairs cut out before midnight and the room went quiet enough that Damayanti could hear the last trucks on the bypass carrying early chilli towards the coast. She had drafted the board slide four times. The first said 81 per cent and she deleted it because it was true. The fourth said "between 37 and 68 per cent, and we cannot yet be more precise", and she deleted that too, because it was also true and sounded like a company admitting it had never known what it sold.

On the table were Kalpana's nine reports, Devashish's range, Ronit's ceiling, Kishore's slide and Brinkman's question, still unanswered. She thought about the induction slide — every claim on an Upaja passport can be walked back to a field and to a laboratory record that exists — and about the fact that in nine years nobody had asked whether Upaja had done the walking. She turned off the lamp at twenty past one and went down into the wet October air with all of it still open.

Ikya Sahakara Systems: What the Brand Actually Promises

A Case for Discussion · Go-to-Market, Growth & Monetisation · Brand Fundamentals for Product Managers

It was a little past nine on Wednesday, 4 February 2026, when Harish Kattimani, Head of Product at Ikya Sahakara Systems, closed his laptop in the company's office on Khanapur Road, Belagavi, and signed for a thick envelope from the Karnataka Milk Federation: the request for proposals for a unified milk-procurement-and-payout platform across its district unions. Bids were due by five in the evening on Friday, 20 February — sixteen days away. Harish's team had built the one feature everyone believed would win it: instant, UPI-linked payout the moment milk was tested at the village collection centre. The pilot data on his desk suggested that feature also had a way of quietly breaking the promise Ikya had spent seven years keeping. He had sixteen days to decide what went into the bid.

1. Ikya Sahakara Systems

Ikya was founded in 2018 by three Belagavi engineers tired of watching commission agents shortchange farmers on fat and SNF (solids-not-fat) readings at village collection points — the two measures on which every rupee of milk price is calculated. Ikya builds Automatic Milk Collection Units: an electronic analyzer at the village Dairy Cooperative Society (DCS) that reads fat and SNF in seconds, prices milk against the union's rate chart, and pushes the transaction into a cloud ledger, bypassing the paper khata-book and the agent's discretion. Farmers see the price the instant their can is tested; the payout, until now, settles the next morning after a supervisor reviews the batch file.

Seven years in, Ikya serves three of the federation's district milk producers' unions — Belagavi, Bagalkot and Gadag — covering 2,090 village societies, 159,000 farmer accounts and roughly ₹956 crore a year in payouts (Exhibit 1). Its pitch has always been one sentence on the induction slide: the number on the screen is the number that lands in the account. That promise, not any screen or app, is what Ikya sells. Nandini, the federation's consumer brand, is the face farmers see on the can; Ikya is the invisible plumbing, and trust in that plumbing is the whole commercial asset. NPCI's UPI rails have made faster settlement the natural next feature across the category, including for Stellapps Technologies, whose mooPay module now reportedly offers same-evening settlement.

2. The situation

The RFP covers roughly a dozen district unions beyond the three Ikya already runs, worth an estimated ₹42 crore over three years, and its evaluation rubric gives explicit marks for settlement speed — a response to demands that money move as fast as milk does. Tanuja Chougule, Ikya's Sales Head, has spent a month building the bid narrative from her home office in New Jersey, on calls starting 7 a.m. in Belagavi and running near midnight for her. She is also the company's contact with its US-based Series A investor, who has told the board that one new union this quarter matters for the next funding round. To Tanuja, it separates a competitive bid from a losing one.

Nagappa Yaligar, Engineering Lead in Pune, piloted Instant Payout for sixty days across forty DCS in one Belagavi taluk before recommending against a company-wide launch. Harshitha Mugali, the data scientist in Toronto, spent three weeks on the logs. Her finding, in Exhibit 2, was not that Instant Payout caused more errors — analyzer drift, duplicate cattle-tag scans and operator mistakes produce the same error rate whichever way settlement runs. What changes is that the morning review, which used to catch errors before the bank file went out, no longer sits between reading and account. A UPI push cannot be recalled like a batch file, and a small, real share of pilot transactions reached farmers wrong with no way back.

3. The people

Harish Kattimani — Head of Product, Belagavi. Owns the decision; must reconcile sales' narrative with what the pilot showed.
Tarun Gouda — Co-founder & CEO, Belagavi. Needs a signed union for the fundraising conversation; trusts Harish but cannot ignore the board.
Tanuja Chougule — Sales Head, New Jersey. Wants Instant Payout as the headline feature to match Stellapps.
Nagappa Yaligar — Engineering Lead, Pune. Wants ninety more days for a reconciliation window before wider rollout.
Harshitha Mugali — Data Scientist, Toronto. No stake in the outcome; her analysis is the evidence others argue over.

4. Exhibit 1 — Ikya's footprint across its three district unions

5. Exhibit 2 — What the sixty-day pilot actually showed

Exhibit 2 is Harshitha's argument: the error rate is unchanged by speed, but the safety net disappears once settlement turns instant. Of every 2,40,000 transactions, 1,200 are flagged, 240 turn out real, 96 unrecoverable — a pattern that recurs at any scale.

6. The options

Option 1 — Instant Payout live everywhere at go-live

Make it the flagship feature for every farmer account Ikya serves, matching Stellapps head on. Upside: highest win probability, cleanest pitch for sales and the board. Cost: all 159,000 accounts, and several times that after the tender, carry the pilot's error pattern from day one.

Option 2 — Instant Payout only where hardened, T+1 elsewhere

Launch it for the 640 DCS already refreshed for connectivity and analyzers — 82,680 accounts, 52 per cent of the base — with automatic fallback to T+1 elsewhere, disclosed plainly in the bid. Upside: real differentiation, no unguarded exposure. Cost: a less dramatic pitch and roughly twenty-five days to audit the pathways first.

Option 3 — Delay Instant Payout out of this bid

Bid on Ikya's seven-year record of accurate payouts; introduce Instant Payout only after Nagappa's ninety-day, ₹65 lakh reconciliation fix is proven. Upside: the promise stays fully intact. Cost: conceding the speed criterion to Stellapps outright, and weakening the growth story Tarun needs for fundraising.

Exhibit 3. Decision economics of the three options
OptionEst. win probabilityExpected bid value (₹ crore)Farmer accounts exposed at go-live
1 – Instant everywhere55%23.101,59,000 (100%)
2 – Phased instant50%21.0082,680 (52%)
3 – Delay instant30%12.600 (0%)

Expected bid value is win probability × the ₹42 crore contract value; rows are alternatives, not a sum.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What promise has Ikya been making to farmers and unions for seven years — does it live in the technology or the process around it?
  2. Does Exhibit 2 show Instant Payout is less accurate, or that it removes a safety step protecting the same error rate? Why does that matter for choosing an option?
  3. Using Exhibit 3, what is Harish trading between contract value and the size of the promise at risk? Should the highest expected value always win a brand-sensitive decision?
  4. If Harish picks Option 2, what must be true operationally, and in how the union is told, so the phased promise does not become the next one Ikya fails to keep?

8. A note for the learner

Brand fundamentals come down to one question: what promise does the product make, and are today's decisions building it or spending it? For Ikya the promise was never speed — it was that the number on the screen is the number that lands in a farmer's account, with no error between the two. Exhibit 2 is where a good answer starts: settlement speed does not change the 0.5 per cent flag rate, it only removes the review that used to catch it before money moved. That turns a technology question — can Instant Payout ship — into a brand question: can it ship only where the safety net is in place.

Option 1 borrows against seven years of trust to fund one sales pitch; a single well-publicised wrong payout at roughly fifty times pilot scale (2,090 societies against the pilot's 40) would cost far more in the unions' confidence than the ₹1.34 lakh notional stake suggests, and spent brand equity, unlike expected contract value, does not renew next quarter. Option 3 protects the promise perfectly but risks the tender and the fundraising story the company needs to survive — refusing all risk is not automatically responsible, since no promise is kept by a company not there to keep it. The defensible path is Option 2: it extends the promise rather than trading it away — the number you see is the number you get, and where we cannot yet guarantee that in minutes, we say so and stay with the process that does. Harish should pair it with two written commitments: dated milestones for extending hardened coverage union by union, and a cap below which Instant Payout will not fire until Nagappa's fix is live everywhere — so the promise Ikya sells in February is the one it keeps in December.

Disha Insight Cloud: Writing the Positioning Statement

A teaching case on deciding what a product is, before an audience decides for you.

1. Bengaluru, Monday 28 September 2026

Devika Tandon, VP of Product Marketing at Disha Insight Cloud, had four days to finish a single sentence: for whom, what category, what benefit, unlike what. That sentence would go on the homepage, into the sales deck, into the renewal scripts Faiza Thakkar's team used from Singapore, and onto the slide behind Devika when she walked on stage at SaaSBOOMi Annual in Bengaluru on 6 October to answer, in front of press and prospects, the question: what is Disha Insight Cloud?

Two deadlines pressed on her at once. The keynote was one. The other was quieter but larger: on 1 October, Faiza's team would begin the Q3 renewal cycle — eighty accounts, worth ₹12.28 crore of the company's ₹42 crore in annual recurring revenue, each needing someone to say, convincingly, why the account should keep paying Disha instead of switching to CleverTap or MoEngage. Devika did not want that answer improvised call by call.

2. What Disha Insight Cloud sells

Disha Insight Cloud was founded in Bengaluru in 2019 by three engineers who had built messaging tools inside a mid-sized food-delivery company. It sells a customer engagement and retention platform to Indian direct-to-consumer brands — the kind of company that sells online the way boAt or Mokobara do, running its own Shopify or WooCommerce storefront alongside Amazon and, increasingly, ONDC listings, and using Unicommerce to manage inventory. Disha's product plugs into that stack and sends push, SMS, email and WhatsApp messages to bring customers back. By September 2026 it had roughly 410 paying customers and ₹42 crore in annual recurring revenue, competing for every deal against CleverTap, MoEngage, WebEngage and Netcore — four well-funded, well-known engagement platforms, each with a broader feature set and a longer track record.

Eighteen months earlier, Trisha Fonseca, Disha's lead data scientist in Toronto, had shipped something none of the four competitors had: a model reading a brand's live stock feed that predicts, for each customer, whether the product they buy repeatedly is about to go out of stock — and, if so, triggers a save action before the customer churns out of frustration rather than disloyalty. The team called it the inventory-intelligence module. Nothing on Disha's website or deck said the company was built around it.

3. What had actually been happening

Disha's official positioning statement, unchanged since 2021, still read: for D2C brands running lifecycle marketing, Disha Insight Cloud is the customer engagement platform that unifies push, SMS, email and WhatsApp campaigns, unlike point-tools that cover only one channel. Every rep's deck opened with it. But Farhan Dastur, Disha's head of enterprise sales in New Jersey, had noticed his best reps quietly not using it. When a prospect already ran CleverTap or MoEngage — by 2026, most did — leading with "unified campaigns" invited a comparison Disha usually lost. His top reps led with the inventory story instead, and Farhan had the win-loss numbers to show it worked (Exhibit 1). He wanted it written down, not left to whichever rep reinvented it.

Faiza Thakkar, running customer success from Singapore across Asia-Pacific and Middle East accounts, saw the other side of the same gap. In quarterly reviews, several of her largest, most exposed accounts — including Tariq Farooqui at Sadaf Home & Living LLC, a Dubai-based home-goods distributor and Disha's largest cross-border account — had asked, more or less directly, what Disha did that CleverTap didn't. Her team logged this as a churn-risk flag, clear enough by September to put in front of Devika (Exhibit 2). Daniel Thorne, Disha's lead product designer in Berlin, had meanwhile paused an onboarding redesign: he could build the first screen around campaigns or around inventory alerts, not convincingly both, and needed the hero capability decided before the Q4 release froze.

4. The people

Devika Tandon — VP Product Marketing, Bengaluru. Owns the statement; presents it publicly in eight days.

Farhan Dastur — Head of Enterprise Sales, New Jersey. Wants the inventory pitch made official for every rep, not just his best ones.

Trisha Fonseca — Lead Data Scientist, Toronto. Built the model; wants the category name to reflect it, for customers and for hiring.

Daniel Thorne — Lead Product Designer, Berlin. Needs one hero capability before the Q4 onboarding redesign freezes.

Faiza Thakkar — Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Runs renewals for the accounts most likely to leave if they can't say what makes Disha different.

5. What the numbers said

Exhibit 1 covers every enterprise opportunity qualified in H1 FY27 (April–September 2026), split by pitch used.

Exhibit 1 — H1 FY27 enterprise opportunities, by pitch used
Pitch usedOpportunitiesWonLostWin rateAvg. ACV (₹ lakh)ARR won (₹ lakh)
"Engagement platform" (standard deck)71145719.7%14.0196
"Inventory-intelligence" (improvised)25131252.0%22.0286
Total / blended96276928.1%17.9482

Win rate = Won ÷ Opportunities. Avg. ACV rows are per-deal averages within that pitch; the total row is the blended average (₹482 lakh ARR won ÷ 27 deals won = ₹17.9 lakh). ARR won = Won × Avg. ACV.

The gap was stark: the improvised inventory pitch, used on barely a quarter of opportunities, won at more than double the rate of the standard deck and at 57 per cent higher contract value, producing 59 per cent of the half-year's ARR won from just 26 per cent of the opportunities.

Exhibit 2 shows the renewal cohort Faiza's team would call from 1 October, by tier.

Exhibit 2 — Q3 FY27 renewal cohort (Oct–Dec 2026), by segment
SegmentAccountsARR at stake (₹ lakh)Flagged "unclear differentiation"Flagged share
Enterprise D2C18612950.0%
Mid-market D2C544321425.9%
Cross-border / UAE8184562.5%
Total801,2282835.0%

Flagged share = Flagged accounts ÷ Accounts in that segment. ARR at stake of ₹1,228 lakh (₹12.28 crore) is 29.2 per cent of Disha's ₹42 crore total ARR.

The risk sat exactly where the money was: Enterprise and Cross-border accounts, worth ₹796 lakh of the ₹1,228 lakh at stake, were flagged at 50 and 62.5 per cent, against 25.9 per cent for Mid-market — the same accounts, Farhan's numbers suggested, where the inventory-intelligence story already won.

Exhibit 3 sketches where the four named competitors and Disha itself actually sat.

6. The options Devika was weighing

A. Hold the current statement

Keep the 2021 positioning — "the customer engagement platform that unifies push, SMS, email and WhatsApp" — and add inventory-intelligence as a lower feature bullet. No retraining, no rewrite of Daniel's brief. The cost: Disha stays inside a comparison it wins only 19.7 per cent of the time, and nothing changes for the 50 and 62.5 per cent of Enterprise and Cross-border accounts already unable to say why they should stay.

B. Reposition fully around inventory-intelligence

Rewrite the primary statement: for D2C brands selling on Shopify, Unicommerce and ONDC, Disha Insight Cloud is the inventory-intelligence layer that turns stock signals into retention actions, unlike CleverTap and MoEngage, which run engagement campaigns with no visibility into what's actually in stock. Carry it into the website, the deck, Daniel's redesign and Faiza's script. It matches every number in Exhibits 1 and 2. The cost: it must be retaught company-wide, and some Mid-market buyers may not recognise themselves in it.

C. Two statements, one per tier

Keep the engagement-platform language for Mid-market, where flagged risk is lowest, and use the inventory-intelligence statement only for Enterprise and Cross-border, where it already wins. No segment is asked to accept language that doesn't fit it yet. But the same product now makes two different "unlike" claims to two buyer groups, doubling the collateral Devika must produce, and reopening the question whenever a Mid-market account grows into Enterprise.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using the template for [who], [product] is the [category] that [benefit], unlike [alternative], write the statement implied by each option. Which one could Devika defend, unscripted, to a customer already running CleverTap?
  2. Exhibit 1 shows a 32.3-point gap in win rate between the two pitches. What in the case explains why Disha's sales team had not already standardised on the pitch that wins more?
  3. Exhibit 2's renewal risk sits in the segments carrying the most ARR. How should that shape which buyer the statement is written for, versus which buyers simply get different proof points under it?
  4. If Daniel's onboarding redesign isn't ready by the Q4 freeze, should the words or the product experience ship first, and what does that cost Farhan, Faiza and Trisha?

8. A note for the learner

A positioning statement is not a summary of everything a product does; it is a claim about who the product is for, written so specifically that its "unlike" clause is falsifiable. That makes Option A untenable: it competes on CleverTap and MoEngage's own axis, and Exhibit 1 shows how that comparison ends — 19.7 per cent, against 52.0 per cent in the same data.

The harder choice is between B and C. A positioning statement names one primary buyer, not every buyer the product happens to serve; segmentation belongs downstream, in the messaging hierarchy under the statement, not inside its own "who" and "unlike." Option C solves that hierarchy problem by writing two statements instead — the same product telling two buyer groups two different things it is "unlike," a distinction Farhan's reps would struggle to hold across adjacent calls, and one that breaks the moment a Mid-market account grows into Enterprise.

The evidence points to Option B, scoped correctly: write the primary statement for the Enterprise and Cross-border buyer, exactly where the win-rate advantage (52.0 versus 19.7 per cent), the ACV advantage (₹22 lakh versus ₹14 lakh) and the renewal risk (50 and 62.5 per cent flagged) all point at once. Mid-market buyers need the same claim carried through with lighter proof points, not a second, competing statement — a messaging-hierarchy decision for later. That gives Devika one sentence, defensible with numbers, for the SaaSBOOMi stage and for Farhan's and Faiza's teams before the renewal calls begin.

Hastakshar Contract Cloud: The Sentence Before the Board

A case on what a company is allowed to call itself once the money, the code and the name have all been chosen.

1. Pune, Sunday 4 October 2026, 11.20 p.m.

Anuradha Kaikini had thirty-one slides ready for the board meeting that opened at ten the next morning, and one was blank but for a heading: Positioning. Below it sat the skeleton every product marketer there had learned to fill in — for whom, what category, what benefit, unlike what. She had written eleven versions since Thursday and deleted them all.

The sentence was not a marketing artefact this time. Two funds wanted a Series B narrative memo before diligence, and the memo began with the category the company claimed. That claim would propagate: into the pricing page relaunching on 10 October, into an insurer's tender due 9 October, into Hemal Acharya's sales kickoff in Austin on 13 October, and into how 268 customers were renewed. The evidence Anuradha had spent September collecting had arrived in volume, and it disagreed with itself.

Navratri was a week away, the last pandal scaffolding stacked against the wall below her window. Her notebook held three candidate sentences, each defensible, each expensive, and a fourth line she had circled twice: we are not actually arguing about words.

2. How Hastakshar came to be what it is

Hastakshar Contract Cloud was founded in Pune in 2019 by Kabir Ahluwalia, who had run legal operations at a large Indian insurer, and Advait Kulkarni, an engineer from a payments gateway. The name — hastakshar, signature — was Kabir's, chosen in a week when the founders believed the product was an Indian alternative to DocuSign and Adobe Acrobat Sign: cheaper, Aadhaar eSign-native through UIDAI's licensed providers and at ease with the Information Technology Act.

By the 2021 Series A they had learned that e-signature alone was a feature, not a company: incumbents were competent at it and per-signature pricing was collapsing. So the round — ₹62 crore, led by a growth fund whose partner, Ashwin Karnad, still sat on the board — was raised on contract lifecycle management. Indian legal teams, the deck argued, drafted in Word, signed on one tool, stamped through another and stored contracts nowhere. Hastakshar would be the one workflow from draft to repository.

Then came the decision that shaped everything Anuradha could now say. In mid-2022, with eighteen months of runway and one engineering team, Advait could build either a drafting and negotiation layer — clause library, template governance, redlining, the items CLM buyers score, estimated at ₹4.2 crore — or deep integrations into state e-stamping systems, so a loan agreement could be stamped at the correct duty inside the workflow that signed it. Kabir chose stamping: customers already paid for it manually, in franking queues and courier runs, and nobody else had it. Four years and ₹8.4 crore later Hastakshar was live in fourteen states with no clause library, and the CLM story it sold was hollow in exactly the places buyers scored.

3. The industry Hastakshar sells into

Three forces shaped the Indian market by 2026. The first was digital lending: RBI's guidelines had pushed regulated lenders into digital onboarding, and a digital loan still ends in a stamped, signed, evidentiarily sound instrument — lakhs of documents a month across NBFCs, small-finance banks and insurers regulated by IRDAI. The second was fragmentation: stamp duty is a state subject, collected under the Indian Stamp Act and state amendments, with e-stamping routed through SHCIL, Protean eGov and treasury portals. The third was the DPDP Act.

Against that, the competitive set depended on what Hastakshar said it was. Described as e-signature, it met Leegality, Digio, SignDesk, Zoho Sign and DocuSign — all benchmarked on price per envelope. Described as contract lifecycle management, it was scored on a feature matrix it partly failed. Described as compliance infrastructure, it had almost no competitors, and almost no buyers with a budget line by that name.

The exposure was not only Indian. In 2024 an Abu Dhabi group, Hadaf Construction LLC, bought the platform for subcontractor agreements across the UAE and Oman and grew into the largest single account, at ₹248 lakh of ₹4,380 lakh in recurring revenue, or 5.7 per cent. Hadaf paid for seats, workflow and a repository, and nothing for stamping: Indian stamp duty does not exist there.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

The belief through 2023 was that stamping was an on-ramp: land operations, expand to legal with CLM seats. Ketaki Ambekar's customer-success team in Kuala Lumpur reported the first counter-evidence in late 2024. Account after account, the stamping workflow was bought by a compliance or operations head, ran at volume, renewed reliably — and never travelled to the legal team. The legal teams that did buy seats had bought them first, in a separate motion, and were likeliest to leave when a global CLM vendor arrived with a clause library.

By March 2026 Aniket Havaldar, the data lead in Vancouver, could show the mix drifting (Exhibits 1 and 2). Subscription revenue — the high-margin line the Series A story rested on — was growing at roughly a quarter of the rate of stamping revenue. Nobody read this as a positioning problem: it was a sales-mix problem, and Hemal was asked to hire two enterprise reps.

Two events in July 2026 broke that reading. Hastakshar reached the final two of a large private bank's CLM tender and lost on the scored matrix, on drafting gaps Advait's roadmap would not close before 2028. And Karnataka revised its cap on e-stamping service charges, cutting the realised fee per document there from ₹128 to ₹110 — 14.1 per cent, worth about ₹90 lakh a year at current volumes. The category Hastakshar claimed was one it kept losing in; the category it earned in answered to fourteen states that had never agreed on anything.

5. The people

Anuradha Kaikini, VP Product & Product Marketing, Pune. Owns the statement and the slide; believes the company has addressed the wrong buyer for three years. Has not said she wrote the 2024 refresh reaffirming the CLM language, so reversing it reads as her error.

Kabir Ahluwalia, co-founder and CEO, Pune. Wants the Series B on a software multiple, which he believes needs subscription revenue and the CLM category. Chose stamping in 2022 and never links that choice to the CLM gap. Has not said one fund has floated a lower valuation if transaction revenue keeps rising.

Hemal Acharya, Head of Enterprise Sales, Austin. Wants the compliance-execution pitch made official because his team wins with it; is paid on bookings, not margin or deal size. Has not mentioned that his two largest 2026 deals were legal-team CLM sales, or that his reps retagged old opportunities after hearing what Exhibit 4 compared.

Ketaki Ambekar, Customer Success Lead, Kuala Lumpur. Wants one sentence her team can repeat across nine time zones, and holds the retention data favouring the compliance buyer; her bonus tracks gross retention, which that segment flatters. Has not said she stopped introducing legal teams, whose requests she could never get built.

Advait Kulkarni, VP Engineering, Indore. Quotes the drafting layer at ₹6.8 crore and fifteen months — the 2022 module repriced. Would rather build three more state integrations. Has not said three senior engineers will leave if the next eighteen months are more government portals.

Hiral Kamath, Lead Product Designer, Amsterdam. Cannot design the first screen until the category is settled: execution products open on a document queue, CLM products on a repository. Wants a rename. Has not said she briefed the agency on Exhibit 5, order of statements included.

Aniket Havaldar, Data Lead, Vancouver. Produced Exhibits 1 to 3 and refuses to recommend a statement, warning in writing that Exhibit 4 shows what was pitched to whom, not what wins. Thinks the retagging makes it unusable but will not say so, because Hemal defends his headcount.

Ashwin Karnad, board member, Mumbai. Wants a category the next round's buyers already believe in; says regtech comparables trade below CLM ones. Sits on the board of a company selling to the same compliance buyer. Has not said which revenue line he would sell first if the round failed.

6. Exhibits

Two of the six pointed in opposite directions.

Exhibit 1 — Revenue mix and gross margin, annualised run rate, September 2026 (₹ lakh)

Source: finance close, 26 September 2026. Stamp duty is collected in trust for state governments and is not revenue; execution-line direct cost is collection-centre charges, certificates and bank fees.

Exhibit 3 was the one Ketaki quoted most and Kabir liked least. Alone, it says the compliance buyer is the best customer Hastakshar has; against Exhibit 1, that the best-retaining customer sits on a thirty per cent margin.

Exhibit 3 — Accounts and retention by economic buyer, September 2026

International accounts, Hadaf included, sit in the legal row, carry no stamping revenue, and hold ₹498 lakh of the ₹1,140 lakh subscription line.

Exhibit 4 is the cut Hemal wanted; Aniket asked it not be shown alone.

Win rate, decided = Won ÷ (Won + Lost), so the total row is 39 ÷ 102 = 38.2 per cent; on a won ÷ all-opportunities basis the total is 39 ÷ 130 = 30.0 per cent. Avg ACV rows are per-deal averages; the total is blended (₹853 lakh ÷ 39 wins).

Exhibit 4b — The same 130 opportunities, split by when the pitch was recorded

The 31 untagged opportunities were classified in a survey sent to eleven reps on 18 September, after Exhibit 4's comparison had been described to the sales team. Win rates here are decided-only: execution deals tagged after the outcome won 14 of 21, or 66.7 per cent, against 8 of 20, or 40.0 per cent, where the tag preceded the result.

Exhibit 5 was Hiral's: trusted least, hardest to dismiss.

Exhibit 5 — Message test, Indian buyers, August 2026 (n = 142)

Fielded by an agency from a buyer panel, briefed by Hiral Kamath; statements shown in fixed order, S1 first, unrotated. Of 142 respondents, 96 came from firms below ₹500 crore turnover and 46 from the larger firms the enterprise motion targets. S2 scored the highest clarity and the lowest willingness to pay.

Exhibit 6 shows a mechanism Anuradha had not expected, and suspected mattered more than any pitch data: buyers file the product into a category of their own, and that category sets the price.

Exhibit 6 — Formal tenders and RFPs, H1 FY27, by the category the buyer scored Hastakshar in
Category the buyer usedRFPsShortlistedWonARR won (₹ lakh)Avg ACV of wins (₹ lakh)ARR won per RFP (₹ lakh)
E-signature / document signing38191111010.02.89
