RFP-led opportunities only: 28 of the 39 wins in Exhibit 4 came through a tender, carrying ₹523 lakh of the ₹853 lakh won; the other 11 averaged ₹30.0 lakh. Category is the tender's own heading, not Hastakshar's pitch; total-row averages are blended. Shortlist rate was 15 of the 22 compliance tenders, or 68.2 per cent, against 14 of 41 in CLM.

Read across, Exhibit 6 says three incompatible things at once. Its rates are wins per tender entered, not per decided deal. Scored as CLM, Hastakshar wins 6 of 41, or 14.6 per cent, but at ₹39.0 lakh a deal. Scored as compliance it wins 9 of 22, or 40.9 per cent, at ₹17.0 lakh. Scored as e-signature it wins respectably and is paid ₹10.0 lakh for identical software. Compliance returns most per tender, ₹6.95 lakh against ₹5.71 lakh — but only 22 such tenders existed in six months, because no analyst firm publishes that category for finance teams to budget against.

7. Voices

"We are a CLM company that happens to be very good at stamping. Tell the funds we are a compliance utility and we price ourselves at a services multiple, with a thirty per cent margin line as the core business."

Kabir Ahluwalia, product and GTM review, 24 September

"My reps do not lose on the compliance pitch. Sixty-one days, twenty-two wins. I do not need a survey to read my own pipeline."

"Your pipeline tells you which deals you chose to pitch that way. Not the same sentence."

Hemal Acharya and Aniket Havaldar, forecast call, 26 September

"Every call where I say 'lifecycle' is a call where the customer asks about the clause library and I change the subject. Nine people, three time zones. Give them something true."

Ketaki Ambekar, email to Anuradha, 29 September

"You cannot put 'lifecycle' on a homepage above a logo that reads signature. Buyers are not confused about us. We are."

Hiral Kamath, design review, 1 October

"We renewed because your workflow holds our subcontractor agreements across two countries and our auditors accept it. Nothing in our contract mentions Indian stamp duty. If this becomes an Indian compliance product, tell me early — our March commitment is a clause library."

Khalid Ansari, Group Legal Head, Hadaf Construction LLC, quarterly review, 2 October

8. The options as Anuradha sees them

A. Hold the CLM statement and treat execution as proof

For enterprise legal teams, Hastakshar is the contract lifecycle management platform that takes an agreement from draft to stamped, signed execution in one workflow, unlike e-signature tools that stop at the signature. Protects the ₹1,140 lakh subscription line, the ₹39.0 lakh price point and Hadaf's roadmap commitment. Needs Advait's ₹6.8 crore module to be credible, and asks Ketaki's team to keep using a word customers do not know.

B. Reposition around compliant execution

For compliance and operations heads in regulated Indian businesses, Hastakshar is the compliant execution layer that stamps, signs and files every agreement to the duty rules of fourteen states, unlike contract suites that leave stamping outside the system. Matches the win rates, the retention and the revenue mix — and the ₹17.0 lakh price point. Writes 43.7 per cent of subscription revenue out of the story; hands the valuation to fourteen state fee schedules.

C. Two products, two statements

Split the platform in name: an execution product for compliance buyers, a lifecycle product for legal teams, each with its own statement and price book. Nobody hears the wrong sentence. But one engineering team serves two roadmaps, Hemal's reps must pick a story in the first minute of every call, and the question of what Hastakshar is returns unanswered to the board.

D. Name a new category

Contract execution infrastructure. S3 in Exhibit 5 is a first draft: best willingness to pay, middling clarity, no budget line anywhere. Category creation takes eighteen to twenty-four months before a tender carries that heading; Hastakshar has sixteen months of cash.

All four assume the statement is Anuradha's to write. Advait's estimate and Kabir's 2022 fork suggest it merely records a product decision made four years ago and never revisited; Hiral's objection suggests the binding constraint is a name on a logo; Exhibit 6 suggests the buyer's procurement template sets the category, not the vendor's homepage. Anuradha had written all three in the margin without working out which, if any, dissolved the choice.

9. The deadline and the constraints

The board met at ten on Monday 5 October. Hastakshar held ₹31.2 crore of cash against a net burn of ₹1.95 crore a month — sixteen months, if the mix did not shift the margin further. The memo was due to the funds by 17 October. Subscription ARR stood at ₹11.4 crore of the ₹43.8 crore total, or 26.0 per cent, against a story assuming ₹40 crore of subscription ARR by FY29 and a blended margin above sixty per cent; today's is 46.3 per cent.

The hard edges: renaming would cost about ₹2.6 crore in trademarks, domains and re-papering 268 agreements that name the licensed product. Hadaf's master agreement committed a clause library by March 2027, with a termination right if it slipped. The insurer's tender due 9 October was headed Contract Lifecycle Management — Empanelment. Fourteen state integrations were live, and the top three states carried 8,50,000 of the 12,00,000 documents stamped in H1 FY27, or 70.8 per cent. And the drafting module could not be funded out of the current plan without cutting two state integrations or the two enterprise reps Hemal had just hired.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Write each option in the form for [who], [product] is the [category] that [benefit], unlike [alternative]. Which clause does the real work, and which does each option quietly leave blank?
  2. Exhibits 4 and 4b describe the same 130 opportunities. What does each support, and what would you need before allowing either into the pack?
  3. Exhibits 3 and 6 disagree about which buyer is best. Is that about evidence, about time horizon, or about what "best" means to whoever produced the exhibit?
  4. Exhibit 6 implies the buyer's procurement heading sets the price for identical software. If so, what can a positioning statement change, and over what period?
  5. Hadaf is 5.7 per cent of ARR and much of the reason the subscription line exists. Must a positioning statement include the largest account, and what happens to Ketaki's renewals if it does not?
  6. It is Monday morning: one slide, four minutes. What does Anuradha put on it, what does she tell the board she cannot yet decide, and what would she have to be wrong about for that recommendation to destroy the company?

At 11.50 p.m. Anuradha typed a fifth sentence, borrowing the "who" from Option B and the "category" from Option D, and read it aloud to an empty room. It was clear and it was true, and she could not name one buyer in Exhibit 6 who had written a tender under that heading. She left the slide blank and shut the laptop.

Go-to-Market, Growth & Monetisation · Positioning, Messaging & Product Marketing

Writing a Positioning Statement

The sentence is cheap. What it commits a company to — which customers, which comparison, which promise engineering must keep — is not: a capital-allocation decision that happens to be written in prose.

1. Two rooms in Hubballi, eleven days apart

On 14 July 2026, off Gokul Road in Hubballi, Keerthi Nadgir opened a review with a sentence she no longer believed. Nadgir was vice-president of product and marketing at Chandana Load Exchange, a spot-freight marketplace founded in 2021 where despatchers post intercity truckloads and fleet owners bid for them. In the quarter ended 30 June 2026 its shippers posted 1,84,000 loads, of which 66,240 — a fill rate of 36 per cent — were matched. At ₹30,000 per matched load that was ₹198.72 crore of gross merchandise value, earning ₹7.95 crore at a 4 per cent take rate.

The offending sentence sat on Chandana's home page: "India's largest verified truck network." Defensible — 41,600 verified trucks, 23,800 active that quarter — and worthless, naming no customer, category or alternative. Kotresh Angadi, her co-founder and chief executive, wanted it kept because investors quoted it; Kalyani Shettar, of Chandana's Series B fund, wanted something sharper before the next raise. The uncomfortable part, which Nadgir had already found, was that the segments deserving the sharpest sentence were not the ones carrying the volume.

Eleven days later, four kilometres away, Charan Yerramilli faced the mirror image. He ran product marketing at Kaarvaan Fleet Systems, which since 2019 had sold large shippers an enterprise transport management system bundled with an in-cab telematics device: by 30 June 2026, 74 customers, 26,300 instrumented trucks, ₹59.2 crore of annual recurring revenue, an average contract value of ₹80 lakh. It had just run two quarters of one sales motion against one list under two different sentences about what the product was. Making the newer one official meant telling the board that Kaarvaan's category was the wrong one.

2. The idea, and the four camps that will not agree about it

A positioning statement is one declarative sentence fixing four commitments: the target (a customer describable precisely enough to buy a list of them), the category (the frame within which that customer judges the product), the benefit (the outcome that matters most to them), and the alternative plus the reason the product beats it. The canonical form — for [target], [product] is the [category] that [benefit], unlike [alternative], because [differentiator] — is a forcing device: each slot narrows the next, so a team writing one honestly discovers what it had been refusing to decide.

Four camps agree on little beyond the word. Al Ries and Jack Trout, in Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind (1981), put the position in the prospect's head, not the product: they would sign that perception, not capability, is the asset managed, and would not sign that a claim must be earned by what the product verifiably does. Geoffrey Moore, in Crossing the Chasm (1991), made it a template tied to a beachhead segment and a whole product — one target, one compelling reason, and no holding several positions at once. April Dunford, in Obviously Awesome (2019), inverted the order of work: start from the alternatives customers consider, derive the differentiated capabilities, then choose a category deliberately. She would sign that the category is chosen, not inherited, and would not sign the template as a starting point. Byron Sharp and the Ehrenberg-Bass tradition, from How Brands Grow (2010), dispute the premise: brands in a category share buyers heavily, perceived differentiation is weak, and growth comes from availability across a broad base.

Moore and Sharp recommend opposite actions on the same data: narrow until the sentence bites, or accept that a narrow sentence forfeits reach you will never recover.

3. Mechanics: the statement as an allocation model

Expert practice does not begin with words. It begins with a table costing each candidate target, because the "who" slot is the only one with a revenue number attached. Nadgir built hers from settlement data across five despatcher segments, using each segment's trailing-four-quarter fill rate to estimate how much of its volume Chandana's supply pool could serve.

The two tables rank the segments differently, and that gap is the argument. Auto components and garment export hold 18,300 of the 77,160 reachable loads — 23.7 per cent — and 9,024 of the 26,712 matched loads, or 33.8 per cent. Yet they produce ₹127.0 lakh of the ₹177.3 lakh of monthly contribution, 71.6 per cent. Agri traders, the largest segment by account count at 1,150, contribute ₹0.7 lakh a month. Only now do the other slots become tractable. Choosing auto components and export garments makes reliability of placement, not price, the benefit that matters, because a tier-2 supplier whose line stops loses far more than the freight bill. That benefit selects the alternative: these despatchers do not compare Chandana with a rival app but with the commission agent they have used for fifteen years, who guarantees a truck by handing the load to a sub-broker they never meet. The differentiator must therefore be something a broker structurally cannot offer. Nadgir tested four candidates on 120 despatchers.

The lowest-rate claim, important to 78 per cent, scores worst: a near-zero on uniqueness or belief destroys the product, which is why teams ranking claims by importance alone pick the weakest available.

4. When the discipline applies, and when it misleads

The conditions are testable claims. The customer has a comparison set. Chandana passes: despatchers compare it against a named broker. Kaarvaan passes: buyers evaluate it against Chakrapath Logistics Suite and the transport module they already own. The product can keep the promise. Chandana can verify owner-operators because it holds the registration and permit trail; otherwise the winning claim is a lie with a 69 per cent belief score. The segment is reachable as a segment. Auto-component despatchers can be listed and called; "shippers who value reliability" cannot.

The idea misleads in three situations. Before product-market fit, a statement freezes a guess and attracts evidence for it. Where the category does not exist in buyers' minds, the "unlike" clause has no referent. And where buying is habitual — Chandana's driver-side app competes with a truck owner's messaging group and his nephew — salience beats differentiation.

5. Hard edges: two sides, two products, one regulator, one device

A two-sided marketplace has two statements, and the binding constraint is that they be jointly deliverable. Chandana's despatcher sentence promises a verified owner-operator; its fleet-owner sentence promises return loads within four hours of unloading. Those promises compete for the same supply, because verification removes the sub-broker layer that produced the fastest return-load matches. An expert writes both on one page, then decides which side takes the harder promise.

Multi-product firms hit the seam vertically. Kaarvaan sells a transport management system, a telematics device and a freight-audit module; the temptation is one corporate sentence covering all three, which yields "the integrated logistics platform" and communicates nothing. Mature companies answer with a positioning architecture: a narrow statement per product, plus a thin corporate line whose only job is coherence for analysts and recruits. They say the corporate line drives the product lines; in practice the reverse.

Regulation and hardware constrain the sentence more than software teams expect. Kaarvaan's audit module reconciles a carrier invoice against a satellite trace and the e-way bill record under the goods and services tax regime. It is tempting to promise "compliance", but compliance is the shipper's statutory obligation, which no vendor can assume, so the benefit slot must say evidence. Because the device ships through installers, the position must survive a fitter in a Hosapete yard who has read nothing; Kaarvaan printed it on the installation checklist. For an AI-native entrant such as Chintan Dispatch AI, which prices spot loads automatically, the benefit is probabilistic, so the sentence must carry the distribution — "prices 85 per cent of loads within 4 per cent of the settled rate".

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The category slot is a budget decision, not a label

Naming a category commits the firm to the cost of being credible inside it: calling Chandana a freight operating system in 2024 obliged it to answer questions about contracted rates and integration that a load exchange never faces. The tell: an expert asks what the category obliges the roadmap to build within two quarters, and reads "nothing" as evidence it was chosen for the deck.

The "unlike" is chosen by the customer, not the team

Teams name the competitor they fear; buyers compare against what they used last. Chandana's real alternative was a commission agent, a business no slide of theirs had mentioned. The tell: an expert asks the last twenty deals, won and lost, what they would have done otherwise.

Importance is not differentiation

The lowest-rate claim mattered to 78 per cent of despatchers and scored 4.3 per cent. The obvious reading — lead with what customers care about most — ignores exclusivity and belief. The tell: an expert insists on uniqueness and believability scores beside importance.

A statement that costs nothing to say is worth nothing

The test of a position is what it gives up. "India's largest verified truck network" excluded no customer and conceded no ground, which is why it survived three years unargued. The tell: an expert asks which customers it sends elsewhere, and treats one with none as description.

Contribution, not volume, drives the target slot

Cement offers 27,900 reachable loads a month and ₹32.8 lakh of contribution; garment export offers 6,000 loads and ₹48.5 lakh. The tell: an expert demands the cost-to-serve column before agreeing to a target.

The sentence is internal; the market never reads it

A positioning statement is a decision record, not copy. Chandana's sub-broker clause appeared on no hoarding, yet it set which lanes sales pitched and what onboarding verified. The tell: when the debate turns to phrasing, the expert redirects it to what changes on Monday.

Repositioning has an asymmetric cost curve

New customers under a new sentence are cheap to win; the existing base was acquired under the old one and never consented. Chandana's change cost 4,100 of 19,400 active trucks — 21 per cent — in two quarters. The tell: an expert costs a reposition on the retention side first.

Ownership is the hidden failure mode

The statement is written by product marketing, funded by the chief executive, delivered by sales and made true by engineering. Where nobody owns the reconciliation, three sentences run at once: the board's, the website's, and the one the best salesperson improvises. The tell: read all three side by side.

7. How it differs by product type and by stage

In consumer products the target is one person and the alternative is often a habit, so the sentence argues against inertia. In business-to-business software the target splits: Kaarvaan's economic buyer is a finance chief who cares about freight cost leakage, the daily user a transport manager who cares about not being blamed. One benefit slot rarely satisfies both, and the expert answer is a statement per buying role reconciled by a shared differentiator. In enterprise deals the "unlike" clause must also satisfy a procurement committee, so it must be verifiable. Hardware positions must survive a channel that will not read them; AI positions must quote a distribution rather than a promise.

Stage changes the use more than the content. Before product-market fit the statement is a hypothesis register; through growth it is the allocation model above; at scale its function is to justify refusing work, and its risk is that each quarter's initiative widens it by one clause until it means nothing. The mechanics are identical throughout; only the evidence moves.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Kaarvaan: the same funnel, two sentences

Framing A was the sentence Kaarvaan had raised its Series B on: "For logistics-intensive enterprises, Kaarvaan is the integrated transport management system that digitises your entire freight operation, unlike legacy on-premise systems." Framing B named a narrower buyer and promise: "For manufacturers spending over ₹50 crore a year on outbound road freight, Kaarvaan is the freight-cost assurance system that matches every carrier invoice to a satellite trace and an e-way bill before it is paid, unlike a transport management system, which records what you were billed but cannot prove the trip happened."

Framing A — "integrated transport management system"48096362469.262372

Counts and new ARR are sums; average contract value in the total row is ₹1,406 lakh ÷ 17 = ₹82.7 lakh. A median of two medians is not meaningful, so it is left blank.

The narrower sentence bought fewer conversations and more business. Framing A opened 96 of the 480 accounts approached, 20 per cent; Framing B only 72 of 480, 15 per cent. But 40 of those 72 meetings qualified — 55.6 per cent, against Framing A's 36 of 96, or 37.5 per cent — and 11 of the 40 qualified opportunities closed, 27.5 per cent, against 6 of 36, or 16.7 per cent. End to end, Framing B converted 2.29 per cent of approached accounts against 1.25 per cent, at ₹94 lakh of average contract value rather than ₹62 lakh, producing ₹10.34 crore of new recurring revenue against ₹3.72 crore — 2.78 times as much from the same list. At ₹1.15 crore of cost per arm per quarter, cost per win fell from ₹19.17 lakh to ₹10.45 lakh, or from 30.9 per cent of first-year contract value to 11.1 per cent.

Kellerbach: the same product, a different alternative

Kellerbach Speditions GmbH, a mid-sized German freight forwarder with an India desk, ran a three-month pilot over 1,150 trips at an average billed freight of ₹54,000, a total of ₹6.21 crore. Reconciliation found ₹41.4 lakh of that billed freight — 6.7 per cent, or ₹3,600 per trip — unsupported by any trace of the trip having happened as invoiced. Konrad Neuwirth, the procurement head, signed quickly, but for a reason Yerramilli had not written into the sentence: Kellerbach's comparison was its own auditors, who sampled 2 per cent of invoices by hand, so what closed the deal was coverage of the whole population rather than a sample.

Chandana, 2024: a category change that cost a fifth of the supply

Chandana had run this experiment already and lost. In October 2024, after an investor observed that load boards were valued as brokers while platforms were valued as software, Angadi repositioned it as "India's freight operating system". Posted volume rose as predicted, from 96,000 loads in the quarter ended September 2024 to 1,08,000 by March 2025, up 12.5 per cent. Everything else fell: fill rate from 33 per cent to 26 per cent, matched loads from 31,680 to 28,080, down 11.4 per cent, and gross merchandise value from ₹87.12 crore to ₹78.34 crore, down 10.1 per cent, even though average freight value edged up from ₹27,500 to ₹27,900.

"Operating system" attracted enterprise shippers wanting contracted annual rates and integration; their loads were longer-haul and more specific, so the fill rate on incoming demand collapsed. Fleet owners, who had joined for short-haul return loads, found fewer and stopped opening the app: 4,100 of 19,400 active trucks went dormant within two quarters, leaving 15,300. The supply side had never been told, and it was the supply side that priced it. In April 2025 Chandana restored "spot load exchange" as its category word, keeping one artefact of the experiment: contract-rate benchmarking, sold as a paid add-on. Fill rate recovered to 31 per cent by June 2025, 34 per cent by September 2025 and 36 per cent by June 2026.

9. Failure modes, their early warnings and the cost of a late catch

Category inflation. Early sign: the category word reaches the fundraising deck before a customer's mouth. Diagnostic: name five buyers who used it unprompted. Caught late, the cost is the supply-side collapse above, 21 per cent of active trucks. A benefit the product cannot verify. Early sign: sales asks for a case study that does not exist. Diagnostic: what evidence would a sceptical procurement committee accept? Caught late, it surfaces as churn at renewal. Optimising the top of the funnel. Early sign: meetings rise while qualified opportunities do not — Framing A's pattern. Diagnostic: track meeting-to-qualified conversion by framing, not by channel. Repositioning without the base. Early sign: a new sentence ships with no cohort analysis. Diagnostic: which customers chose us for what we are about to stop saying? Caught late, the churn lands one to two quarters after a launch already declared a success.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does narrowing grow the business or cap it? The Moore-and-Dunford position holds that a sharp position is the only way a firm with finite resources gets chosen at all, and Kaarvaan's 2.78-times revenue advantage on an identical list is the evidence it rests on. The Ehrenberg-Bass position holds that such results are real but local, that category share growth comes from light and non-buyers reached at scale, and that narrow positions win tests while losing decades. For the first to be wrong, Framing B's advantage would have to decay as Kaarvaan saturates manufacturers spending over ₹50 crore on outbound freight. For the second to be wrong, Chandana's concentration — 23.7 per cent of loads carrying 71.6 per cent of contribution — would have to be typical.

Is the category chosen or assigned? Dunford's position is that the category is the most powerful lever available, since it sets the comparison set and therefore the criteria. The opposing position, which Chandana's 2024 experience supports, is that buyers assign categories from what they already understand, and a firm insisting on one they do not hold pays for the education and cannot usually afford it. For Dunford to be wrong, deliberate category changes would have to succeed rarely relative to attempts; we observe mostly survivors and nobody has the denominator.

Does the template help or hurt? Defenders argue it forces four decisions teams otherwise avoid; Dunford objects that it lets a team produce a grammatical sentence with no analysis behind it. Both are true of different teams. The compromise practitioners reach is to do the analysis in tables and write the sentence last — what Nadgir did and Chandana's 2024 effort did not.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this writes the sentence, circulates it and moves on. Someone who has internalised it starts from a cost-to-serve table and treats the sentence as its output; asks what it forbids before asking whether it is true; names the alternative in the last five lost deals from memory; knows the reposition cost to the base first; and accepts a smaller top of funnel when the arithmetic downstream is better.

12. What each of them decided

Nadgir recommended, and Angadi accepted on 25 July 2026: for auto-component and garment-export despatchers shipping time-critical intercity loads, Chandana is the spot load exchange that places a verified owner-operator on the lane within four hours, unlike a commission agent, who hands your load to a sub-broker you never meet and cannot hold to account. The network claim survived as a proof point inside the sentence, and agri acquisition spend, worth ₹0.7 lakh of monthly contribution, stopped. Shettar's condition was that fill rate for the two named segments be reported separately each quarter, so the promise could be falsified.

Yerramilli made Framing B official for new business in August 2026 but did not retire Framing A for the 57 existing customers — ₹45.14 crore of the ₹59.2 crore book, an average of ₹79.2 lakh — who had bought a transport management system and would renew against it. Kaarvaan ran two sentences, with a six-quarter sunset.

Discussion questions. (1) Chandana's target carries 71.6 per cent of contribution on 23.7 per cent of reachable loads. When does that concentration become a vulnerability rather than focus, and what would you measure to know?

(2) Framing B produced 24 fewer first meetings per 480 accounts, and in one quarter the shortfall would have shown before the revenue advantage. What governance holds the line through that interval?

(3) Chandana lost 21 per cent of its active trucks to a category change aimed at the demand side. Whose job was it to notice, and where should authority over a category word sit?

exp20v2-pmm.positioning.statement:
Go-to-Market, Growth & Monetisation · Positioning, Messaging & Product Marketing

Writing a Positioning Statement

For a customer you can name, in a category you have chosen, unlike an alternative they were about to pick instead.

1. A slide rewritten four times

In the last week of March 2026, Manpreet Sidhu, vice-president of product marketing at Manzil Credit Systems, walked into a board meeting above a car showroom on Ferozepur Road, Ludhiana, carrying a single slide she had rewritten four times overnight. Manzil, launched in September 2023, paired a mobile lending app with a partner NBFC (non-banking financial company) regulated by the Reserve Bank of India, extending credit lines of ₹15,000 to ₹3,00,000 to borrowers across Punjab's smaller towns. The app had 6,00,000 downloads; 90,000 — 15 percent — had converted into activated borrowers who had completed KYC and drawn at least one disbursal, carrying an average outstanding of ₹60,000 each, for a live loan book of ₹540 crore.

Respectable numbers, which was why Rupinder Chahal, the board member representing Manzil's Series B investor, had not yet asked the question everyone could feel coming: why had the cost of acquiring each activated borrower drifted upward for six straight months, even as weaker-underwriting entrants grew faster on smaller budgets? Co-founder Harpreet Grewal had asked Manpreet to open with an answer, not a diagnosis. Her slide had one sentence on it, and thirty minutes to defend it. If the sentence was wrong, the fix would not be a cheaper channel — it would mean Manzil had spent two and a half years telling the market the wrong thing about itself.

2. The idea

A positioning statement is a single, testable sentence stating who a product is for, what category it belongs to, what benefit it delivers, and what alternative it beats for that customer, and why. It follows a template close to: "For [target customer], who [has this need], [product] is a [category] that [benefit]. Unlike [alternative], [product] [differentiator]."

The idea that a product occupies "a position" — a specific place in a prospective customer's mind, defined relative to alternatives already sitting there — was named by advertising strategists Al Ries and Jack Trout in their 1981 book Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind. The fill-in-the-blank sentence that turns that idea into something a team can write, test and argue about was formalised a decade later by Geoffrey Moore in Crossing the Chasm (1991), for companies moving a product from enthusiastic early adopters to a larger, skeptical mainstream market with no patience for vague claims.

The statement solves a recurring problem: people who build a product understand it in far more feature-by-feature detail than any customer will, and that detail, unfiltered, produces marketing that lists everything a product does and communicates nothing about why any one person should care. The sentence Manpreet needed to say without sounding glib was this: "A positioning statement is not what we say about the product — it is the one sentence that tells us who has to want it, and who else they were about to choose instead."

3. How it actually works

Writing a positioning statement means filling five slots in a fixed order; each constrains the ones that follow. The first is the target: not "anyone who needs a loan," but a specific, describable customer. Manzil's data showed its best-performing cohort was self-employed traders and small manufacturers in towns like Jalandhar and Bathinda — not the salaried gig workers the old app-store copy had chased. The second is the need, stated as a job to be done, never a feature: these traders wanted working capital they could draw when a supplier demanded advance payment and repay when a sale cleared, repeatedly, without restarting paperwork each time.

The third slot names the category — the shelf in the customer's mind the product sits on — and this is the slot practitioners skip past too quickly. Calling Manzil a "loan app" put it beside a single-use payday product; "revolving credit line" put it beside a bank overdraft, inviting different expectations about reuse and fees. The fourth is the benefit, an outcome rather than a mechanism: "approved once, redraw for a year without reapplying," not "instant disbursal," a feature rival Mool Money already owned more convincingly. The fifth, the "unlike" clause, names the alternative the target was actually about to choose — never a generic "the competition" — since the sentence works only as a comparison against something already in the customer's head. The step teams most often skip is returning to the first slot after writing the fifth: if the differentiation matters only to a narrow subset of the named target, the target was drawn too broadly.

4. A worked example, twice

Manpreet's team ran the comparison as a controlled test, not a debate. Over a thirty-day window in February 2026, two variants of app-store copy and search-ad creative sent traffic to the same underwriting flow, with the ad budget split evenly at ₹15,00,000 per arm. Variant A kept the launch sentence: "For anyone who needs cash fast, Manzil puts money in your account in minutes." Variant B carried the sentence built from the five slots above, naming Mool Money as the alternative traders were actually switching from.

Total30,00,00045,000—6,250——

Variant B's narrower copy cost more per install (₹75 versus ₹60) but converted nearly twice as well (18.75 percent versus 10 percent), so it activated a borrower for ₹400 against Variant A's ₹600. Together the arms spent ₹30,00,000 to activate 6,250 borrowers, a blended ₹480 per activated borrower — Variant B alone was already a third cheaper than the sentence Manzil had run for two and a half years.

Manpreet then tested how sensitive that answer was to one change: narrowing the target further, from "self-employed traders and small manufacturers" to only traders holding a GST registration, a proxy for a more established business. This cut installs to 12,500, a 37.5 percent fall, but lifted activation to 24 percent since the remaining traffic fit the underwriting model more precisely, yielding 3,000 activated borrowers — 20 percent fewer than un-narrowed Variant B — at the same ₹15,00,000 spend. Cost per activated borrower rose to ₹500, up 25 percent from ₹400, despite the better conversion rate. The arithmetic forces a lesson intuition would miss: a sharper target converts a larger share of what it reaches, but if it also shrinks how much it reaches, cost per activated customer can still rise. Precision and reach are different knobs, and a sound decision watches both.

5. What a learner has to become aware of

It is not a tagline

A positioning statement is an internal working sentence; a tagline is the polished external output a copywriter derives from it. Manzil's "unlike Mool Money" clause never appeared on a billboard, but it disciplined every piece of copy that did.

The category is a promise about the comparison set

Choosing a category is not describing a feature; it is choosing which shelf of expectations the customer judges the product against. Calling Manzil a credit line rather than a loan silently promised reuse — a promise underwriting then had to deliver, not just marketing.

The "unlike" clause needs a real, current alternative

The alternative named must be one the target is actually choosing today, not a straw man invented to flatter the product. If traders were mostly switching from a moneylender, not Mool Money, the statement would be arguing against the wrong opponent.

It is a hypothesis, not a finding

It reads like a conclusion but should be treated as a claim to be tested, exactly as Manpreet tested Variant A against Variant B with real spend and real outcomes rather than settling it by seniority in a room.

It cannot fix a product that does not deliver

Wordsmithing cannot manufacture a benefit the product lacks. Had servicing actually required a fresh bureau pull on every redraw, no statement claiming "no reapplication" would have survived the first repeat borrower's experience.

Confused with mission, and premature before real data

A mission statement is aspirational for years; positioning is tactical, rewritten as competitors shift. And before a company has enough data to know its best customers, writing one freezes a guess into false certainty — Manzil could only name its target credibly after two and a half years of repayment data.

6. Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and stage

In a consumer product like Manzil, the "who" is a single named end-user, and "unlike" names another consumer product or an informal behaviour, such as borrowing from a moneylender. In B2B, the target often splits into an economic buyer and a day-to-day user, the benefit is expressed in return on investment or compliance rather than convenience, and "unlike" often names a manual process, since the true incumbent is the customer's own status quo. In a marketplace, positioning must be written twice: Manzil's NBFC partners needed a statement about portfolio quality, borrowers one about reuse and speed, and the two had to stay compatible.

Stage changes how the statement is used more than what it contains. At Manzil's stage it was a hypothesis tested cheaply on a slice of one month's budget, and Manpreet could afford to be wrong for thirty days. In a large lender, the same change touches trained call-centre scripts and existing customers who chose the product under the old promise, so it is piloted in one city for a quarter first.

7. Common mistakes

Listing features instead of naming one benefit

Symptom: the "statement" runs four sentences and mentions five capabilities. Misunderstanding: treating positioning as a condensed spec sheet, not a single promise. Cheapest diagnostic: ask a satisfied customer to repeat it from memory in one breath; if they cannot, it carries too many features to be a position.

Refusing to name a real alternative

Symptom: "unlike" says "anything else out there" or "traditional methods." Misunderstanding: naming a rival feels like it makes the product look small, when refusing actually leaves the sentence with nothing to be true against. Cheapest diagnostic: ask ten recent customers what they would have used instead; a converging answer is the alternative that belongs in the sentence.

Optimising acquisition against the wrong target

Symptom: installs and clicks look healthy while activation quietly worsens, as happened to Manzil under Variant A. Misunderstanding: measuring cost per install rather than cost per activated customer, which lets a broad sentence look cheap while underwriting rejects most of what it attracted. Cheapest diagnostic: segment cost and activation by creative variant, not only by channel.

8. What good looks like

Consider Sukhwinder Dhillon, who runs an auto-parts shop in Ludhiana's Field Ganj market and became exactly the customer Variant B was written for. He did not need cash "fast" in the abstract; he needed to draw ₹70,000 to pay a supplier ahead of a festival order, and to draw again six weeks later without a branch visit or fresh paperwork. When the app-store listing, the support scripts and the loan officers' talk tracks all carried the same sentence — a revolving credit line, unlike a single-use cash app that made him reapply every time — his experience matched what had been promised, and he returned for a second draw unasked. Good positioning is recognisable less by clever wording than by this quiet coherence across the ad, the app and the person servicing his account.

9. What Manpreet decided

Manpreet recommended the board adopt Variant B as Manzil's standing statement across every channel, rather than the further-narrowed, GST-only version. The narrower version converted better and kept borrowers returning for a second draw at nearly two and a half times Variant A's rate — but it cut addressable installs by more than a third, and a company still building its loan book could not trade that much reach for a 25 percent rise in cost per activated borrower. Her compromise: run the GST-narrowed sentence only on the highest-intent paid search terms, while broader Variant B carried the app-store listing, organic search and the loan officers' scripts. Harpreet Grewal approved it that morning; Rupinder Chahal's question about rising acquisition cost had, in effect, already been answered.

The natural next topic is the messaging hierarchy: translating one statement into different messages for app-store copy, a collections script and a loan officer's talk track without any drifting from the sentence underneath. Category design, and the harder problem of changing a position without losing customers who chose the product under the old promise, both build on the same five slots. Two questions worth sitting with: how would you find out who customers actually compare you to today, rather than who you assume; and when a narrower position converts better but reaches fewer people, whose call is that trade-off?

Launch Communications and PR

What is the story of this launch, and who tells it?

1. A Wednesday in late September

On the last Wednesday of September 2026, Poorvi Sancheti, Head of Product Marketing at Prerna Wearables, sat with a sixteen-page embargo plan she was not yet willing to sign off. In eighteen days, on 14 October, Prerna would put the Prana Band 3 — its third-generation fitness band, the first with continuous blood-oxygen and stress tracking — in front of the press. The board's target was blunt: 40,000 pre-orders in the first ten days, twenty-nine per cent above the 31,000 units the Prana Band 2 had sold in its own first ten days two years earlier. Behind that number sat a ₹85 lakh communications budget, eighteen technology reviewers promised review units a week before launch, forty creators already briefed on posting windows, and a rival, Fire-Boltt, rumoured to be readying its own launch the same week.

What worried Sancheti was the plan's silence on what story the eighteen reviewers were actually meant to tell. The briefing deck ran to forty slides of specifications — sensor accuracy, battery hours, water resistance — and not one sentence answering the question a features list cannot answer on its own: why does this matter now, to this person, more than it did yesterday. Press coverage would happen regardless of what she did; the only question left open was whether it carried Prerna's account of the launch or one assembled by a reviewer with forty minutes and a deadline.

2. The idea

Launch communications and PR is the deliberate, sequenced work of getting independent voices — journalists, industry analysts, creators, and a company's own existing customers — to tell a consistent, favourable, and true account of a product launch before, or instead of, the company simply telling people itself. It is distinct from advertising, which is paid and controlled outright, and it is distinct from the launch itself, which is the operational act of making a product available. PR supplies something advertising structurally cannot: borrowed credibility. A reviewer's sentence carries weight a company's own press release does not, precisely because the reviewer is presumed to have no obligation to say it.

The modern choreography of embargoes, exclusive briefings, and staged reveals took shape in Silicon Valley's technology press of the 1980s and 1990s, an era in which marketing strategist Regis McKenna — working with Apple and Intel — helped popularise the idea that positioning a product's story mattered as much as the product itself, and in which a growing trade press became powerful enough to make or break a launch weekend on its own. The single sentence Sancheti could repeat without sounding glib: launch communications is choosing, in advance, which independent voices tell the story, in what order.

PR routes a message through an independent voice the audience already trusts; advertising delivers the same message directly, with full control but none of that borrowed credibility.

3. How it actually works

Sancheti's team worked through six steps, in order, and the order mattered more than any single step. First came the narrative spine: not a features list but a single tension — why has continuous stress tracking on a ₹3,600 band not been possible until now, and what changed. Everything downstream had to serve that one sentence. Second, the team split the story by audience: the trade reviewer wants sensor engineering explained in falsifiable detail; the general reporter wants the market-size angle (India's wearable category, worth an estimated ₹9,000 crore in 2026); the creator wants something demonstrable on camera in under ninety seconds; the existing Prana Band 2 owner wants a plain answer to "should I upgrade."

Third came the asset kit — press release, technical briefing deck, eighteen review units couriered under signed non-disclosure agreements, a FAQ, and, easy to skip, an executive spokesperson trained on the one question everyone hoped no reporter would ask (here: why battery life had fallen from six days to four). Fourth was sequencing against an embargo — an agreed date and time before which no outlet may publish, so coverage lands in one window rather than trickling out unevenly. Fifth was briefing spokespeople on exactly three message pillars, deliberately no more, because a fourth is the one a nervous spokesperson forgets under stage lights and improvises around. Sixth, and the step most plans leave implicit, was staffing the first forty-eight hours after embargo lift for rapid response, since a single early negative review can set the narrative before a company has said a word.

The narrative spine is fixed before Day −14; everything else is sequencing.

4. A worked example

Sancheti's media plan reduced to a funnel she could defend line by line. Eighteen embargo reviews, averaging 2.5 lakh readers each, gave a gross press reach of 45,00,000. Forty seeded creators, averaging 1.5 lakh followers each, gave 60,00,000. Prerna's own channels — email, app push, and site traffic — added 8,00,000 more. Each channel converts differently: press clicks through at 1.2 per cent because a review sits inside a long article; creator audiences click at only 0.5 per cent, entertainment first; owned channels convert at 4 per cent because the audience already opted in. Of those who click, press converts to a pre-order at 22 per cent (pre-sold by the review), creators at 18 per cent, and owned traffic at 30 per cent — the highest-intent audience of the three.

ChannelReachCTRClicksConversionPre-orders
Press (18 embargo reviews)45,00,0001.2%54,00022%11,880
Creators (40 seeded)60,00,0000.5%30,00018%5,400
Owned (email, app, site)8,00,0004.0%32,00030%9,600

Reach and clicks sum down the column; CTR and conversion are blended rates, not sums, and are computed from the totals (1,16,000 ÷ 1,13,00,000 = 1.03%; 26,880 ÷ 1,16,000 = 23.2%).

Twenty-six thousand eight hundred and eighty pre-orders, against a target of 40,000, left Prerna at 67 per cent of goal — roughly ₹9.68 crore of the ₹14.4 crore the board had modelled, at ₹3,600 per unit. At a spend of ₹85 lakh, that is roughly ₹316 per pre-order. Sancheti's second pass asked a sharper question: which input, moved alone, closes the gap fastest? More reviewers barely helped, since press reach was already large relative to its conversion rate. But lifting press click-through from 1.2 to 2.0 per cent — sharper headlines and one clear call to action, not more coverage — raised press clicks to 90,000, press pre-orders to 19,800, and the campaign total to 34,800, or 87 per cent of target: a better sentence in eighteen reviews mattered more than twenty-two additional reviews would have.

5. The nuances a learner must hold onto

Earned, owned, and paid are not interchangeable

PR is earned media: an independent party chooses to cover the story, unpaid, and can choose not to. The moment money changes hands for a placement — a paid creator post, a sponsored article — it becomes paid media wearing earned media's clothes, and the Advertising Standards Council of India requires it to be disclosed as such. Conflating the two misleads a team about how much of its "coverage" is actually trusted.

Embargo is not the same instrument as exclusivity

An embargo gives many outlets the same material at once, bound by a shared publish time; an exclusive gives one outlet the story first, with no simultaneous release to anyone else. The two trade against each other — an embargo buys breadth of coverage in one window, an exclusive buys depth and goodwill with a single masthead at the cost of everyone else's cooperation next time.

Reach is not resonance

A gross reach of 1,13,00,000 sounds decisive, but it says nothing about whether any of those readers believed, remembered, or acted on what they read. The funnel above exists precisely because reach is the easiest number to inflate and the least informative one on its own; conversion, not reach, is what a comms budget should ultimately be judged against.

What PR cannot tell you

Even a clean funnel cannot isolate PR's own causal share of a sales lift when a paid campaign, a price cut, and a competitor's stumble land in the same fortnight. The 26,880 pre-orders attributed above are a plausible allocation, not a controlled experiment; treating the split as certain fact mistakes a model for a measurement.

A story is not a feature list

The mechanism that makes a launch story travel is narrative tension — why was this impossible until now, what changed — not an enumeration of specifications. Forty slides of sensor accuracy answer questions nobody outside the company is asking; the tension is what a reviewer actually quotes.

An announcement is not a launch

Announcing a product and making it purchasable are different events a comms plan can accidentally collapse into one. When coverage runs ahead of availability, the resulting traffic finds nothing to convert, and the credibility cost of "coming soon" falls on the company, not the reviewer.

6. Consumer, B2B, and marketplace — and early versus large

Prerna's approach — mass press, creators, and an embargo choreographed around one on-sale date — is a distinctly consumer pattern. A B2B launch replaces the reviewer with an industry analyst whose opinion moves a buying committee more than any journalist's does, and replaces the creator with a customer reference willing to be quoted by name; a single analyst briefing three weeks before announcement often matters more than the press release. A marketplace launch must tell two stories to two audiences at once — sellers need reassurance about demand and payout terms, buyers need reassurance about selection and trust — and the two must never visibly contradict each other in the same news cycle.

Stage matters as much as category. An early-stage company's PR is usually founder-led and built on personal relationships with two or three reporters who cover the category early; there is no retained agency, only a founder's own credibility. A company at Prerna's scale runs a heavier process — legal review of every claim, a retained agency such as Prachar Communications managing forty creator relationships at once — in exchange for access to premium mastheads a founder alone could rarely reach.

7. Common mistakes

SymptomUnderlying misunderstandingCheap diagnostic
Release lists six co-equal announcements; no clear headlineTreating the release as an internal completeness checklistAsk what one sentence a busy editor would use as the headline
Spokesperson answers in acronyms under pressureAssuming internal vocabulary is public vocabularyRun a mock Q&A with someone outside the category
One outlet publishes early; others refuse the next embargoUnderestimating how reputation-sensitive embargo relationships areCheck whether the same three or four outlets keep getting burned
Coverage runs, but the buy flow is down or out of stockTreating comms and commerce readiness as separate workstreamsRun the buy flow end to end 24 hours before embargo lift

Each of these is cheap to catch and expensive to leave uncaught. Sancheti's own near-miss was the first: the forty-slide deck she rejected on that September Wednesday would have handed eighteen reviewers a features list and let each one invent their own headline — some of them, inevitably, less flattering than the one Prerna would have chosen for itself.

8. What good looks like

Two Prana generations later, the team that had learned from Band 3 ran the Band 5 launch differently. The narrative spine — one sentence about why continuous tracking finally worked at this price — was fixed before a briefing deck existed. Reviewers received identical material and published within one six-hour window, because embargo lift time had been checked against warehouse readiness three times, not once. The spokesperson carried three pillars into every interview and, asked the one hard question about a supply constraint, answered it directly instead of deflecting into jargon. Nothing was exotic; the difference was that every step the first launch had left implicit — spine, ops sync, rehearsed hard question — was now written down.

9. What Sancheti decided

Sancheti did not ask the board for a larger budget. Her sensitivity analysis had shown that a sharper headline and call to action across eighteen existing reviews closed more of the gap to 40,000 than twenty additional reviewers would have. She redirected two lakh rupees from the creator line toward message testing with the press contacts, tightened the briefing deck from forty slides to one narrative spine and eight supporting slides, and moved the embargo-lift rehearsal with operations from one check to three. What she took from the exercise was a standing instinct, not a fixed number: before adding reach, ask whether the story earns the reach it already has. The next topics worth studying are the messaging hierarchy PR is meant to carry, and the discipline of launch planning that keeps commerce and communications on the same clock. Two questions worth sitting with: if reach without resonance does not move a buyer, what should a communications budget be judged against? And how would you brief a spokesperson to survive the one question everyone hopes nobody asks?

Rasayan Chemist Cloud: The CareLoop 2.0 Launch

Launch communications and PR — what is the story of this launch, and who tells it?

1. Monday, 21 September 2026 — Madurai

Vidya Ramanathan, VP of Marketing and Communications at Rasayan Chemist Cloud, closed her laptop after a ninth read of three draft press notes and admitted none felt right. In four days, on Friday afternoon, she was due on a board call to recommend one way to announce CareLoop 2.0 — Rasayan's first product built for patients, not pharmacists — before the Navratri-to-Diwali fortnight, when chemist footfall, and loyalty enrolment with it, would peak. Get the story right, and Rasayan could turn a hard month in the pharmacy-tech press into an opening against chains many times its size. Get it wrong, with a rival's data leak still in the papers, and it risked scrutiny a nine-person marketing team could least afford.

2. Company background

Rasayan Chemist Cloud was founded in Madurai in 2019 by Venkatesh Pillai, a chartered accountant who had managed finance for a fifty-store pharmacy chain and tired of loyalty ledgers kept in exercise books. It sells a subscription platform to regional pharmacy chains too small to build their own technology and too large to run on paper — typically twenty to a hundred and fifty stores across Tamil Nadu and Kerala. Its product runs one loyalty programme across a chain's outlets, sends refill reminders by SMS and WhatsApp, and, since 2024, holds an e-prescription vault: a prescription scanned once at a partner counter, checked against Schedule H rules, and reusable at any other partner store. Rasayan does not sell to patients directly like Tata 1mg, PharmEasy or Netmeds, nor compete with the in-house systems Apollo Pharmacy or MedPlus built themselves; it sits underneath the family-run, mid-sized chains that make up most retail pharmacy counts in the two states. By August 2026 the platform was live in 1,240 stores, with 9,50,000 loyalty members and 3,10,000 e-prescriptions processed monthly (Exhibit 1). A blended fee of roughly ₹15,000 per store a month, plus a small per-prescription charge, brought monthly revenue of ₹210.8 lakh — an annualised run-rate near ₹25.3 crore — funded so far by one institutional round and the founders' own capital, well short of a venture-backed e-pharmacy app's budget.

3. The situation

CareLoop 2.0, code-complete since July, layered two consumer-visible features onto a product that had always lived behind the counter: a loyalty wallet a patient could check on her own phone, and a Health ID-linked prescription vault built on the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission's sandbox, so a prescription written in Madurai could be refilled at a partner chemist in Kochi. It was the first Rasayan feature a patient, not a pharmacist, would open — the first time Rasayan's own name, not the shop's, would appear in someone's hand. That made how the launch was told, and to whom first, genuinely different from anything Vidya had handled.

The question had sharpened three weeks earlier. On 14 August, a national e-pharmacy app — never publicly named beyond a regulator's notice — disclosed that prescription records for more than two lakh customers had been exposed through a misconfigured server, drawing press coverage and a reminder that the DPDP Act, 2023's consent obligations applied in full to health data. Pharmacy owners on Rasayan's advisory calls began asking, unprompted, how CareLoop stored consent records. Venkatesh wanted the incident treated as an opening: a smaller, cleaner platform could look more trustworthy than the giants, provided the launch said so soon, ahead of an investor talk in October. Vishnu Subramaniam, running data and trust from Chennai, wanted the opposite. His review, closed 10 September, found only 61 per cent of active e-prescription users had completed the newer, ABDM-aligned consent flow; he wanted no consumer journalist near CareLoop until that number was much higher, fearing a reporter finding the gap that had sunk a competitor. Winston and Vimala read the same three weeks differently again, and by Monday, Vidya had three drafts and four colleagues each convinced theirs was the only responsible reading.

4. The people

Venkatesh Pillai — Co-founder and CEO, Madurai

Wants a story loud enough to turn August's headlines into an advantage before a MedPlus-sized chain copies the feature, and a story for his October investor meeting.

Vimala Krishnan — Head of Pharmacy Partnerships, Coimbatore

Manages renewals with chain owners whose shop names sit above the counter, not Rasayan's; fears a branded campaign sidelines them and costs her November's renewals.

Winston Varghese — Regional Operations Lead, Kerala, Kochi

Kerala holds only 430 of 1,240 stores; needs momentum for his year-end target and wants a launch timed to the tail of the Onam season.

Vishnu Subramaniam — Head of Data and Trust, Chennai

Owns DPDP and ABDM consent compliance; his review found only 61 per cent consent-flow completion, and wants no consumer press until that is much higher.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 shows how uneven Rasayan's footprint is between its two states, a fact the comms plan must answer for before choosing one national moment over several regional ones.

Exhibit 2 lays out the three costed options, each implying a different answer to Vishnu's 61 per cent problem.

Exhibit 3. All dates 2026. The Navratri–Diwali window, though after the deadline, is why it exists: chemist footfall and enrolment rise sharply through the fortnight.

6. The options

Option A: Wait and go quiet first

Announce to trade press only — pharmacy-association bulletins, B2B publications — at ₹6.0 lakh, holding consumer press until Vishnu's number clears an agreed threshold. Cheapest, and Vishnu's own choice, since it removes the risk of a journalist finding the same gap. Its cost is opportunity: at 8,000 projected sign-ups it does little for Winston's Kerala target or Venkatesh's October story.

Option B: Launch big, now

Hold a flagship press and influencer event in Chennai, at ₹42.0 lakh, aimed at trade coverage plus health and pharmacy influencers, projected to reach 18,00,000 impressions and 54,000 sign-ups. This gives Venkatesh his clearest investor narrative and the fastest volume. Its cost is exposure at the worst moment: it puts CareLoop before the same press still asking data-leak questions, while 39 per cent of users have not completed the newer consent flow.

Option C: Sequence the story by state

Launch through regional trade press and micro-influencer partnerships in Tamil Nadu, the larger, established base, at ₹16.0 lakh, projected at 6,50,000 impressions and 22,000 sign-ups; hold Kerala's louder push for a few weeks later, once the consent number has moved. It costs more than A and reaches fewer than B, but keeps chain owners' shop names prominent for Vimala, gives Venkatesh a quieter but credible October story, and buys Vishnu the weeks he needs, opening before the festive window closes.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What does the still-live data-leak story change about the risk of a large launch, for a company Rasayan's size versus a larger platform?
  2. Does Exhibit 1's gap between Tamil Nadu's 810 stores and Kerala's 430 argue for one national launch, or state by state?
  3. In Exhibit 2, Option B costs most yet its cost per sign-up is similar to the others. What does that figure leave out when reach and risk differ this much?
  4. Whose interest — Venkatesh's, Vimala's, Winston's, or Vishnu's — should set the sequence, and what evidence would you cite to defend it to the other three?

8. A note for the learner

Launch communications and PR asks a narrower question than "should we launch": given a plan and messaging hierarchy that already exist, what is the story, and who is told first? The plan does not invent positioning; it sequences the telling of it, and that sequence carries its own costs, as Exhibits 2 and 3 make concrete.

A well-reasoned answer uses both exhibits together. Exhibit 1 shows Rasayan is really two markets at different stages; Exhibit 2 shows Option A has the lowest total spend, Option B the largest reach, and Option C the lowest cost per sign-up (₹72.7, against Option A's ₹75.0) — three options winning on three different metrics, so no single figure should decide. Exhibit 3 supplies the binding constraint — a still-fresh competitor failure and a 61 per cent consent number — raising the cost of being loud before Vishnu's work is done.

One defensible path is Option C. A Tamil Nadu-first trade launch lets Rasayan say something true and checkable — scale, chain-owner endorsement, careful handling of health data — while Vishnu closes the consent gap, then holds Kerala's louder moment for the weeks before Navratri, once that number no longer invites comparison to August's headline. It costs six times Option A yet still gives Venkatesh an investor story by October, and less than half of Option B while removing its biggest risk: a journalist finding an unfinished consent flow during a launch built to draw journalists. What makes it defensible is not that it is safest or cheapest, but that its sequence matches the facts — trust addressed before growth.

Rasayan Chemist Cloud is a fictional company created for teaching purposes. All figures are illustrative.

Baithak Space Systems: The India Office Utilisation Index

A launch story that got better as a headline and worse as a relationship.

1. Sunday night, 4 October 2026 — Bhubaneswar

Chitrangada Mohapatra had the number on a sheet of paper in front of her, and it had not improved in six hours of looking at it. Forty-eight point five per cent. On the fullest day of an average week, fewer than half the desks Baithak Space Systems could actually see held a human being. Six weeks earlier the same pipeline had said sixty-three per cent, and she had built a launch around that figure — a benchmark called the India Office Utilisation Index, an exclusive with a national business daily, an analyst programme, a chart she could picture being screenshotted into every leasing deck in Gurugram.

At eleven the next morning she was due to give Baithak's board a recommendation. The Index was still the best earned-media asset the company had ever had; it was simply now telling a different story, and one that several of the clients who supplied its data would rather nobody told at all. Her team of eleven had ₹82 lakh of uncommitted budget for the year and four costed options. What she did not have was a defensible answer to the question Indrajit Behera would ask first: whose story is this, and who gets to tell it?

2. Company history

Baithak Space Systems was founded in Bhubaneswar in 2018 by Indrajit Behera, who had spent nine years in facilities management for an IT services campus, watching three thousand people badge into a building whose landlord could not say at quarter-end how many of its floors had been used. Baithak's first product was unglamorous: a booking layer that sat on whatever access-control hardware an operator already owned, reconciled it against the billing ledger, and produced a monthly occupancy report a landlord could read. It sold to operators too large for spreadsheets and too small to build software, and later to their landlords.

One decision from 2022 still shapes everything. To win scale quickly, Baithak signed a three-year white-label agreement with Nirvaan Workspaces, then a fast-growing operator in seven cities. Nirvaan got the platform under its own branding at roughly half list price; Baithak got volume and a sensor deployment it could never have funded alone. Clause 11.4 forbids Baithak from publishing, in any form, analysis derived from Nirvaan's centres without prior written consent. The deal renews or lapses in January 2027.

The consequence is double-edged. Nirvaan supplies 44,000 of the 1,15,900 instrumented desks in Baithak's base — 38.0 per cent of the Index's raw signal — while Baithak's name appears nowhere a Nirvaan member can see it. An agency survey in July 2026 put the problem plainly: of 180 occupier and facilities decision-makers polled across six cities, just 11 named Baithak unaided, or 6.1 per cent. The Index was conceived partly as the cure for that invisibility.

3. The industry

India's flexible-workspace market has spent three years turning from a start-up curiosity into a listed asset class. Awfis Space Solutions listed on the NSE and BSE in 2024; Smartworks and WeWork India followed, and the quarterly absorption notes from CBRE, JLL, Knight Frank and Colliers are read as macro indicators rather than trade gossip. SEBI-regulated REITs — Embassy Office Parks, Mindspace Business Parks, Brookfield India — hold Grade-A portfolios in which flexible operators are among the fastest-growing tenants, and global capability centres have absorbed floorplates in Bengaluru and Hyderabad at a pace that keeps headline vacancy low even where daily usage is thin.

That gap — between leased and used — is Baithak's commercial argument and its political problem. An operator's valuation rests on seats sold; Baithak measures seats sat in. The two have never been close, and until now the difference stayed inside a client's monthly PDF.

Two regulatory facts bear on the launch. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs the badge, Wi-Fi and camera-derived data from which utilisation is computed; Baithak's position is that the Index uses aggregated, de-identified counts, but clients' consent notices to their members vary widely in coverage. And for a listed REIT, a third party publishing a utilisation series on its buildings raises an awkward question about disclosure of information that could move a unit price. Neither has a settled answer in Indian practice, which is what makes both dangerous in a press cycle.

Baithak is no longer purely Indian. Ipsita Rath runs customer success from Singapore across four Southeast Asian accounts, and Marhaba Estates Group of Dubai, a family-owned landlord with eleven towers, is the largest overseas contract at ₹2.40 crore a year, or 5.6 per cent of group revenue. Its chairman wants his buildings in no published benchmark.

4. The situation in detail

The Index began in February 2026 as an internal artefact. Chandrima Goswami, chief product officer in Kolkata, wanted a cross-client benchmark so an operator's monthly report could say "your Thursday utilisation is nine points below comparable centres" rather than report a number in a vacuum. Renewals improved wherever the benchmark line appeared.

In May, Indrajit asked the next question: if this keeps a client, can it make Baithak famous? Chitrangada's answer, in a memo dated 2 June, was yes, with conditions — a defensible sample, permissive contracts, and a story clients would want to be part of. On that memo an agency was retained, a production budget approved, and conversations opened with a national business daily about a first-look exclusive.

On 12 August the board saw the first cut: peak-day utilisation of 63.0 per cent, average weekday utilisation of 51.0 per cent. Indian flexible offices were fuller than the work-from-home commentary suggested, and Baithak had the receipts.

What has since turned out to be wrong is the number itself. Charulata Das, who leads data science from Toronto, had been rebuilding the ingestion pipeline for unrelated reasons and reported on 22 September. Three defects had inflated the series. Members badging at both a turnstile and a floor door were counted twice. Hot-desk bookings counted as occupancy whether or not anyone checked in — in her sample, roughly a third never did. And a timezone offset had folded Singapore centres into the Indian weekday buckets. Corrected, peak-day utilisation fell to 48.5 per cent and Friday to 27.4 per cent (Exhibit 2).

Two more beliefs collapsed in the same fortnight. On 26 September the daily's editor asked for the methodology note and sample composition before committing — a reasonable request that would surface Exhibit 3. And on 29 September Nirvaan's chief marketing officer wrote to Ishani Pradhan, warmly, to say how much Nirvaan valued the partnership, and to remind Baithak of clause 11.4.

5. The people

Chitrangada Mohapatra — VP, Marketing and Communications, Bhubaneswar

Owns the recommendation. Argues that a benchmark nobody trusts is worse than none, and that the corrected number is the better story.

Not saying: she wrote the 2 June memo whose conditions have not been met, and a quiet launch reads internally as her failure.

Indrajit Behera — Co-founder and CEO, Bhubaneswar

Wants the loud launch. Believes invisibility is the binding constraint on enterprise deals, and that a Series C conversation in early 2027 needs a category-defining asset.

Not saying: he has already described the Index to two investors, using 63.0 per cent.

Chandrima Goswami — Chief Product Officer, Kolkata

Built the benchmark for retention, not publicity. Would ship the analytics module on its merits and leave the Index client-only for two more quarters.

Not saying: her roadmap slipped twice this year, and a product-only launch puts her team, not marketing, on October's critical path.

Ishani Pradhan — Head of Enterprise Sales, Gurugram

Opposes publication in any form that identifies segments. Carries the Nirvaan renewal and four of the fourteen enterprise accounts into January.

Not saying: her variable pay is weighted to renewals, and the Index helps the half of her pipeline she is not measured on.

Chiranjib Nayak — VP, Engineering, Hyderabad

Neutral on the launch, firm on sequencing: the corrected pipeline needs four more weeks of parallel running before he will certify any published series.

Not saying: he flagged the turnstile double-count in a March ticket, triaged low and closed.

Ipsita Rath — Head of Customer Success, Singapore

Reports that Southeast Asian clients ask for the module constantly and for the benchmark never. Wants the launch built around the product, the Index as evidence.

Not saying: Marhaba's chairman told her publication would end the relationship, and she has put that in no written record.

Notes that against ₹43.24 crore of annualised group revenue no option on the table is material to the P&L, but losing Nirvaan and Marhaba together would be.

7. Voices

"We are not publishing a number, we are publishing a category. Nobody remembers the second-best index."

Indrajit Behera, leadership call, 24 September

"I can defend 48.5. I cannot defend calling it India. Put the sample table in the release or take my name off the methodology note."

Charulata Das, email to Chitrangada and Chandrima, 23 September

"Ishani — small point. Our members were told their badge data supports building operations. A newspaper chart is not building operations. Clause 11.4, for reference."

Nirvaan Workspaces, CMO, to Ishani Pradhan, 29 September

"Four clients this quarter have asked when they can buy the analytics module. Zero have asked for a benchmark of the Indian market. I keep raising it and keep being told it is a marketing question."

Ipsita Rath, customer-success review, 25 September

"If the series is wrong twice it is not a series, it is a press release with axes. Four weeks of parallel running."

Chiranjib Nayak, engineering standup, 23 September

"Everyone is arguing about whether to publish. Has anyone asked whether a facilities head in Hyderabad reads the business pages before shortlisting a vendor?"

Indranil Chatterjee, chat thread, 30 September

8. The options as Chitrangada sees them

Option A — Keep the Index inside the client base

Publish the corrected series to clients only and brief three trade outlets without figures, at ₹9.5 lakh. It honours every contract and leaves ₹72.5 lakh unspent. It also concedes the category to a consultancy that will publish something similar within two quarters, and gives Indrajit nothing with which to correct his investors.

Option B — Publish the Index in full

Give the daily its exclusive and run the analyst programme, spending ₹64.0 lakh of the ₹82 lakh remaining. Largest reach by a wide margin, and the corrected number is newsworthy. It also requires excluding Nirvaan's 44,000 desks — which would move the published figure by an amount nobody has computed — or securing a consent Ishani believes will not come thirteen weeks before a renewal.

Option C — Co-brand with a property consultancy

Let an established research house own the methodology and the masthead; Baithak supplies data and takes a credit line, at ₹38.0 lakh. It borrows the credibility Exhibit 3 cannot supply and gives clients a neutral counterparty. It also hands away the asset and may leave Baithak in eight-point type beneath another logo — the 2022 problem, repeated.

Option D — Launch the product, hold the Index

Announce the module with customer proof points and no market-wide claim, at ₹22.0 lakh. It is what Ipsita's clients ask for and what Chandrima can support, and it keeps January open. It also makes four months' spend look like nothing, and Chitrangada cannot say what story it tells beyond "we shipped a feature".

All four share an untested assumption: that the launch's audience is the press. Exhibit 4 measures reach and leads; nobody has asked what a facilities director on a Hyderabad campus reads before shortlisting a vendor, and Indranil's question has gone unanswered for five days. It is also possible that the real asset was never the Index but the fact that Baithak can compute it — and that the messaging hierarchy she wrote in June, which puts market authority first and product capability third, is in the wrong order.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board call is at eleven on Monday 5 October. Durga Puja closes the Kolkata and Bhubaneswar offices for most of the third week of October, and the agency says any launch not committed by 9 October slips past Diwali into November — the quarter-end window, when the consultancies publish and the business press has no appetite for a fifth utilisation chart.

Money binds least: ₹82 lakh of a ₹2.10 crore annual marketing budget remains uncommitted, against ₹58 crore of cash and a burn of ₹1.9 crore a month — a little over thirty months of runway. People bind harder: eleven in marketing, two already on the module launch. Contracts bind hardest — clause 11.4, the 140 operator agreements silent or restrictive on publication, and Exhibit 5's unaudited consent coverage, which counsel flags as the material gap.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What is the story of this launch? State it in one sentence, and say who it addresses.
  2. Exhibit 2 shows a headline improving as a story while worsening as a relationship. Which effect should weigh more in a launch-communications decision?
  3. Exhibit 4's cost per lead clusters between ₹23,750 and ₹29,091 while reach varies enormously. What is that column hiding, and what would replace it?
  4. Exhibits 3 and 5 describe the same base and point in opposite directions. If you had to publish anyway, what would you disclose, and in what order?
  5. The 2022 white-label deal bought scale at the cost of voice. Is the Index the right instrument for recovering it, or is Baithak solving a 2022 problem with a 2026 launch?
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Chitrangada do, what does she say to the board, and what does she say to Nirvaan, Marhaba and the daily — and in which order?

11. Sunday night, continued

Around midnight Chitrangada reopened the June memo and read her three conditions: a defensible sample, permissive contracts, a story clients would want to be part of. On the evidence in front of her, none held. That should have settled it. What kept her at the table was the thought that all three would still fail in January, and in April, and that waiting for a clean version of this decision was itself a decision — one she would have to defend to a board that had last seen a very different number.

She drafted an opening line for the deck, deleted it, and drafted it again. Outside, the last Puja pandal frames were going up along the road to the office. The call was in eleven hours.
