Launch Communications and PR

What is the story of this launch, who tells it, in what order — and what does the sequence cost when it is wrong?

1. Two rooms, eleven days apart

On the morning of 31 October 2026, Ishani Kalbag, who runs product marketing at Ishaara Observability Cloud in Bengaluru, carried a single slide into a room holding her chief executive, her general counsel and a machine-learning lead who had not slept much. Ishaara sells incident telemetry to large engineering organisations: ₹186 crore of annual recurring revenue, 340 enterprise customers, fifty-four per cent of revenue from India, twenty-seven per cent from the Gulf and Southeast Asia, nineteen per cent from Europe. On 11 November it would announce Signal Graph, a layer that reads a running system's telemetry and proposes a root cause an on-call engineer can act on. The board wanted ₹42 crore of new pipeline attributable to the launch within the quarter.

The slide held eleven numbers: the change in median time-to-resolution for each closed-beta customer. The median improvement was forty-one per cent — seventy-eight minutes to forty-six. Three of the eleven improved by more than half; two got worse. Marketing wanted the forty-one per cent in the headline; the general counsel wanted it in a footnote. Kalbag's view was that the number was not the problem, the sequence was. Ishaara had briefed no analyst, and in enterprise software an analyst who first hears a claim from a customer rather than the vendor writes about the vendor's process, not the product.

Eleven days later, on 11 November, Ketaki Khandekar sat in Kiraaya Machinery Exchange's Pune office with a different arithmetic. Kiraaya is a two-sided rental marketplace for construction and farm machinery — backhoes, compactors, tractors, mostly small owners' second-hand fleets — with ₹410 crore of annualised gross transaction value and an 8.5 per cent take rate, or ₹34.85 crore of net revenue. On 3 December it would launch Kiraaya Assured in eleven cities: inspected machines, insurance-backed substitution, a published deposit schedule, against a target of ₹96 crore of incremental transaction value across two quarters.

Khandekar had run this launch before, badly. In July a three-city pilot spent ₹28 lakh on demand communications and generated 512 rental requests against an inspected fleet averaging seventy-eight machines. Only 188 of the 512 were fulfilled — 36.7 per cent — because a fourteen-day rental at sixty per cent utilisation lets seventy-eight machines serve about 187 rentals in eight weeks, and no press release changes that. Cost per fulfilled rental: ₹14,894. The story had been true, well told, and six weeks early.

The two decisions look unrelated. They are the same one: who tells this launch's story, to whom, in what order, and against what the company can deliver on the day the telling lands.

2. The idea, and the four camps that hold it differently

Launch communications is the deliberate sequencing of who says what about a product release, across voices the company does not own. Public relations is the subset concerned with earned coverage: journalists, analysts, creators and named customers, none paid for the sentence they produce. The defining property is borrowed credibility. A reviewer's claim is believed partly because the reviewer could have declined to make it; a company's identical claim is discounted because it could not.

The practice was invented to solve an attention-allocation problem. Through the 1980s and 1990s a small technology trade press held effective veto power over a launch weekend, and strategists of the Regis McKenna school — whose work with Apple and Intel popularised the notion that a product's story is part of the product — formalised the embargo: identical material to many outlets at once, under a shared publication time. Al Ries and Jack Trout's positioning literature supplied the content side; Geoffrey Moore supplied the enterprise variant, in which the reference customer and the analyst, not the journalist, move a buying committee.

Four camps now disagree, substantively rather than stylistically.

The narrative-first camp holds that a launch's purpose is to install a frame. It would sign: six pieces sharing one frame beat forty that share none. It would not sign: reach is the primary measure of a launch.

The demand-generation camp treats communications as the top of a measurable funnel. It would sign: a programme that cannot be tied to pipeline within ninety days should be cut. It would not sign: unmeasured brand effects justify the spend.

The analyst-relations camp, dominant in enterprise software, would sign: in a category Gartner and Forrester cover, two notes outrank twenty articles. It would not sign: trade press moves an enterprise buying committee.

The direct-publishing camp, shaped by developer tools and direct-to-consumer brands, would sign: the company should be its own primary publisher, and press is a lagging indicator. It would not sign: an embargo is necessary.

A fifth position, held mostly by general counsels, is that launch communications is claim governance — the artefact a regulator reads back to you. It would sign: every external number must survive a hostile reading. It would not sign: PR's job is pipeline.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Expert practice has a shape. First the spine: one sentence naming the tension the launch resolves, written before any asset exists. Kalbag's was that an on-call engineer at three in the morning does not need more dashboards, she needs a defensible hypothesis. Second, the voice map: which independent party is decisive for which audience, and what each needs in hand. Third, inventory and lead times, because analyst calendars run in quarters and a reference runs through the customer's legal department. Fourth, claim substantiation a hostile reader can check. Fifth, sequencing against readiness — supply, stock, sales capacity, support scripts. Sixth, the rapid-response roster for the first seventy-two hours.

The quantitative treatment most practitioners never write down is a fidelity ledger: take each piece of coverage, count the three briefed message pillars, and ask how many appear. Ishaara's eighteen pieces gave fifty-four pillar slots; twenty-five were filled.

4. When the idea applies, stated as claims you can test

Four conditions carry most of the weight. One: there exists an independent voice the buyer already consults before purchase. For Ishaara this is plainly true — platform engineering leaders read analyst evaluations and peers' incident write-ups. For Kiraaya it is partly true: a contractor hiring a backhoe consults the dealer and two WhatsApp groups, not a newspaper, though regional trade press shapes what the machine owner believes about Kiraaya's solvency.

Two: the product is available, or the gap is short and stated. True for Ishaara, whose software ships on the announcement date. Dangerous for Kiraaya, whose July pilot failed precisely here: the announcement was real, the inspected supply was not.

Three: the claim survives hostile reading. Ishaara's forty-one per cent is a median across eleven customers with two regressions, and survives only if stated with its denominator. Kiraaya's "insurance-backed substitution" survives only where a substitute machine exists in that city and class.

Four: earned coverage is cheaper per unit of qualified attention than buying it. This fails more often than practitioners admit. Where the audience is small and identifiable — 600 named accounts — field outbound converted at 15 per cent, ten times the press meeting rate, and PR is simply the wrong instrument. The idea is actively misleading in three situations: regulated products where a journalist's paraphrase creates liability the company owns; enterprise categories where the buying committee has never read the outlet; and any launch whose real constraint is operational capacity, where coverage converts unservable demand into public disappointment.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Two-sided launches are hardest, because communications to one side is communications to the other. Kiraaya could not tell contractors "every Assured machine is inspected" without telling owners "your machine may fail", so the owner-facing programme ran first. Of 8,400 registered machines, 3,360 were enrolled for the sixty-two-point inspection, 2,352 passed, and 2,100 of the 2,352 that passed — 89.3 per cent — were listed under Assured; 252 were withdrawn by owners who rejected the deposit terms.

Solid line: fulfilment capacity implied by inspected machines. Dashed line: requests generated by demand communications. The discipline is that the solid line leads the dashed one at every point — the inverse of the July pilot.

Regulated launches invert the usual advice: the release is written for the regulator first and the reader second, because a claim a journalist paraphrases loosely still belongs to the company. Indian consumer launches run against the Advertising Standards Council of India's disclosure rules for paid creator posts, financial products against SEBI and RBI expectations on performance claims, data claims against the Digital Personal Data Protection Act. Hardware plus software launches split the story in time: the object is reviewable on day one, the software promise is not, and reviewers score the unit in front of them. Multi-product launches face the seam problem — three business units each owning a pillar, producing a release with no headline. Mature companies say a launch council solves this; what they do is let one executive decide which product gets the headline that quarter and pay the others in internal currency.

AI-native launches concentrate all of these. The claim is statistical, variance across customers is wide, and the honest presentation is a distribution rather than a number.

Bars are grouped by outcome band, not one per customer. The headline claim — 78 minutes to 46, a 41 per cent fall — is the median; the distribution is what a hostile reader asks for.

6. Nine things that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Coverage count is a supply metric. The tell is a clip report sorted by outlet, presented as a result. It measures how many editors found the story usable — press relationships, not demand. The obvious reading, more clips more effect, fails because the clips appear whether or not a single reader acts.

The embargo sells simultaneity, not secrecy. Experts assume leakage and design for it; the value is that ten outlets publish into one window, so the category conversation has a single day. The tell is a team treating a leak as catastrophic rather than a schedule change.

An exclusive is paid for in the next launch. The tell is a comms head keeping a ledger of which mastheads were passed over and when. Granting one outlet the story costs the others' cooperation next time, so the question is never whether it is worth it now but across the next three launches.

Analyst inventory has quarterly lead times. Competent practitioners book a briefing; experts know the note they want is scheduled against a research agenda set months earlier, and being late means the next window, not a smaller mention. The tell is a launch date chosen from an engineering calendar alone.

Reference customers are a supply chain with a legal bottleneck. The constraint is almost never enthusiasm; it is the customer's legal review, which takes weeks and can be withdrawn at any point. The tell is a named-customer slide with no approval date beside each name.

The hardest question belongs in the briefing, not the FAQ. Volunteering the weakness — two of eleven beta customers got slower — shortens its negative half-life: disclosed by the vendor it is a paragraph, discovered later it is the headline. The tell is a Q&A whose difficult answers have never been said aloud to a stranger.

Owned channels are over-credited by last-touch attribution. Ishaara's owned line converted at 2.5 per cent against press at 1.5 per cent, which looks like superiority and is partly sequence: many of those contacts read the analyst note first. Experts read owned channels as harvesting, and resist the conclusion that earned coverage can be cut.

Silence on day two becomes the story. The absence of a statement is read as an answer. The tell is a rapid-response roster ending at close of business on launch day, precisely when the first substantive criticism appears.

The story's geography must match the shelf's. National coverage of a product stocked in six cities converts interest into irritation. The tell is a media plan drawn by reach and a distribution plan drawn by city, with nobody holding both.

7. How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer categories the reviewer and creator are decisive, the launch is a single dated event, and the constraint is stock. In B2B and enterprise the analyst and reference customer are decisive, the launch is a quarter-long campaign rather than a day, and the constraint is sales capacity: coverage producing meetings nobody can take is waste. Platforms and marketplaces must publish two stories that cannot contradict each other in the same news cycle, supply story first. Hardware adds irreversibility — a review unit is a permanent verdict on one revision, and the shelf cannot be patched. AI products differ in one real respect: the claim is distributional, so the credible artefact is an evaluation with its denominators, not an adjective. Practitioners overstate the differences in the mechanics — spine, voice map, substantiation, readiness, rapid response are the same everywhere.

Stage changes who speaks more than what is said. A seed-stage company's launch comms is the founder plus three reporters who cover the category early, and its advantage is candour. At Ishaara's scale the same programme requires legal review, analyst scheduling and a retained agency — here Ilhaam Public Affairs — which buys notes and mastheads a founder cannot reach, at the cost of a blander first draft. The pathology of scale is that the approval chain lengthens until the spine is sanded into a sentence nobody would quote.

8. Three worked examples

Ishaara, November 2026. The analyst-first sequence produced the funnel in section 3: 300 meetings, 72 opportunities, ₹30.18 crore of pipeline against a ₹42 crore target, at ₹1.9 crore of cost. Two analyst notes reached 480 accounts and produced 12 opportunities at an average contract value of ₹58 lakh, the highest of any channel — the empirical core of the analyst-relations camp's claim.

Ikshu Beverage Works, an exclusive against an embargo. Ikshu, a Nashik bottler of cold-pressed cane juice, launched twice in 2026. In March it ran a fourteen-outlet embargo: fourteen pieces, 1,60,00,000 of gross reach, average piece length 310 words, fourteen of forty-two pillar slots filled — 33.3 per cent — while distribution covered 6,200 of 41,000 target outlets, 15.1 per cent. In September it ran an exclusive with one business daily plus eleven syndicated pickups: twelve pieces, 1,30,00,000 of reach, 18.8 per cent less, but an anchor piece of 1,450 words and twenty-six of thirty-six pillar slots filled, 72.2 per cent. Coverage was confined to six cities where distribution had reached 9,400 of 11,000 target outlets, 85.5 per cent. Branded search in launch week rose from 2,40,000 to 3,10,000, up 29.2 per cent, and modern-trade offtake ran at twenty-three bottles per store per week against fourteen, up 64.3 per cent, on ₹31 lakh against ₹44 lakh — ₹238 per thousand of reach against ₹275. The cost came later: two March outlets declined the September briefing.

Kiraaya's July pilot, and the recovery. The failure is stated above: 512 requests, 188 fulfilled, 36.7 per cent, ₹14,894 per fulfilled rental, an average Assured rating of 2.9 out of 5. The diagnosis was not poor communications but demand communications sequenced ahead of inspected supply. Khandekar stopped demand comms for five weeks, inspected 500 machines at a 68 per cent pass rate, adding 340 listings to the 210 then live to reach 550 — weekly capacity of 165 rentals — and restarted at lower intensity. Requests settled at 138 a week with 112 fulfilled, 81.2 per cent; the residual gap was mismatch by machine class and city, not aggregate shortage. Six weeks cost ₹19 lakh for 672 fulfilled rentals, or ₹2,827 each — a 5.3-fold improvement, achieved by changing the order of operations rather than the message.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Comms ahead of capacityRequests rising faster than fulfilmentWhat is our weekly fulfilment ceiling on launch day?Kiraaya: 63 per cent of requests unmet, ratings at 2.9
Headline-free releaseSix co-equal announcements, no rankingWhat one sentence would an editor use?Fidelity falls toward the 29.6 per cent pickup rate
Unsubstantiated statistical claimA single number with no denominatorWhat is the distribution behind this median?Correction cycle plus a lost analyst relationship
Reference pipeline collapseNamed logos with no approval datesWhich references are signed, as of today?Loss of the highest-ACV channel two weeks out
Day-two vacuumRapid-response roster ends at 6 p.m.Who answers the first critical piece, and how fast?The critic's framing becomes the category's framing

Each row has the same structure: a cheap question before the launch date replaces an expensive discovery after it. The two most often skipped are the first and the last, because both belong outside the comms team — operations and support — and neither appears in the comms plan's table of contents.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Embargo, exclusive, or neither. The embargo camp's evidence is that simultaneity concentrates attention, which matters when a competitor may launch the same week. The exclusive camp points at Ikshu: fidelity more than doubled, from 33.3 to 72.2 per cent, on a smaller budget. The direct-publishing camp holds that both instruments protect journalists' interests rather than the company's. The embargo camp is wrong if attention no longer concentrates in a single window, which is increasingly arguable; the exclusive camp is wrong if relationship debt compounds faster than the fidelity gain.

Whether PR should be measured on attributable pipeline. The demand-generation camp notes that Kalbag's table drove a real decision. Its critics say the channel split is an allocation, not a measurement: earned coverage cannot be geo-held-out cleanly, and last-touch crediting moves value from press to owned channels. The critics are wrong wherever a holdout design is genuinely available; in a national launch it rarely is.

How much of an AI claim to publish. One camp argues for the median with the distribution attached, on the grounds that variance disclosed is variance defused. Another argues that publishing two regressions out of eleven hands competitors a quotation that outlives the product's improvement. What is not defensible is publishing the median while holding the distribution in reserve: it surfaces eventually, and its late arrival converts a statistical fact into a credibility question.

Founder as spokesperson. For: candour and specificity travel, and a founder answers the hard question without escalation. Against: concentration risk — the story becomes a person, and that person's next unrelated remark becomes the product's problem. Unresolved, because both effects are real and neither is measurable in advance.

11. What mastery looks like

Mastery shows in three ways. Experts fix the spine first and refuse to let the briefing deck become a specification list. They read the launch date as a constraint imposed jointly by analyst calendars, legal review, inspected supply and warehouse readiness, and move the date rather than the story. And they staff the first seventy-two hours most heavily, not least. Asked what a launch achieved, they answer with a fidelity rate and a conversion rate before a reach number, and say plainly which part of the result they cannot attribute.

12. What each protagonist decided

Kalbag kept 11 November, briefed both analyst firms under non-disclosure six weeks ahead, and published the forty-one per cent median with its full distribution — eleven customers, two regressions — in the release rather than a footnote. She reallocated ₹11 lakh from press to doubling customer reference sessions, on the arithmetic that references create pipeline at 1.3 per cent of its value against 8.8 per cent for incremental press, closing the gap to the board's ₹42 crore target from 71.9 to 91.6 per cent.

Khandekar inverted her July order of operations. Owner communications ran from week minus six, demand communications began at week minus two with 1,340 machines listed, and the 3 December embargo lifted against 2,100 inspected machines — weekly capacity of 630 rentals against 420 requests. Fulfilment averaged about 450 rentals a week across the two quarters — 11,700 rentals at ₹46,000, or ₹53.82 crore, 56.1 per cent of the ₹96 crore target — on the argument that a fulfilled rental is worth more than a fulfilled forecast.

1. Ishaara's analyst channel produced the highest average contract value and the smallest reach. Under what conditions would you spend the entire launch budget on two analyst relationships — and what would you lose?

2. Kiraaya's recovery improved cost per fulfilled rental 5.3-fold without changing the message. What does that imply about how launch communications performance should be attributed between story and sequence?

3. Ikshu gained fidelity and lost two media relationships. Price that trade: what would the March outlets' cooperation have been worth at the next launch, and how would you know?

13. Going deeper

Launch planning and launch mistakes supplies the readiness gates that made Kiraaya's second attempt work. Messaging hierarchy is the artefact whose fidelity this page measures — without it there are no pillars to count. Writing a positioning statement forces the spine into one testable sentence before briefing anyone. Naming products and features decides whether a journalist can headline your name. Brand fundamentals for PMs explains why borrowed credibility accrues or decays. Category design is the narrative-first camp's long game. Sales enablement converts the meetings a launch creates. Packaging and on-pack communication is where Ikshu's story survives or dies, eighteen inches from a shelf.

Ehtiyaat Audit Cloud: Five Promises at One Factory Gate

A Product Marketing case — Ludhiana, Punjab

1. Sunday night on Gill Road

At a quarter past eleven on Sunday, 4 October 2026, Jasleen Grewal was the only person left on the second floor of Ehtiyaat Audit Cloud's office on Gill Road in Ludhiana. Eight sheets of A3 were taped along the conference-room partition, one for each surface on which the company spoke to a customer, from the website and the sales deck to the Punjabi one-pagers channel partners carried to job-shop owners and the investor deck Zorawar Dhillon used in September. Jasleen, Director of Product Marketing, had asked an intern to highlight in orange the first benefit claim on each. There were five different orange phrases across the eight sheets.

At nine the next morning the messaging council met — a forum Jasleen had proposed in June, which had so far produced two adjournments. On Friday, 9 October, the board pre-read went out, and on 16 October the board would approve two things at once: a ₹210 crore Series C, whose lead investor had asked why the company described itself four different ways in four documents, and a ₹2.85 crore rebrand budget that assumed the messaging question was settled. On 12 November, Ehtiyaat opened a twelve-metre stand at the OSH India expo in Mumbai; the graphics printed on 20 October. She had four drafts of the sentence that sat above everything, and believed none of them.

2. How Ehtiyaat came to be, and the promise it signed away

Zorawar Dhillon grew up in the Ludhiana bicycle-parts trade; his family's press shop in Focal Point supplied handlebar stems to Hero Cycles and Avon Cycles. In March 2016 a fire in a neighbouring unit killed two workers, and Zorawar watched his father produce three years of statutory registers — Form 12, Form 21, the accident register — written up in one night by an accountant who did this for eleven units in the same lane. The registers were not false so much as unrecorded until needed. Ehtiyaat Audit Cloud was incorporated in February 2017 by Zorawar and Jaspreet Sidhu, a Bengaluru engineer he met at a supplier-quality workshop. The name, from the Urdu and Hindi word for caution, was chosen because Zorawar wanted something a foreman would say aloud.

The first product was unglamorous: a tablet app that turned Factories Act registers and state checklists into timestamped, photo-backed entries, so a plant could show an inspector a live record rather than a reconstructed one. Enterprise customers followed from 2019, beginning with a Ludhiana textile group and a Faridabad auto-components maker supplying Maruti Suzuki, which wanted one dashboard for eleven plants.

Then came the decision that still shapes every sentence Jasleen writes. In November 2021, with ₹17 crore of revenue and a sales team of nine, Ehtiyaat signed a five-year co-marketing and data agreement with a large general insurer's industrial-risk division. Ehtiyaat would compute from platform data a 0–100 plant risk index branded the Suraksha Score; the insurer would band a premium discount to it and distribute Ehtiyaat through its branches. The agreement, which runs to 31 March 2028, obliges Ehtiyaat to lead all co-branded material with the premium-saving claim; early exit costs ₹4.50 crore and forfeits renewal rights over the channel's base. In 2021 this looked like distribution for free. By 2026 roughly one rupee in eight arrived attached to a promise Jasleen's own data no longer supported.

3. The industry as it stands in 2026

Indian factory safety is governed by an unfinished transition. The Factories Act 1948 and the state Factories Rules still bind most plants, administered by state Chief Inspectors of Factories and the Directorates of Industrial Safety and Health, with DGFASLI setting guidance and PESO licensing pressurised plant. The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code of 2020 is meant to subsume much of this, but states have notified rules at very different speeds, so a group with plants in four states runs four compliance calendars. Above that sits a commercially sharper layer: SEBI's BRSR Core assurance, which pushes safety disclosure into the value chain, and European buyer regimes — CSRD and supply-chain due-diligence law — which reach Jalandhar sports-goods exporters and Ludhiana hosiery units through purchase-order clauses rather than any Indian regulator. Ehtiyaat also serves eleven plants in Jebel Ali and Sharjah, and worker photographs brought the DPDP Act into the roadmap.

Competitively, Ehtiyaat sits in a gap. Global EHS platforms — SAP's EHS module, Enablon, Intelex, Sphera — win the listed conglomerates and price accordingly, while Zoho and Freshworks have taught mid-market Indian buyers to expect a self-serve trial and a price on the website. Between them are perhaps forty thousand registered factories too large for a spreadsheet and too small for Enablon, and two hundred thousand smaller units whose relationship with compliance is a visit, a file and an afternoon. Ehtiyaat has tried to serve all of them.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Exhibit 1 sets out the sequence; three of its beliefs have not survived.

The first was that the Suraksha Score measured safety. It was built in 2021 from what the platform could see — checklist completion, closure time, training records, inspection frequency — and validated against one year of insurer claims data on 240 plants. Zarina Virk's team re-ran it in August 2026 across the 1,180 channel plants; the result is Exhibit 6, in which the score sorts plants by incident level quite well and explains their improvement hardly at all. Incidents are self-reported, and the more diligent a plant, the more completely it reports. Zarina's note called the score "a good description of how a plant keeps records and a weak prediction of whether a worker gets hurt". The insurer has not seen it.

The second was that the MSME app would grow into the enterprise business. Ehtiyaat Saathi launched in January 2025, Hindi-first and with a free tier, and by August 2026 had 2,80,000 installs. Of those, 61,600 completed onboarding — 22 per cent — and 15,400 of the 61,600 ran a second audit within sixty days, 25 per cent. Only 4,620 of those 15,400 bought the ₹14,999 annual plan, 30 per cent, which is 1.65 per cent of installs and ₹6.93 crore of the ₹7.00 crore MSME line in Exhibit 2A. Jagmohan Randhawa's channel data shows the app sells on one sentence: the owner will not be embarrassed when the inspector arrives. The enterprise segment will not pay for that sentence, yet the app's growth is read inside the company as evidence for a promise it does not support.

The third was that the sales organisation knew which message worked. Exhibit 5 is the CRM's own account: opportunities tagged by the lead message the rep says they used. Read naively it declares premium savings the winner; read carefully it says something else, because insurer-channel opportunities arrive pre-qualified from a branch manager, they close small, and the tag is applied after the outcome is known. Exhibit 4, Jasleen's July buyer survey, puts premium savings last among EHS managers. Both sit in the pre-read, and nobody has reconciled them.

7. Voices

"Put 'nobody gets hurt on our watch' at the top and let the sub-heads do the rest. If we lead with paperwork we are a forms company, and forms companies sell for four times revenue."Zorawar Dhillon, messaging council, 18 September 2026

Renaming it in-product is a contract question, not a design question."External counsel, forwarded by Jaspreet Sidhu, 29 September
"My two Gulf renewals happened because we produced one report their European buyer accepted. Nobody in Ludhiana thinks that is the product. It is the only reason those accounts stayed."Jyoti Bajwa, customer-success review

8. The options as Jasleen currently frames them

  1. Lead with the outcome. Adopt Zorawar's promise on all eight surfaces, with incident reduction as the headline pillar and compliance, effort and reporting beneath it. It is the story the Series C wants, the claim Exhibit 6 supports least, and a banner Zarina has said she cannot defend.
  2. Lead with inspection certainty. "You will never be caught unprepared." It is what the largest revenue segment says it buys and what the product demonstrably does. It leaves the group sustainability buyer — 50 per cent of whom rank BRSR readiness first, and who sit in the accounts Jyoti renews — reading about inspectors when the problem is a customer's questionnaire.
  3. Segment the promise. Run two promises, an enterprise platform story and a Saathi story for the channel: Jeevan's portfolio argument in disguise. It doubles the surfaces to maintain with a team of six and two vacancies, and the insurer leaflet belongs to neither.
  4. Hold one promise and one set of pillars, vary only the proof. Fix the promise and three pillar names everywhere and let the evidence beneath each change by reader: inspection records for plant heads, the buyer report format for group finance, the premium band for the insurer channel. It satisfies the contract's letter without letting the premium claim become the promise. It requires six surface owners to hold wording constant against their own incentives, and it does not say what the promise is.

Jasleen wrote the options on Saturday and by Sunday had begun to distrust the list itself. Every one assumes the company should have a single voice at the top and differ below. Jeevan's remark about portfolio, and Jyoti's about a side feature carrying two renewals, suggest the argument is not about wording at all: it is about what Ehtiyaat sells and to whom, dressed as a question about a banner.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The council meets Monday, 5 October; the pre-read closes Friday, 9 October; on 16 October the board approves or refuses the ₹2.85 crore rebrand budget, of which ₹0.62 crore is the website, ₹0.48 crore collateral and translations, ₹0.55 crore sales enablement, ₹0.70 crore in-app strings, and ₹0.50 crore the expo and channel kit. Stand graphics print on 20 October; OSH India opens on 12 November.

The constraints are harder than the dates. The insurer agreement runs to 31 March 2028 and costs ₹4.50 crore to exit, against ₹11.00 crore of FY2026 revenue and 1,180 plants whose renewals the channel controls. Any incident-reduction claim must survive a diligence team that has asked for the underlying data. Product marketing is six people with two roles unfilled since July, and the Hindi and Punjabi versions are rewrites. Jeevan's rule-packs for two OSH Code states slip into Q4, so nationwide readiness is not yet true, and the DPDP Act makes any proof point built on worker photographs a matter for counsel before it is a matter for copy.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Reading Exhibit 3 alone, what has gone wrong — and is five claims across eight surfaces a failure, or the predictable result of eight owners doing their jobs well?
  2. Exhibits 4 and 5 disagree about the premium message. What would you need to know to decide which to believe, and what if you could not find out by Monday?
  3. Exhibit 6 came from Ehtiyaat's own analysts and omits two cautions from the pre-read. What obligations does that create for Jasleen, and for Zarina, in the next eleven days?
  4. Exhibit 2B shows 1,180 plants generating ₹11.00 crore and 412 generating ₹48.00 crore. Should a promise be weighted by customers or by revenue, and what does each cost?
  5. Jeevan believes this is a portfolio question in messaging clothes, and Jyoti's Gulf renewals hint at a promise nobody has proposed. Is any of the four options the right frame, and if not, what should Jasleen put to the council instead?
  6. It is Monday morning. What should Jasleen do, in what order and with whom — and when the board asks on 16 October why the company describes itself four ways, what exactly should she say?

11. Sunday, later

Jasleen took the eight sheets down a little before one and stacked them face up, the orange phrases showing. She thought about the two workers in the lane behind the press shop in 2016, whom Zorawar named in every all-hands, and about the sentence owed by Friday: it had to be true for a hosiery unit with nine workers in Ludhiana, for a group finance head in Mumbai filling a BRSR annexure, and for a branch manager in Kanpur holding a leaflet he did not write. She turned off the light and did not choose.

Messaging Hierarchy Under Load: Promise, Pillars and Proof When Fourteen Surfaces Disagree

1. Two decisions, nine days apart

On 9 September 2026 Vandita Sarpotdar taped fourteen pages to a wall in Vyavastha Procurement Cloud's Bengaluru office: the opening claim of each of the company's fourteen public surfaces. Vyavastha sold indent-to-payment software to Indian mid-market manufacturers and ended August with 320 customers and ₹96 crore of annual recurring revenue — an average contract value of ₹30 lakh. One number had moved. In the six months to 31 August 2026 it worked 480 qualified opportunities and closed 105, a win rate of 21.9 per cent; in the same months of 2025 it worked 412 and closed 107, or 26.0 per cent.

Vyavastha's head of product marketing counted five answers to what the company was for: control of spend, speed, auditability, ease of implementation, and an "autonomous procurement function" in the chief executive's conference talk. Only five of fourteen surfaces led with a claim mapping to the promise approved eighteen months earlier — concordance of 35.7 per cent. Her chief revenue officer, Varad Chitnis, diagnosed it differently: reps knew the promise but not which of five pillars to lead with before which of three buyers, so they led with all five, and the first-call deck had grown from nine slides to twenty-three.

Nine days later Oindrila Basak faced the same problem with harder edges. Oas Water Systems, founded in Pune in 2021, sold a connected purifier whose sensor measured how loaded the filter actually was rather than how many days had passed. Hardware cost ₹14,500, an annual maintenance contract ₹3,600. In the six months to 31 August 2026 Oas sold 62,000 units across four channels and signed 27,187 contracts, a blended attach rate of 43.9 per cent: ₹89.9 crore of hardware revenue, ₹9.79 crore of subscription revenue, ₹99.69 crore in all. Attach decided whether Oas was a hardware or a subscription business.

Oviya Rajagopalan, her growth head, read the exhibit precisely: a customer who bought a specification had not bought a relationship with a service company, while one who bought a sensor that tells the truth about filter life had bought a promise somebody must keep. Both own the same machine.

2. The idea, its history, and the four schools

A messaging hierarchy has three levels. At the top sits one promise: a sentence stating the change the product makes for a named buyer, phrased so the buyer could repeat it. Beneath it sit two to four pillars, the reasons the promise is true, distinct in a testable sense: each answers an objection no other pillar answers. Beneath each pillar sits proof: evidence a sceptic can check without the company's help. It is a document about claims, not words: the claim layer is common property, the wording is not.

Three lineages arrived at this shape. Rosser Reeves argued in Reality in Advertising (1961) that a proposition without a reason to believe is a slogan, which 1970s agencies formalised as the copy platform. Corporate communications produced the message house — roof, pillars, a foundation of facts — because it let twenty spokespeople survive unpredictable questions without contradicting one another. The third lineage is academic: Gutman's means-end chain (1982) showed buyers ladder from a concrete attribute, through its consequence, to the value they hold. A hierarchy is that ladder written top-down. Geoffrey Moore (1991) and April Dunford (2019) supply the layer above.

The positioning-first school, taught in marketing-rooted programmes at Kellogg and Cornell Johnson, signs that when two surfaces disagree the fault lies in the positioning document, not the writers; it will not sign re-deriving the hierarchy per surface from data. The narrative-first school signs that a buyer commits to a shift in the world rather than a benefit; it denies that the top of the hierarchy is a benefit sentence at all. The direct-response school signs that the winning marketplace headline owes nothing to the winning line in an enterprise call, and denies that a written promise overrides a tested winner. The distinctiveness school, following Byron Sharp and Ehrenberg-Bass, signs that most buyers in low-involvement categories never process a reason to believe; for it, consistency means asset consistency, not claim consistency.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Two steps in expert practice are usually left implicit, and both are quantitative. Step one is to write the promise as a sentence a competent competitor would refuse to print. Vandita discarded "control of spend for finance leaders" because Tally, Zoho and SAP Ariba could all print it. What survived was narrower: "Nothing gets committed before the person who owns the budget has seen it."

Step two is pillar distinctness, a property of pairs, so the work scales with pairs: for k pillars there are k(k−1)/2. Vyavastha's inherited hierarchy had five pillars — cycle time, spend visibility, compliance, single source of truth, ease of adoption — and so ten pairs. Four failed the test of whether one objection was answered by both: spend visibility and single source of truth both answered "I cannot see what my plants have committed". Collapsing them left three pillars and three pairs, none failing. Intuition scores items; the defect lives in a pair.

Step three is proof, under a rule most teams learn late: every proof point carries a date and an owner, because proof decays. Vyavastha's cycle-time proof was a before-and-after across 41 customer instances, dated June 2026, median indent-to-purchase-order time falling from eleven days to one. Its compliance proof was not a claim but the statutory rails it wrote to — GST e-invoicing and TReDS — verifiable by any auditor.

Step four measures how the pillars distribute across the room, which decides whether a hierarchy survives a sales force. In July 2026 Vyavastha put its three pillars to 360 decision-makers, asking for the single most important reason to change systems.

Two things follow; only the second is usually noticed. Spend visibility wins, at 38.9 per cent, but on a plurality of barely two-fifths, and the within-role concentrations are stronger than the ranking: 74 of 120 finance heads choose spend visibility, 61 of 120 procurement heads cycle time, 65 of 120 plant IT managers statutory rails. A team reading only the total row leads wrongly before three-fifths of those it meets. Worse, a reader shown a pillar they did not choose reclassifies the product: plant IT managers given a spend-control opening filed Vyavastha under finance and forwarded it there.

4. When it applies, and when it misleads

Condition two deserves most attention: its failure is the commonest reason a hierarchy is imposed where it does not help. Consistency is about accumulation: a buyer meeting the same claim in four registers arrives at the fourth half-convinced, while a nine-minute marketplace shopper accumulates nothing. But C2's failure relocates the argument rather than ending it. The Oas customer meets many surfaces after buying — the app, the filter-life alert, the booking flow, the renewal reminder — and their consistency with the original claim decides whether maintenance reads as a continuation or an upsell. Exhibit 1's 43-point attach spread is post-purchase consistency appearing in a revenue line.

Three situations make the idea misleading. For a ₹20 biscuit, pillars and proof address a process the buyer does not perform; in a repositioning, holding a claim steady is the obstacle; in a wide platform one promise forces an abstraction too high to carry information.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

Multi-product is the first seam. When Vyavastha launched Payables in March 2026, 64 of its 320 customers bought both products within six months, a cross-sell rate of 20.0 per cent. One hierarchy covering both would have produced a promise about "spend management" that neither buyer recognised. Vandita adopted the arrangement mature companies operate while publishing something tidier: a thin company promise, a hierarchy per product, and a rule that no product claims a pillar another owns.

Two-sided situations break the rule more fundamentally. Oas is two-sided in a way its org chart concealed: the dealer channel is 3,100 independent installers averaging four units each. A homeowner wants to know when the water stops being clean; an installer wants repeat service revenue without callbacks. These cannot ladder to one promise without one being insulted by it, so the honest structure is two hierarchies sharing one foundation of proof.

Regulation constrains the proof layer rather than the promise. Under BIS rules and the Advertising Standards Council of India's substantiation expectations, "lowest service cost in class" needs a comparison producible on demand, so Oindrila's team replaced it with arithmetic the customer can check. Three years of Oas cost ₹14,500 for the unit plus ₹3,600 a year, or ₹25,300, and at twelve litres a day over 1,095 days produce 13,140 litres — ₹1.93 a litre. The calendar-replacement competitor at ₹12,900 plus ₹4,800 a year comes to ₹27,300, or ₹2.08. The difference is ₹2,000 over three years and 15 paise a litre: smaller than marketing wanted, and defensible.

Hardware plus software produces the seam that cannot be engineered away. Oas carton artwork takes nineteen weeks to shelf, so a box printed in February still sells in December while the app ships fortnightly. The box carries the promise and at most one pillar; the app carries the proof. AI-native products face this on a shorter clock: Vyavastha's extraction model improves weekly, making an accuracy percentage the worst possible pillar and a good dated proof point.

Product marketing writes the hierarchy; the web team tests its way to a different promise within two quarters because its metric rewards that; sales adds a fourth pillar in the field; partners rewrite everything, as Exhibit 5 shows. What mature companies operate, as against what they publish, is less a message house than a claims register: approved claims, each with proof, owner and expiry date, audited on a schedule.

6. Eight nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The promise must be losable. A promise no competitor would refuse to print is a category description; the tell is that it fits three rivals' homepages unnoticed. "Nothing gets committed before the budget owner has seen it" passes, because it excludes every system that cannot interrupt a purchase order.

Pillar order follows when objections arrive, not importance. Competent practitioners rank by importance; experts rank by where in the buying process the objection surfaces. The tell is a deck whose pillar order does not match the first twenty minutes of questions: Vyavastha's statutory-rails pillar was third in importance, first in chronology.

Proof has a shelf life and needs a date beside it. The tell is a benchmark quoted without a date, which usually means the number is older than the person quoting it believes.

Consistency is of the claim, not the wording. "Fastest deployment" and "fast to deploy" are not consistent: one is a superlative needing a competitive comparison, the other a description. The tell is a legal review objecting to what marketing thought a synonym.

The first audience is internal. The test is whether a tired rep on a bad line can produce it from memory. Asked to state the promise unprompted, 11 of 42 Vyavastha reps gave the documented one before the rewrite, 26.2 per cent, and 38 of 42 afterwards, 90.5 per cent. The tell of failure is a document nobody quotes.

Different pillars on different surfaces is not inconsistency. Different promises is. The obvious reading, identical openings everywhere, is the error that costs most money. Ask a surface owner which pillar they lead with and what the promise is: a good answer differs on the first, matches on the second.

Superlatives move risk rather than removing it. A superlative transfers risk to legal, which transfers it to the customer as a footnote; the tell is a footnote longer than the claim.

A hierarchy is a compression artefact, and difficulty compressing is information about the product. Teams pad to three pillars because frameworks say three; the tell is a third pillar with the weakest proof and the most adjectives. When a promise will not come out in one sentence, the cause is usually a product doing two unrelated things for two buyers, and the expert escalates to strategy, not to a copywriter.

7. Across product types and company stages

The mechanics are identical in every setting below; most writing about messaging by product type describes differences in readers and revision costs, not method. Four things genuinely vary: how many people must be convinced, how many surfaces a buyer meets, how fast proof decays, and how expensive a surface is to change.

In consumer products the buyer decides alone and quickly, so the distinctiveness school's evidence bites hardest and most of the pillar layer goes unread. In business software it must survive two or three readers with different first-choice pillars, so proof must be swappable under a stable pillar — an ROI model for finance, an architecture diagram for IT. In enterprise it must survive security questionnaires, hence the compliance pillar no marketer would have chosen. In marketplaces one promise gives way to two hierarchies sharing proof; in hardware the constraint is print lead time; in AI, proof decays in weeks. Stage cuts across all of it: before product-market fit a hierarchy is a hypothesis log; at Vyavastha's stage the first rep cohort learned version one; at scale it becomes governance.

8. Three worked examples

One: the cost of leading with the wrong pillar

Vandita tagged all 480 opportunities from the six months to 31 August 2026 by whether the first-call deck had led with the pillar matching the primary buyer's role.

At ₹30 lakh average contract value the 105 wins are ₹31.5 crore of new recurring revenue. Had all 480 converted at the matched-pillar rate of 30.0 per cent, Vyavastha would have won 144 deals, 39 more, worth ₹11.7 crore. Vandita did not claim that as recoverable: the tagging was retrospective, and the matched group was plausibly the group where the rep understood the buyer better in every respect, so the gap conflates message choice with rep skill.

Two: making the AI claim a proof point, not a pillar

Varad's team wanted a fourth pillar for the invoice-extraction model, whose field accuracy had reached 94 per cent on a July 2026 sample of 12,000 invoices from 41 customer instances. Vandita refused the pillar and took the number as dated proof under cycle time. A pillar answers a standing objection, and no buyer had objected that the product lacked a model; they objected that approvals took eleven days. A pillar must also outlast its surfaces; within two months the figure had moved to 96 per cent.

Three: where the approach failed, and the recovery

In September 2025 Oas did what the consistency argument superficially recommends: Oindrila mandated one headline, "Water you can prove", on every surface including marketplace listings, replacing the specification-led title used since launch. Over six weeks the listings took 184,000 sessions and conversion fell from 4.6 per cent to 3.4 per cent: 8,464 units at the old rate against 6,256 at the new, a shortfall of 2,208 units, or ₹3.20 crore of hardware revenue at ₹14,500 each. Brand-tracking scores improved, which made the decision hard to reverse.

A marketplace listing is a matching surface, not a persuasion surface: a shopper filtering on "RO UV 12 litre" will not click a title without a specification. The November 2025 recovery put the specification back in the title, where conversion recovered to 4.5 per cent, and moved the sensor proof into the first bullet and image. Marketplace attach rose from 22 to 31 per cent; against 24,800 marketplace units, that is 2,232 extra contracts worth ₹80.35 lakh in the half-year.

9. Failure modes and their early warning signs

Claim drift. The warning is support macros quoting a benefit in no approved document; the diagnostic is to ask six surface owners separately to write the promise in one sentence. Caught late it looks like 35.7 per cent concordance and a win rate down four points.

Pillar inflation. The warning is pillar count rising after every roadmap review; the diagnostic is to name the objection each pillar kills and count duplicates pairwise. The cost shows up as a deck of twenty-three slides, which nobody logs as a messaging symptom.

Proof decay. The warning is a live deck citing a benchmark two releases old; the diagnostic is to ask of any number its date and who can reproduce it. Caught late, an evaluator disproves it in the room and the loss is every other number's credibility.

Flattening. The warning is the pattern Oas saw: brand metrics improving while conversion falls on the highest-volume surface. The diagnostic asks whether every surface's reader arrives doing the same thing. The cost was ₹3.20 crore in six weeks.

A promise written for the investor. The warning is a category word no customer uses: "autonomous procurement function" appeared in the keynote and in no respondent verbatim. The diagnostic: has a customer said it back to you?

An unowned hierarchy. The warning is that nobody can name who approves a change. Unowned hierarchies are not violated; they are quietly reverted.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

One promise, or one per audience. The single-promise position rests on accumulation and on Exhibit 6; at its strongest, a company with three promises has no promise, because the sales force picks per call and the market hears noise. The segmented position rests on Exhibit 3: no pillar takes more than 38.9 per cent of first choices, so a promise built for the modal buyer is wrong for the majority. For the first camp to be wrong, buyers would have to rarely compare notes across roles; for the second, the cost of several promises would have to exceed the gain — a question almost nobody measures.

Documented consistency, or tested winners per surface. The direct-response case is Oas's ₹3.20 crore: the tested headline won where it mattered most and the document overrode it. The documentarian case is Exhibit 1's attach spread: that headline optimised a metric the test could see and degraded one it could not, because attach is measured months later. The disagreement is about whether measurement covers the consequences.

Whether proof does any work. The Ehrenberg-Bass position, on long panel data on repeat purchase in packaged goods, is that reasons to believe are mostly unread and that distinctive assets plus availability explain growth. The counter-evidence sits in considered purchases: a ₹30 lakh contract, or a household's drinking water, where a verifiable third-party number changes behaviour. It would take evidence that proof-rich creative wins in high-frequency categories to move one camp, and that enterprise buyers ignore substantiation to move the other.

Who owns it. One camp holds the hierarchy belongs to product marketing, because only PMM sees every surface; another to sales, because a hierarchy no rep uses is decoration; a third to brand, because the promise outlives every product. Varad's position was the second: a promise the field will not say is an opinion. Vandita never conceded it; they ran the register jointly.

11. What mastery looks like

Asked about messaging, experts ask first what is printed on the surface most expensive to change — the carton, the contract template, the partner portal — because that constrains everything above it. They write dates beside numbers unprompted, can say what their promise gives up, and treat a promise that gives up nothing as unfinished. They let surfaces differ in wording and refuse absolutely to let them differ in claim. And when a promise resists being written, they raise a product question rather than book another workshop.

12. The decisions, and questions for discussion

Vandita kept one promise and published a surface key against it: the same three pillars everywhere, with the opening pillar set by the primary reader's role — spend visibility for finance-facing surfaces, cycle time for procurement, statutory rails for the RFP boilerplate. She refused Varad's fourth pillar, made model accuracy a dated proof point, and set concordance as a launch gate, moving it from 5 of 14 surfaces to 13 of 14.

Oindrila declined to unify headlines. Oas would keep channel-specific claims under one rule: every surface must carry the filter-sensor proof within its first three lines or first image. She moved the promise onto the carton for the next print run, accepting a nineteen-week lead time that leaves the current box wrong until the first week of February 2027, and commissioned a separate installer hierarchy. Her open question is the one Exhibit 1 cannot answer: whether the 43-point attach spread is caused by the claim on the surface or merely correlated with the customers each channel attracts.

For discussion. First: Vandita's 13-point win-rate gap conflates message choice with rep skill. Design the cheapest experiment that separates them, and say what result you would accept. Second: Oas's flattening experiment improved brand metrics and cost ₹3.20 crore in six weeks. When would that have been the right trade, and how long would you run it to know? Third: choose between a hierarchy 90 per cent of your sales force can state from memory and one measurably better at converting, and say what the choice implies about who the hierarchy is written for.

13. Going deeper

Writing a positioning statementThe layer above; a promise that will not compress fails here.
Naming products and featuresThe most permanent surface; a wrong name is unfixable.
Brand fundamentals for PMsThe distinctive-asset argument limiting the claim layer.

Landing pages and conversion copyWhere flattening shows up first.

Ojasvi Aqua Network: One Promise, Six Surfaces

A Product Marketing case — Surat, Gujarat

1. The Friday deadline

On the morning of Monday, 5 October 2026, Urvi Shah sat in the third-floor conference room of Ojasvi Aqua Network's headquarters at Sachin GIDC on the southern edge of Surat, looking at six open tabs: the company website, the Ojasvi farmer app's Play Store listing, the exporter sales deck, the trade-fair booth artwork, a WhatsApp broadcast draft for farmers, and the investor pitch deck for the firm's Series B round. As Vice-President of Product Marketing, Urvi had been asked by founder and CEO Abhay Solanki to produce, by Friday, 9 October, one messaging brief that all six surfaces would follow. Two events made the deadline firm. The biennial India International Seafood Show, run by the Marine Products Export Development Authority (MPEDA), would open in Kochi on 6 November, with Ojasvi exhibiting to exporter buyers for the first time. The same week, Abhay would begin roadshow meetings with growth-stage investors for the Series B. Whatever Urvi wrote down would soon be read by exporters, farmers, and investors alike.

2. Ojasvi Aqua Network

Abhay Solanki had founded Ojasvi Aqua Network in Surat in 2019 after watching, as a young supply-chain manager for a diamond and textile trading family, how little organised cold storage existed for the shrimp and pomfret moving out of Gujarat's Veraval and Porbandar harbours. The company began as a B2B service: it built refrigerated storage hubs and reefer-truck routes, and helped exporters document catch records against the Coastal Aquaculture Authority's farm-registration rules and the European Union's IUU (illegal, unreported, unregulated fishing) catch-certification rules, both preconditions for shipping to EU and US buyers under FDA seafood import rules. That compliance service remained Ojasvi's largest line. In 2023 it added a second line, supplying packaged fish and shrimp to retail chains such as Reliance Fresh and to D2C seafood brands like FreshToHome and Licious. In 2024 it launched a third: a farmer-facing app, also called Ojasvi, through which registered farmers could book cold-storage slots, get water-quality alerts, and sell harvest to Ojasvi's processor network at a listed price. By the close of FY2026 the network ran nineteen hubs across three states, serving 18,400 farmers, as Exhibit 1 shows, and had grown revenue to ₹302 crore.

Exhibit 1 — Cold-chain hubs and registered farmers by state, FY2026

Source: Ojasvi Aqua Network operations dashboard, September 2026. Andhra Pradesh hubs cluster around Nellore and Kakinada, India's largest shrimp-farming belt.

3. What the audit found

Ahead of the seafood show, Urvi had commissioned a message audit: a plain read of what each surface actually told a customer to expect. The results, in Exhibit 3, unsettled her. The exporter deck led with cold-chain reliability and compliance, aimed at buyers worried about a consignment being turned back at port. The investor deck led with scale, citing the nineteen hubs and 18,400 farmers as a defensible moat. The trade-fair banner, already printed in draft, carried a generic tagline about "freshness you can trust" that named none of it. The app listing and the WhatsApp broadcasts to farmers led with price: a claim that farmers could earn "up to 31 per cent more" than selling to the local trader, or arhatiya. That claim troubled Ashish Pandya, the head of analytics, because it held for only a sliver of farmers. Of the 64,000 farmers who had installed the app in the past two quarters, 11,520 — 18 per cent — completed activation (KYC plus a first sale); of those, 6,912, or 60 per cent, were still active ninety days later. Ashish's verified data showed that across those 6,912 farmers, average price realised was 14 per cent above the local mandi price — real and defensible. Only the top decile, roughly 691 farmers with direct processor contracts, came near the 31 per cent uplift behind that line. Aarushi Desai, running the farmer platform from Ahmedabad, needed activation to climb toward the board's 25 per cent target, and believed an honest price story would do more for that than a freshness tagline.

4. The people around the table

Abhay SolankiFounder & CEO — SuratA single scale-and-trust story he can repeat unchanged to Series B investors, exporters, and the press in the same week.
Anish VyasHead of Exporter Sales — VisakhapatnamCompliance and cold-chain reliability up front; exporter buyers, he says, stop reading if farmers appear before certification does.
Aarushi DesaiHead, Farmer Platform — AhmedabadA farmer-first promise built on the verified 14 per cent uplift, to lift activation from 18 per cent toward the board's 25 per cent target.
Ashish PandyaHead of Analytics & Trust — MumbaiWhatever number appears anywhere must be one he can defend to an investor's diligence team or a farmer's neighbour.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 2 explains why this matters now. Exports are still the largest line at ₹186 crore but the slowest-growing, up 31 per cent. The farmer platform, smallest at ₹22 crore, grew fastest at 83 per cent, and domestic retail and D2C supply grew 68 per cent to ₹94 crore. The audiences Ojasvi has spoken to least consistently are exactly the ones it now depends on for growth, even as exporters still pay most of the bills.

Exhibit 3 — Messaging hierarchy: fragmented today, one hierarchy proposed

Exhibit 3. Top row: the wording actually found on each surface during the September 2026 audit. Bottom row: the hierarchy Urvi is weighing, in which promise and pillar names stay fixed and only the proof beneath each pillar is localised to the reader.

Exhibit 3 makes visible what the audit only listed. The top row shows six surfaces answering different questions — reliable, big, fresh, lucrative — with no shared vocabulary, so a buyer reading the investor deck then the trade-fair banner would not recognise the same company. The bottom row sketches the alternative: one promise and three pillar names fixed everywhere, with the proof beneath each pillar drawn from whichever number is honest for that reader.

6. The options

  • A. Lead with the investor and exporter story everywhere. Adopt Abhay's promise — "India's most trusted aquaculture traceability network" — with scale-and-compliance pillars on all six surfaces, farmer app included. Upside: one quotable line for the Series B roadshow and for exporters who decide fast on a trade-show floor. Cost: farmers get an abstract corporate line instead of a price number, and Aarushi expects activation to fall further short of 25 per cent.
  • B. Lead with the farmer price story everywhere. Put the verified 14 per cent uplift and a "fair price, every catch" framing on all six surfaces, investor deck included. Upside: a message tied to real transaction data and to the fastest-growing part of the business. Cost: exporters and investors, who need compliance and scale first, may read Ojasvi as smaller than its ₹302 crore of revenue supports.
  • C. One promise, three fixed pillars, proof localised by surface. Keep one promise and three pillar names — cold-chain integrity, verified traceability, fair price discovery — everywhere, letting the proof beneath each pillar change with the reader: hubs and tonnage for investors, CAA and EU IUU records for exporters, the 14 per cent uplift for farmers. No audience gets an irrelevant argument, yet any two surfaces read as one company. Cost: six surface owners must hold the wording constant even when they disagree on which proof matters most.

7. Questions for discussion

  • What, concretely, has gone wrong across the six surfaces, and why is Exhibit 3 evidence of a messaging problem rather than six teams simply doing their jobs?
  • Why should the gap between the 14 per cent verified uplift and the 31 per cent top-decile uplift matter to how Urvi frames the fair-price pillar, even for an investor who never opens the farmer app?
  • What would each stakeholder in Section 4 say is wrong with the other three's preferred option, and whose objection matters most against the 9 October deadline?
  • If you were Urvi, which option would you take into Friday's meeting, and what would you say if Abhay still preferred Option A?

8. A note for the learner

Messaging hierarchy is the discipline of keeping one promise, a small set of pillars, and their supporting proof consistent across every surface a customer might encounter. It does not require identical sentences everywhere — a banner and a WhatsApp message cannot carry the same words — but it does require that the promise a reader infers, and the pillars beneath it, be the same story wherever they look. Ojasvi's audit shows the failure mode: six surfaces, none dishonest alone, together telling three different companies' stories.

A well-reasoned answer works from the distinction the exhibits set up: promise and pillars are the fixed architecture, proof points are evidence, and evidence is expected to differ by audience without breaking the hierarchy. Options A and B make the same mistake in opposite directions, each forcing one audience's proof into the promise slot for every audience. Option C is defensible because it alone treats promise and pillars as company-wide and proof as audience-specific. It does not remove the coordination problem — Anish, Aarushi and Ashish still must agree on wording, and Abhay must accept that the investor deck will name farmers before it names hubs — but it gives Urvi a structural answer for Friday, and lets every number in Exhibits 1 through 3, including the gap between 14 and 31 per cent, be used honestly rather than hidden.

Positioning, Messaging & Product Marketing

Messaging Hierarchy: Keeping Promise, Pillars and Proof Straight Across Every Surface

On the morning of 3 March 2026, Wamika Raut, head of product marketing at Waadaa Wellness Foods, a Gurugram-based nutrition company, opened four documents side by side on her screen. One was the app team's draft screen for the new WhoteinBar launch. One was the copy the D2C website team had written for the same product. One was a shelf-talker design bound for 4,000 modern-trade stores. The last was a sales deck her national sales head, Warun Bhalla, planned to show buyers at Reliance Retail and DMart that Friday. Each document made a different claim about why WhoteinBar was worth buying. The app said "80% less sugar." The website said "the taste you already love." The shelf talker said "India's most-tested protein bar." The sales deck said "verified 20 grams of protein, third-party lab checked." None of the four were false. All of the four were, in a buyer's head, a different product.

Waadaa's first bar, WhoteinBar Classic, had launched fourteen months earlier with exactly this problem, and the postmortem was blunt: trial conversion on the app was 4.0%, on the website 3.0%, and only 12 of 80 buyer meetings, 15%, converted to a stocking commitment. Warun's own view was that the sales team had pitched a "lab-verified" product while the app sold a "diet" product, and a shopper who saw one message on Instagram and a different one on the shelf did not recognise the bar as the same purchase decision twice. Wamika's task now was to decide, before Friday, what the one promise for WhoteinBar would be, what supported it, and what proved it — and to make all four documents restate the same three things in different words.

The idea, defined

A messaging hierarchy is the ordered structure that turns a positioning statement into language people can actually read: a single promise (the one sentence a buyer should be able to repeat back), two to four pillars (the distinct reasons the promise is true, each one a different angle rather than a restatement of the others), and, under each pillar, proof — the checkable evidence that makes the pillar credible rather than asserted. It sits one layer below positioning: positioning answers "compared to what, for whom, and why does that matter" in a strategy document's language; messaging hierarchy arranges that answer into the words a headline, a slide and a sales rep's opening line will actually use, in a fixed order, so a website, an app screen, a shelf talker and a sales deck all draw from the same three-layer document instead of each writer inventing their own.

The habit of backing a claim with a named reason predates product marketing by decades — Rosser Reeves was already arguing, in 1950s advertising, that a claim needs a "reason to believe" the audience can check, not just a slogan. What product marketing courses at Kellogg and Cornell Johnson teach today, following practitioners such as April Dunford after 2019, is writing promise, pillars and proof down as one fixed document, so several teams writing several surfaces translate from the same source rather than each re-deriving the pitch from memory. The sentence Wamika could say in a room without sounding glib was this: "A messaging hierarchy is the one promise, the reasons it is true, and the proof for each reason — written once, so every surface says the same three things in different words."

How it actually works

Building the hierarchy is a sequence, and skipping a step is what had gone wrong with WhoteinBar Classic. Wamika's team worked it in five moves. First, they confirmed the positioning already on file: for health-conscious Indian shoppers aged 22–40 who find whey-protein bars chalky or oversweetened, WhoteinBar delivers verified protein content without the usual taste trade-off, unlike RiteBite or Yoga Bar's mainstream lines. Second, they wrote the promise as a sentence a shopper could repeat, not a slogan: "Protein you don't have to take on faith." Third, they chose exactly three pillars, each answering a different objection a buyer would silently raise — protein content, taste, and price — resisting a fourth pillar for shelf-life or packaging, which were true but not what stopped anyone from buying. Fourth, for every pillar they attached proof a sceptical buyer could check themselves: an NABL-accredited lab certificate for protein, a blind taste-test score against two named competitors, and a per-gram price comparison. Fifth, and the step most teams leave implicit, they wrote a one-page "surface key" translating the same three pillars into each surface's own register — a stat on a shelf talker, a chart in a sales deck, a line in an app screen — while forbidding any surface from inventing a fourth pillar or restating a pillar as the promise itself.

A worked example: which pillar to lead with

Writing the hierarchy is only half the job; deciding which pillar leads on which surface is the other half, and that decision should come from evidence, not instinct. Before Friday, Wamika's team ran a message test: 1,200 respondents, split into three equal cells of 400, each cell shown one candidate headline built from a different pillar and asked whether they would likely buy (top-2-box purchase intent on a five-point scale).

On that reading, every surface would lead with the protein-content pillar. But before locking it, the team cut the same 1,200 respondents by geography — 600 metro, 600 tier-2, 200 per headline in each half — because a national number can hide two different markets pulling in different directions.

The split changed the answer. Nationally, C leads. But inside metro alone, A leads at 65.0% against C's 61.0% — shoppers who already buy protein bars take verified content as given and respond more to taste, while tier-2 shoppers, newer to the category and wary of inflated claims, respond far more to proof (73.0% against A's 57.0%). Trusting only the national average, the app and website — mostly metro traffic — would have led with the weaker message for that audience. The hierarchy stayed the same everywhere; only the pillar placed first changed by surface.

Six distinctions a learner has to sit with

A promise is not a tagline

A tagline is what a brand says to be remembered; a promise is what a buyer must be able to repeat to a colleague to explain why they bought. "Protein you don't have to take on faith" survives being repeated badly. A tagline written for memorability alone often carries no actual claim, which is why it can be catchy and still useless at the top of a hierarchy.

Pillars must be different objections, not different adjectives

"Nutritious," "wholesome" and "healthy" are one pillar wearing three costumes. A real second pillar answers an objection the first does not touch — taste is a different worry from protein content, and price a third, separate from both. Three pillars that all reduce to "it's good for you" are one pillar.

Proof is evidence a buyer can check, not confidence restated

"Trusted by thousands" is not proof; it cannot be checked by the reader. A lab certificate number, a named comparison, a published test score can be. The test is whether a sceptical buyer, given ten minutes, could verify the claim independently — if not, it is not proof, whatever confidence it is written with.

Consistency means the same structure, not identical words

A shelf talker with six words and a sales deck with six slides are not inconsistent for using different sentences. They fail only if the underlying promise, or which pillar is claimed true, changes between them. The hierarchy fixes the skeleton; each surface dresses it differently.

A hierarchy cannot invent a true pillar that is not there

If WhoteinBar's protein content were not independently verifiable, no skillful writing turns "verified protein" into an honest pillar. The framework orders true claims persuasively; it has no mechanism for manufacturing a claim not already substantiated.

It does not tell you whether the product itself is right

A crisp hierarchy makes a mediocre bar sound clear and a great bar sound clear; it does the same work either way. It sits downstream of a product and pricing decision, and a newcomer should ask, before writing one, whether the product actually delivers on the pillars proposed.

Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and early-stage versus scale

The mechanics do not change across these settings, but the audience per surface does. In a consumer product like WhoteinBar, the buyer is one person deciding in minutes, so pillars lean on sensory and price proof. In B2B software, the hierarchy usually has to survive three separate readers — an economic buyer, a technical evaluator, an end user — who weight the pillars differently, so the proof under each pillar (an ROI model, an integration diagram) must be swappable without touching the promise. In a marketplace, supply and demand are two audiences with two different objections, and one promise rarely serves both; most marketplaces run two adjacent hierarchies sharing one brand promise but different pillars per side. Stage matters independently of category: an early-stage company like Waadaa is still testing which pillar converts, so the hierarchy should stay a living document; a large company instead manages the discipline problem of many writers across many surfaces quietly drifting from it, which is why scale brings governance — a single owned document and a review step — rather than more testing.

Common mistakes

Writing the hierarchy after the launch assets, not before. The symptom is exactly Wamika's Tuesday: four finished documents that each sound reasonable and disagree. The error is treating messaging as writing delegated per-surface instead of one source document every surface draws from. The cheapest diagnostic: ask each surface owner, separately, to state the promise in one sentence before the review starts — disagreement surfaces in thirty seconds.

Confusing "more pillars" with "more persuasive." The symptom is a hierarchy grown to five or six pillars once three teams have each added a favourite feature. The error is mistaking a features list for a hierarchy. The diagnostic: read the pillars aloud; if two could be challenged by the same objection, one is redundant.

Proof only the marketing team can verify. The symptom is a proof point like "rigorously tested" with no source a buyer could look up. The error is writing proof for internal comfort, not external verification. The diagnostic: hand the claim to someone outside the company and time how long it takes them to check it — if they cannot, it is not proof.

What good looks like

Six weeks after the deadline, Waadaa's four surfaces still used different words, deliberately: the app opened with a taste-test score, the website with a short video of the lab certificate, the shelf talker printed "20g, lab-verified," and Warun's sales deck opened with the price-per-gram table aimed at buyers who think in shelf economics. What had not changed across any of the four was the promise behind it, or which pillars supported it. When a trade buyer who had seen the shelf talker later sat through Warun's pitch, the two experiences reinforced rather than contradicted each other — the buyer recognised the same claim in a new form, the quiet purpose of a messaging hierarchy.

The decision, and two questions to keep

Wamika chose to lead with the verified-protein pillar nationally, but told the app and website teams — whose traffic was 70% metro — to open with taste and hold verified protein as the second beat, while the shelf-talker and sales-deck teams, facing a mostly tier-2 and trade audience, opened with the lab certificate. Every surface kept the same three pillars in the same order of importance; only the opening beat moved with the audience. Wamika's next step was a quarterly review of the surface key against fresh message tests, rather than writing it once and forgetting it — a hierarchy earns its keep only if someone owns keeping it current as the product, competitors and buyers change. The reader should sit with two questions: when a hierarchy's pillars stop matching the objections real buyers actually raise, who in an organisation notices first — and how would you design a five-minute check, repeatable every quarter, that catches four teams quietly drifting from one promise before a shopper ever notices the mismatch?
