Sales Enablement

Go-to-Market, Growth & Monetisation · Positioning, Messaging & Product Marketing · near-expert treatment

The last mile of positioning: what it costs, how it is measured, why it decays, and the arguments practitioners have not settled.

1. Two decisions, first week of September 2026

On 8 September 2026, Garima Ojha, Head of Product Marketing at Unmesh Quality Systems in Nashik, had two documents open: a requisition for an enablement platform at ₹34 lakh a year, and a deal desk note on Ushakal Lifesciences, an Ahmedabad contract manufacturer evaluating Unmesh's batch-release software for two sites, one of them US-FDA-inspected, ₹48 lakh of annual recurring revenue. Unmesh's rival Urvi Compliance Software had spent a fortnight walking Ushakal's quality head through its 21 CFR Part 11 validation package. Shalini Karn, the account executive, had the same package and had never been shown where it lived.

Behind the deal sat eleven months of a half-built programme. Since October 2025, five of Unmesh's eighteen account executives had been certified on rebuilt battlecards and had those cards surface in the CRM whenever a competitor was named; six more were certified with no surfacing; seven, in two regions whose manager declined the pilot, sold on the old library. Nishant Dwivedi, the Chief Revenue Officer, wanted a revenue-enablement manager under himself; Anurag Pathak, in sales operations, called it a CRM problem. Each described half of it.

The same week, Gopal Ranjan was arguing a different version at Utsav Venue Exchange, a Dehradun marketplace matching banquet halls to event organisers through forty field representatives. In the March quarter, 243 of 3,600 assigned leads became venues transacting within thirty days; in the June quarter, after a scripted module on the objection that killed signings, the figure was 378. Deepak Kesari, his largest supply manager, wanted the script handed to regions; Gopal suspected adaptation was how programmes die.

2. The idea, its history, and the four schools that disagree

Definition. Sales enablement is the deliberate construction and maintenance of the content, tools, training and just-in-time access a revenue team needs for an effective conversation with a specific buyer at a specific moment in a specific deal. Publishing material enables no one: enablement happens when the right sentence, with its proof, reaches the rep in the four minutes it is useful.

The history is traceable. Through the 1990s and 2000s the problem was framed as methodology: Miller Heiman's strategic selling, Solution Selling, the Challenger research, later MEDDICC. These taught selling in general; none supplied the answer to the objection a named rival raised last Tuesday. The 2010s produced the counterpart: the Sales Enablement Society formed in 2013, analysts began tracking enablement as a function, and a category grew up around findability (Highspot, Seismic, Showpad). By the early 2020s the label had drifted again, to “revenue enablement”.

That drift is why four schools share a vocabulary and mean different things. The content-and-tooling school holds that the binding constraint is retrieval, so the work is plumbing. It signs that a card a rep must remember to look for does not exist; not that enablement should change what a rep believes about the buyer. The competency school, from the methodology tradition, holds that enablement is behaviour change, coached and certified. It signs that an unrehearsed answer is no answer; not that a better-organised library moves win rates. The product-marketing school holds that enablement is the last mile of positioning. It signs that no battlecard is more stable than the company's agreement about why it wins; not that enablement is a training function. The sales-operations school holds that an artefact which is not a field or a stage gate in the system of record is an aspiration. It signs that workflow beats narrative; not that prose quality is the lever.

Each school is right about the failure it has cleaned up. Unmesh's experiment matters because it separates two: six reps got the competency intervention alone, five got it with the sales-operations one.

3. Mechanics in depth, and the arithmetic underneath

Expert practice runs a fixed sequence; the steps left implicit are the third and sixth.

Step 1 is inherited: an unsettled hierarchy yields a card that says something different after every rewrite. Step 2 is evidence: win/loss interviews run by someone with no quota. Step 3, most often skipped, ranks objections by the revenue they cost, not how often they are mentioned: Unmesh's old card listed eleven, three never seen in a lost deal, while the one seen in five had no entry. Step 4 is the battlecard: one page per named rival carrying the objection in the buyer's phrasing, the honest answer, the proof, and the trap that exposes the rival without disparaging them. Step 5 maps each objection to a two-minute demonstration branch. Step 6, price guardrails, is least discussed and most diagnostic, because a rep who cannot answer still has price.

That table is an enablement instrument disguised as a finance control: the nine deals in the two deepest bands carried justifications, and six named the same capability objection. Step 7, certification, must be live and expiring. Step 8, surfacing, is what Unmesh's cohorts measure. Step 9 turns the loop monthly, making it a maintenance function, not a project.

Five measures carry a programme, and only the first is about people rather than deals. Ramp time: fourteen of Unmesh's eighteen AEs had six months' tenure or more, and they reached 80% of quota in 9.5 months (the four hired before the programme), 8.5 (the next four) and 6.0 (the six onboarded into it from week one): a hire-weighted mean of (4×9.5 + 4×8.5 + 6×6.0) ÷ 14 = 108 ÷ 14 = 7.7 months across all fourteen, not any cohort. The others are win rate by cohort, cycle length, discount depth and content usage.

The formal treatment is a compounding chain. Chained win rate is opportunity-to-demonstration times demonstration-to-evaluation times evaluation-to-won; revenue is that chain times pipeline times realised contract value, list less discount. Because stages multiply, a programme lifting three of them modestly looks implausibly good, and one lifting only the first two looks like failure.

4. When the idea applies, as testable claims

One: a human intermediary's words change the outcome. True at Unmesh, where a quality head buys after four conversations; true on Utsav's supply side, where a representative sits in a venue owner's office; false on its demand side, where an organiser books without speaking to anyone. Where it is false, enablement collapses into product copy.

Two: a credible alternative is in the room. Unmesh meets Urvi in two-thirds of evaluations; Utsav's reps rarely meet Upvan Events Marketplace, because most venues they visit are on no platform. Utsav's highest-yield artefact is therefore a payout script: its competitor is inertia, which objects differently.

Three: the answer exists but is not retrievable under pressure. This is what makes enablement cheap: Unmesh's package existed, and Karn could not find it while a customer spoke. Four: the deal is winnable on the product as built. Where it is not, enablement misleads, converting a roadmap gap into a training problem, as six of Unmesh's nine deep-discount justifications quietly show.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product. With three products the question becomes “which of ours, in what order”, reps default to what they know, and enablement becomes routing. Mature firms keep one qualification tree, since independent card sets compete for one conversation.

Two-sided. Utsav's reps promise demand the company does not control. A script overstating bookings recruits venues that churn within a quarter: it looks like a marketplace problem and is an enablement defect. An honest script quotes a distribution, not an average.

Regulated. A claim on Unmesh's battlecard can be quoted in a customer's own validation documentation, so claims need regulatory review and must carry only what is evidenced. That slows the loop to weeks, so mature firms split the card: a reviewed claims half, an unreviewed half of traps and questions.

Hardware plus channel. When distributors carry the pitch, enablement extends to people the company neither employs nor certifies, and partner messaging lags the direct team by a release. Firms claiming partner enablement mostly run a portal with a login count.

AI-native. A non-deterministic demonstration cannot be scripted keystroke by keystroke, so the script becomes prompts with known-good inputs plus a recovery move for a poor output; and accuracy claims decay with each model change, so review follows release notes, not quarters. At every seam, whoever runs the loss review owns enablement in practice.

6. Eight nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The unit is the moment, not the artefact. The tell is a manager reporting assets published. An expert times a rep finding the card for a named rival; over twenty seconds means it does not exist. More content is not progress: content and retrieval are separate goods, and only the second is scarce.

A battlecard is a record of losses, not a comparison chart. The tell is a card with no dates and no deal references, just features with ticks. An expert reads it for the phrasing buyers used, clumsier than any marketing prose. Positioning claims something about a market; a battlecard is evidence about rooms.

Certification measures recall; deals require retrieval. The tell is high scores with low usage. Answering at leisure and in the fourth minute of a tense call are different skills, which is why expert programmes certify by live role-play and expire certificates. A passing score predicts readiness as an examination predicts a viva: it does not.

Decay is the default state. The tell is an asset with no owner or review date. Unmesh repackaged in April 2026; of the 61 assets any rep had opened that quarter, 23 still carried the old packaging language. Experts budget maintenance as a standing cost, like a test suite.

Discount depth is an enablement metric, often the cleanest. The tell is an approval queue whose justifications repeat one phrase. A rep without an answer reaches for price, so discount depth proxies for missing answers without surveying anyone. Calling it indiscipline is wrong when one objection recurs in every exception.

Enablement reads the roadmap, and improves the odds only on winnable deals. The tell is an objection log with no field for “no honest answer available”. Experts insist on it, because its count is the best demand signal a product team will get: priced, dated, attributable to named buyers. They read a rising share of capability losses as good news about their instrumentation and bad news for the roadmap. The obvious reading, that enablement should answer everything, teaches fluency about gaps instead of surfacing them.

Ownership is contested because the claimants optimise different failures. The tell is which function conducts the loss interview. Product marketing optimises fidelity and over-produces; revenue enablement optimises behaviour and over-trains; sales operations optimises workflow and under-writes. Experts care less about the reporting line than whether one person can change the card, the CRM field and the certification in a week. It looks like turf; it is latency.

Attribution is confounded, usually by tenure and self-selection. The tell is a cohort boundary that correlates with something else. Unmesh's uncertified cohort sat in the regions whose manager declined the pilot and held its four newest hires, tangling tenure with treatment. Experts fix this by design, staggering rollout by territory, not by caveating a slide. Reading a cohort gap as proof is how budgets get cut.

Between ten and fifty, where Unmesh and Utsav sit, the failure inverts: material accumulates faster than it is retired. Above a hundred the function industrialises and the failure is latency, loss interview to changed card stretching to a quarter. 10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether win rate is a legitimate enablement metric. Against: win rate is driven by pipeline quality, territory, product fit and macro conditions, so crediting enablement invites exactly the confounded claim Unmesh's cohorts illustrate; the defensible metrics are behavioural. For: behavioural metrics are gameable and commercially uninteresting, and a function that refuses revenue measurement is funded as an expense and cut first. Scepticism is wrong if staggered rollouts across matched territories reproduce the cohort gaps; advocacy is wrong if such designs dissolve them.

Whether enablement owns the message or only delivers it. The product-marketing position is that separating authorship from positioning guarantees drift, since whoever sits closest to reps rewrites the story for the room. The revenue-enablement position is that positioning authored far from the field is accurate and unusable, and the rewrite is information, not noise. Settling it needs evidence on whether rewrites improve conversion, which nobody gathers.

Centralised or federated. Federation adapts to local buyers and creates ownership, and yields four versions of the payout promise, one of which will be wrong in a way that costs a venue. Centralisation preserves fidelity and slows the loop. Mature practice fixes claims and frees framing, but that boundary is judgement, not doctrine.

Whether certification is worth its cost. Unmesh's numbers argue for scepticism: certification without surfacing forecasts two extra deals and ₹38.16 lakh. Defenders reply that certification is what makes surfacing useful, since a rep who never rehearsed the answer will not open the card holding it. Unmesh cannot settle it: no cohort received surfacing without certification.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied enablement produces artefacts and reports production. Someone who has internalised it works backwards from a moment, beginning with a loss rather than a template and asking what sentence would have changed the room. They can name the three objections that cost most last quarter, retire material as readily as they write it, and find their numbers' weaknesses before the CFO. And they measure what is scarce: how long what the company knows takes to reach the rep under pressure.

12. What each protagonist decided

Garima Ojha did not buy the platform. She extended CRM surfacing to the thirteen reps in cohorts B and C, since the ₹449.28 lakh gap between scenarios B and C, however confounded, dwarfed a fortnight of Pathak's configuration work. She staggered it, one holdout region now and the other in January, to give the next comparison a cleaner design. On ownership she declined the turf fight, proposing one standing meeting empowered to change the card, the CRM field and the certification in a single week, chaired by product marketing, with the loss review first on the agenda.

Gopal Ranjan kept the claims central and federated the framing: payout and cancellation language, a promise Utsav must keep, was fixed and versioned, while discovery questions, pitch order and local references went to regional managers. He also replaced signings as his headline metric with the 30-day transacting rate.

Three questions for discussion. First: cohort A's reps volunteered and had a better manager, so design a rollout separating the effect of surfacing from the effect of the reps, and say what Garima gives up to run it. Second: the nine deep-discount deals, six naming one missing capability, are roughly ₹40 lakh of foregone value; enablement, pricing or roadmap finding, and who is accountable? Third: Utsav's demand side has no sales force, so does anything here apply, and what does the vocabulary cost anyway?

13. Going deeper

Messaging hierarchy is the input enablement cannot repair: its defects reappear as an unstable battlecard. Working with sales decides whether loss evidence reaches enablement. Enablement for complex sales extends this to committee purchases, where material is sequenced across many conversations. Writing a positioning statement is the hierarchy's smallest unit, where most enablement problems are solved. Naming products and features matters: a feature nobody can name cannot be demonstrated reliably. Brand fundamentals for PMs explains why a claim that survives legal review still may not persuade. Category design is the strategic substitute: change the comparison, not win it. Launch communications and PR aims this material at the market. Packaging and on-pack communication is the physical-goods analogue: the pack is the only enablement a shelf product gets.

Marammat Sewa Cloud: The Battlecard Before Dubai

1. The morning of the loss review

On Monday, 5 October 2026, Inder Bhandari reached his desk off Jaipur Road in Ajmer a little before nine, ahead of the weekly pipeline call. As Head of Sales Enablement, his job was making sure the sales team could explain, defend, and demonstrate what the product did. That morning he knew two things that would make the next twenty-three days difficult. First, the quarter's enterprise loss reviews showed the company had lost four of its last nine large deals, three of them for the same reason: a rep improvising an answer to a technical objection instead of pointing to an agreed, tested one. Second, the most important open deal — a fourteen-branch workshop group in Dubai called Mawasim Auto Care — had its decision call fixed for Wednesday, 28 October, with operations director Omar Al Suwaidi, and Marammat had no collateral built to answer the objections Omar had already raised.

2. A company built on multi-brand workshops

Marammat Sewa Cloud sold cloud software to the workshops that keep India's two-wheelers running: digital job cards replacing the carbon-copy chits still common in the trade, spare-parts inventory tied to distributor catalogues, mechanic productivity tracking, and — its most defensible feature — a warranty-claims module that filed and tracked claims with manufacturers for the workshop. Founded in 2019 by Bhanu Maheshwari, whose family had run a spares counter in Ajmer's Naya Bazaar for three generations, its edge was working across brands: one workshop servicing a Hero Splendor, a Bajaj Pulsar, and increasingly an Ola Electric or Ather scooter ran all three through one system, something no manufacturer's own dealer software offered, since Bajaj, TVS, Hero MotoCorp, Royal Enfield, and Honda Motorcycle and Scooter India each built tools only for their authorised networks. By September 2026 Marammat had 3,400 workshops on the platform, mostly independent operations across Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, and Gujarat, plus a small, fast-growing set of larger chains. Every invoice complied with GST, and every vehicle record followed the DPDP Act's consent rules. Its best-funded rival, Motor Mitra Systems, pitched large chains on deeper warranty integration and an offline-first design.

3. The push upmarket, and where it was slipping

Eighteen months before the loss review, Bhanu had set the company on a deliberate move upmarket, chasing multi-city chains and, if it worked, a first account outside India. A single enterprise account could be worth as much as fifteen SMB accounts, and a strong Gulf reference would open a two-wheeler service market grown with the region's food-delivery boom, where riders for Talabat and Careem ran bikes hard enough to need frequent, documented service. Mawasim Auto Care, fourteen Dubai branches servicing exactly that fleet, was chosen to prove the thesis.

The trouble was that Marammat's sales motion had been built for a different kind of sale. An SMB owner bought after a twenty-minute demo and a handshake; an enterprise buyer ran a structured evaluation with security questionnaires and multiple stakeholders, any one able to veto on a narrow point. Exhibit 2 shows the cost: of nine enterprise deals since April, only three were won, and three of the four losses failed because a rep could not answer, consistently, a question Motor Mitra's rep had already answered with a slide. Omar had raised three such questions with Urvashi Todi, who led enterprise sales from Newark, nine and a half hours behind Dubai most of her day: could the warranty-claims engine validate accurately across Mawasim's manufacturers; would the system hold up through the branches' connectivity drops; and could an Ajmer-based vendor genuinely support Gulf Standard Time. Urvashi had answers to all three — Owen Marsh in Toronto had the accuracy and uptime numbers in a dashboard; Ines Wagner in Berlin had been asked to reskin an old deck but never briefed on the argument it needed — but none of it was assembled into something a rep could trust. Osheen Dhanuka, Singapore-based customer-success lead for Gulf accounts, was already improvising onboarding scripts for the same reason and warned Inder that whatever shipped for Mawasim would shape every Gulf conversation after it.

4. The people

Inder Bhandari — Head of Sales Enablement, Ajmer. Wants a battlecard and demo script a rep can use correctly under pressure, without waiting for a program that cannot ship before 28 October.
Bhanu Maheshwari — Founder & CEO, Ajmer. Wants the Mawasim win as proof the board-approved enterprise push works, but not a rushed fix that costs a bigger reference account later.
Urvashi Todi — Head of Enterprise Sales, Newark, New Jersey. Is on the call with Omar and needs material she can defend live, nine and a half hours from Ajmer's working day.
Osheen Dhanuka — Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Wants whatever ships to survive past the sale, since she inherits the account and is already short of Gulf onboarding material.

6. The options

  1. Hire a dedicated sales enablement lead. Structurally correct for a permanent problem. Per Exhibit 4 it costs ₹18 lakh a year, with a first deliverable six weeks out, past 28 October. It solves next quarter, not this one, and a hire made under deadline pressure risks being the wrong hire.
  2. Build a minimum battlecard for Mawasim now, and generalise it later. Inder pulls the three recurring objections from the loss reviews, gets Owen's numbers and Ines's slide craft into one document within twelve days, and rehearses it with Urvashi and Osheen. Fast and cheap, but built for one deal — unless organised for reuse, the fire drill repeats for the next Gulf prospect Osheen already expects.
  3. Outsource the whole collateral set to a contractor. A fixed ₹4.5 lakh fee buys a fuller deck set in three weeks and frees Inder's time, but Exhibit 4 shows little slack for the two correction rounds a contractor unfamiliar with warranty rules will likely need — risking a polished deck that still errs on the call that matters most.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 2 actually show is missing — a product problem, a sales-skill problem, or an enablement problem?
  2. Why would a battlecard built for the Mawasim objections travel further than one built only to close that deal?
  3. Given Exhibit 3's twenty-three days and the Ajmer–Newark–Dubai time-zone spread, what should happen in week one?
  4. Would you let Inder proceed on Option 2 alone, or commit to Option 1 in parallel — and what does that imply for how Marammat staffs enablement afterward?

8. A note for the learner

Sales enablement answers one narrow question: does the person in front of the customer have the decks, battlecard, and demo script to sell what the company built? Exhibit 2 shows Marammat's problem sits exactly there. Warranty-claims accuracy and offline behaviour were never in doubt — Owen had the numbers — and sales skill was adequate. What was missing was a single, tested answer to three predictable objections, agreed once and reused, instead of improvised fresh under pressure. That gap, not a weaker product, explains three of the four losses and puts ₹56 lakh of pipeline at risk again in Mawasim.

A well-reasoned answer protects the deal without mistaking that for the underlying fix. Option 1 alone cannot ship before 28 October and abandons ₹20 lakh of live pipeline to hope. Option 3 rents speed from someone who must still learn the warranty logic from scratch, with only three weeks and two correction rounds on the deal that matters. The defensible path is Option 2, run so it stops being a one-off: Inder builds the Mawasim battlecard from evidence already in hand, treating the three objections as the reusable skeleton of every future enterprise conversation, and tells Bhanu plainly that a dedicated hire is still the right next commitment — just not the one that can save this call. Enablement is not decoration added after the fact; it keeps a true answer from becoming, on the day it is asked, an improvised one.

Jaanch Fleet Telematics: Who Sells the Driver Score?

A case for discussion. Gorakhpur, October 2026.

1. Sunday night, 11 October 2026

The power cut on Betiahata Road came at a quarter to ten, as it often did on Sundays, and Sarvesh Chaubey kept working by laptop light because the board pack was due at eight. He was Director of Revenue Enablement at Jaanch Fleet Telematics, a title eleven months old that he had argued for himself. On Monday, 12 October, the board would ask one question in some form: why, four months after Jaanch shipped the driver-behaviour product it had bet its software margin on, were only three thousand one hundred vehicles paying for it.

He had four costed options and no view he could defend for ten minutes: every time he settled on one, something in the file contradicted it. The field team, thirty-four people across eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, had shown the product to accounts covering 7,100 vehicles in six months and converted 540 of those vehicles. The five-person inside desk in Basti converted at over five times that rate off a sixth of the pipeline. Lavkush Chaurasia's insurer-led pilot in Nairobi did better still, on numbers too small to trust.

The obvious reading was that the field channel lacked the decks, battlecards, demonstration script and objection answers to sell a behavioural-analytics product, and that fixing this was his job — the company's working assumption since July. Sarvesh had spent the weekend becoming less sure of it, and could not say precisely why.

2. A company that sold boxes first

Jaanch Fleet Telematics was founded in Gorakhpur in March 2017 by Yogendra Tiwari, whose family had run eighteen trucks on the Nepal border routes north of the city and lost enough diesel to pilferage to make the product self-evident. The first version was a box, a SIM and a web page showing where a lorry was. When the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways pushed AIS-140 compliance through the commercial-vehicle fleet, Jaanch had certified hardware ready and salesmen the fleet owners already drank tea with.

By September 2026 it had 48,900 vehicles under subscription across 1,268 accounts, most of them fleets of twelve to ninety vehicles, and a software layer the hardware did not need: fuel-theft alerts, geofences, route-compliance scoring against e-way bill destinations and, from November 2025, a driver-behaviour score.

The decision that constrains everything today was made on Tuesday, 18 January 2022. To win Jhankar Bus Lines of Basti — 3,050 buses, the largest single fleet in the region — Yogendra signed a thirty-six-month agreement at ₹249 per vehicle per month with a clause granting the customer, at no additional charge, every software module Jaanch released during the term. Two further contracts, with Falak Roadlines of Gorakhpur (2,180 trucks) and Jazba Carriers (6,670 trucks), used the same template. Those three cover 11,900 vehicles, 24 per cent of the base: the region's three most quotable logos, entitled to the driver score for free and so unable ever to appear in Exhibit 1 as revenue.

3. The industry Jaanch sells into

Indian commercial-vehicle telematics has three kinds of competitor and no comfortable position in it. At the top, vehicle manufacturers bundle connected-vehicle platforms into new trucks and buses: Tata Motors' Fleet Edge and Ashok Leyland's i-ALERT arrive factory-fitted and cost the operator nothing visible. In the middle sit venture-funded independents; Jaanch's sharpest rival, Jugnu Vahan Systems of Deoria, raised money in 2025 on a dashcam story and demonstrates a camera that watches the driver's eyes, which is easier to show in a meeting than a score.

Two regulatory facts shape the driver score specifically. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, makes a driver's braking, speeding and cornering history personal data about an identifiable individual; Jaanch's counsel advises that the operator is the data fiduciary and Jaanch the processor, but that consent notices in Hindi and Bhojpuri must reach the driver, not merely the owner. And the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority's product-filing regime means no Indian insurer can price a motor policy off the Jaanch Score until it sits inside a filed, approved product. Two have said they are interested; neither has filed.

The global exposure runs through insurance rather than trucks. Fensbury Mobility Underwriters, a managing general agent in London, writes fleet motor programmes in East Africa and wants a score built on worse roads than theirs. Duncan Whitmore, who runs their programmes, wants a validation memo; Lavkush's Nairobi pilot exists to produce it.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Chaalak Score 1.0 launched on Tuesday, 11 November 2025, as a free tab inside the tracking dashboard. Usage looked strong — 61 per cent of accounts opened it at least once in the first month — which the company read as demand. The tab sat on the default landing screen, and a click was not a judgement.

In March 2026 the board approved the FY27 plan, whose largest new revenue line was Chaalak Score sold as a paid module at ₹149 per vehicle per month, targeting 9,000 paying vehicles by 30 September 2026. Version 2.0 shipped on Tuesday, 9 June 2026, with harsh-braking, cornering and over-speed detection reworked and an insurance-grade score band. Between June and September Sarvesh produced a twenty-two-slide deck, a battlecard against Jugnu and a recorded demonstration, all in English, and ran one three-day classroom in Gorakhpur that twenty-six of the thirty-four reps attended.

Three things have since turned out to be wrong. The attach rate the company reported to itself all quarter was the sales-operations figure of 11.2 per cent, which counts accounts rather than vehicles and counts free trials as attached; finance's billing run of Friday, 25 September put it at 6.3 per cent of vehicles (Exhibit 3). The classroom evaluation forms were excellent, and the twenty-six reps who attended converted no better than the eight who did not. And on Friday, 18 September, Eklavya Rai told Sarvesh privately that 2.0's harsh-braking detection was throwing false positives on the unmarked speed breakers between Gorakhpur and Deoria at a rate he called "embarrassing if a customer plots it against his own trip sheets", with a fix due in December. Twenty-four losses in Exhibit 4 are coded to a rep's inability to explain the score; Eklavya thinks the reps were right to be unable to. Figure 1 lays out the sequence; Exhibit 6 shows the result, net additions peaking at 860 in the quarter before 2.0 shipped.

5. The people

Sarvesh Chaubey, 37 — Director, Revenue Enablement, Gorakhpur. Position: the field channel can be made to sell this, but not in fourteen weeks and not on paper. Incentive: his function was justified on the score's attach rate. Unsaid: he believes a third of the reps will never hold a technical conversation about a statistical score.
Yogendra Tiwari, 51 — Co-founder and CEO, Gorakhpur. Position: the ₹149 line must grow before any Series B, because hardware revenue carries a multiple he refuses to accept. Incentive: an investor has told him software ARR is the only number that will be diligenced. Unsaid: he wrote the all-modules-included clause himself and has never discussed it with the board.
Shalini Dubey, 44 — Head of Field Sales, Gorakhpur; 34 reps. Position: her people are paid on devices and core subscriptions; no battlecard changes a commission plan. Incentive: her quota is units, not modules. Unsaid: three of her best reps report that drivers read the score as surveillance, and she has asked them to keep it out of the CRM.
Lalita Ojha, 33 — Head of Inside Sales, Basti; 5 people. Position: give the score to her desk; her conversion is 11.9 per cent against the field's 2.2. Incentive: she has twice asked for the overlay headcount in Exhibit 7. Unsaid: her 620 vehicles came from 41 accounts, mostly inbound, chosen by her.
Eklavya Rai, 39 — Head of Product, working from Deoria. Position: a product needing this much selling is mispackaged; fold it into the base price and let insurers pull it. Incentive: repackaging makes the attach-rate miss disappear. Unsaid: the December fix may not land in December.
Sneha Kesarwani, 31 — Data Scientist, Kraków. Position: the score does separate risk, but Exhibit 5 overstates it: the loss data is mixed-vintage and uncontrolled for vehicle age and route. Incentive: the memo will carry her name. Unsaid: she has already sent a caveated draft to Whitmore's team without telling Yogendra.
Lavkush Chaurasia, 35 — Customer Success lead, international, Nairobi. Position: India cannot prove a behavioural score while its insurers cannot price it. Incentive: his pilot's budget renews in March. Unsaid: 202 of the pilot's 244 converted vehicles sit with one operator, introduced by a broker whose arrangement ends in March.
Duncan Whitmore — Head of Programmes, Fensbury Mobility Underwriters, London. Position: a signed memo by 30 November. Unsaid: Fensbury is evaluating a second vendor.

7. Voices

"My reps sell a box and a monthly rate to a man who knew their father. You have given them a slide that says predictive risk quantification. Change the commission, or change the slide into a price." — Shalini Dubey, WhatsApp to Sarvesh Chaubey, Friday 9 October 2026, 21:14 IST
"Two of my five work score deals only because I take the accounts that ring us. That is not a channel, it is me picking the easy ones. Give my desk the region and I will owe you a different number by January." — Lalita Ojha, weekly revenue call, 6 October 2026
"I cannot sign a memo saying the score predicts claims by a factor of 3.6. A ten-year-old truck on the Basti bypass brakes hard because it is a ten-year-old truck on the Basti bypass." — Sneha Kesarwani, email to Sarvesh Chaubey and Eklavya Rai, 7 October 2026, 14:02 CEST
"We are not asking you to be right, we are asking you to be documented. Unsigned by 30 November and we proceed on the other vendor's data." — Duncan Whitmore, Fensbury Mobility Underwriters, email, 2 October 2026
"Enablement is a symptom word. We shipped a module a fleet owner cannot use on Monday except to shout at a driver, then wondered why the deck was not working." — Eklavya Rai, product review, 8 October 2026
"I need the software line to be a line. Do not come to the board on Monday and tell me the answer is training." — Yogendra Tiwari, to Sarvesh Chaubey, 9 October 2026

8. The options as Sarvesh currently sees them

Option A — equip and certify the field channel. Rebuild the deck around the objections that recur in Exhibit 4, translate the demonstration into Hindi and Bhojpuri, put a live sandbox on forty handsets, certify every rep before the March renewal season. It treats the largest channel as an asset rather than a write-off. It also costs ₹38 lakh against ₹33 lakh of budget, delivers nothing usable for fourteen weeks, and assumes July's classroom failed because it was the wrong classroom rather than because documents do not move a commission-paid seller.

Option B — a specialist overlay desk. Four people selling only the score, pulled into deals by the field reps, at ₹96 lakh a year. Exhibit 2's 11.9 per cent is the argument for it. Whether that rate belongs to the channel or to Lalita's account selection is untested, and an overlay may teach thirty-four reps that the score is not theirs.

Option C — make insurers the channel. Build the validation memo, the explainability pack and the API certification, and let underwriters pull the score through to fleets adopting it for a lower premium. It is the only option in which the buyer has a reason to want the score rather than to be sold it. It is also twenty weeks, and depends on Sneha's controlled run, on an Indian insurer filing a product with the IRDAI, and on Fensbury, which has another vendor and a 30 November date.

Option D — stop selling it separately. Fold the score into Core Track at ₹289 and let the attach-rate problem cease to exist. It concedes the board's FY27 software line, reaches only 17,600 vehicles within a year, and alone acknowledges that 11,900 vehicles already get the module free.

Sarvesh has all four on one page and knows it is wrong somewhere. Every option answers how do we sell the score. None answers Eklavya's question, whether a fleet owner in Deoria has anything he can do differently on Monday because of it; and none answers whose consent, the owner's or the driver's, the product runs on.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets on Monday, 12 October 2026, and will approve one option. Jaanch holds ₹4.10 crore of net cash against a monthly burn of ₹31 lakh — a runway of 13.2 months — and Yogendra intends to open a Series B in February. The all-modules-included clause on 11,900 vehicles cannot be reopened before the Jhankar renewal in January 2028. Fensbury's memo is due 30 November; Sneha will not sign before the controlled run. Any driver-facing consent flow must exist in Hindi and Bhojpuri before the score is sold as a management tool. And the weeks around Chhath in November, when fleets run hardest and drivers go home, are the worst weeks for a classroom and the best for showing an owner what harsh braking costs him.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Which of the four attach rates in Exhibit 3 should the board be shown, and what does the existence of four tell you about Jaanch?
  2. Exhibit 2 shows the field channel converting at 2.2 per cent and inside sales at 11.9. What would you need to know before reading that gap as evidence about enablement?
  3. Exhibit 4 codes 138 of 234 losses. Name the loss reasons you distrust, and say what you would instrument instead.
  4. Sarvesh's function exists to put decks, battlecards and demonstrations in sales' hands. Is that the binding constraint on the ₹149 line — and if not, what is?
  5. Option C makes the underwriter the channel. What must be true of Exhibit 5, the IRDAI filing and Fensbury for that to be a strategy rather than a hope?
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Sarvesh do, in what order, in ten days — and what does he say to a board told all quarter that attach was 11.2 per cent?

By eleven the power was back and Sarvesh had reopened the options sheet again. He had begun the weekend intending to ask for Option A and a larger budget. He now thought Shalini right that a deck cannot outvote a commission plan, Lalita right that her own number was flattered, Eklavya right that the module asks an owner to do something he has no process for, and Sneha right to refuse to sign. All four could be right at once. The cursor sat in the empty field at the top of the sheet, where the recommendation went; and outside on Betiahata Road a loaded six-wheeler took the corner far too hard, and somewhere in a Gorakhpur database a score went down by two points, and nobody would look at it.
exp20v2-pmm.enablement:
Sales Enablement

Go-to-Market, Growth & Monetisation · Positioning, Messaging & Product Marketing

1. A deal Zanjeer Systems cannot afford to lose on a technicality

On 11 August 2026, Amanpreet Rathee, Head of Product Marketing at Zanjeer Systems, a warehouse-management software company headquartered in Vijayawada, read a message from the regional sales lead in Ranchi: Zila Fulfilment Networks, a fourteen-city contract logistics operator, wanted one more call before choosing between Zanjeer and a much larger, internationally known vendor. The deal was worth ₹38 lakh in annual recurring revenue — unremarkable alone, except Zila's decision would be read by four other 3PL groups as a verdict on whether an Indian-built platform could run a warehouse at their scale.

The account executive on the deal, capable and two years in, had done nothing wrong she could name. She ran the standard demo, answered what she was asked. But she froze for a few seconds when Zila's operations director asked how the platform handled a client moving inventory between two warehouses mid-order — a scenario the rival rep had walked through a week earlier with a named reference and a screen recording. Zanjeer's platform could do it; the answer lived three screens deep in a workflow nobody had written down, so she had no confident way to say so live. Amanpreet's problem was not that the product was behind. It was that fourteen account executives across four regions were each reconstructing, deal by deal, knowledge that existed somewhere in the company but had never been organised for live, under-pressure use. That gap has a name: sales enablement, and Amanpreet had eleven days to decide what to do about it.

2. The idea: turning what the company knows into what the rep can say

Sales enablement is the discipline of giving a sales team the content, tools, training and just-in-time access to information it needs for an effective conversation with a specific buyer at a specific moment — distinct from simply knowing the product well. The term crystallised into a named function over the 2010s: the Sales Enablement Society formed in 2013, and platforms such as Highspot, Seismic and Showpad built businesses on the idea that content only helps if it reaches a rep inside the moment they need it, not a folder they never reopen. Before that, most companies treated the problem as solved once marketing shipped a positioning document and sales sat through a training day.

The distinction enablement draws is between knowing and being ready. A rep can pass a quiz on Zanjeer's multi-warehouse feature and still fail to mention it live — recalling a fact at leisure and retrieving it in the fourth minute of a tense call are different skills. The sentence Amanpreet could repeat without sounding glib: enablement is not the deck; it is the guarantee the rep says the right sentence at the exact moment the deal needs it.

3. The mechanics: from positioning to the moment of need

The mechanics run in a fixed order, and most of Zanjeer's failure came from skipping steps, not doing any one badly. It starts with the messaging hierarchy — the company's agreed statement of who the product is for, what problem it solves, and why it wins, ranked from the one sentence a stranger should remember down to the proof points that survive a skeptical buyer. Enablement inherits this rather than inventing it, which is why unsettled positioning produces material that decays within a quarter.

From that hierarchy, product marketing builds battlecards: one page per named competitor, written from win/loss interviews rather than assumption, listing the objections that actually come up, the honest answer, and the specific proof — a client name, a number, a screen — that makes it credible. Zanjeer's battlecard for the large international vendor was eleven months old and had never been updated after three lost deals cited the same objection. Alongside it sits the demo script: a map from each objection to the two-minute sequence that answers it, so a rep navigates to proof under pressure instead of a generic tour. The objection playbook generalises this to procurement, security and implementation-risk questions regardless of which rival is in the room. The step teams skip most often is embedding it inside the CRM at the stage a rep needs it — a card a rep must remember to find is used far less than one surfacing automatically.

4. A worked example: what a certified rep is actually worth

Amanpreet ran a six-week pilot in June 2026, certifying six of Zanjeer's fourteen account executives on the rebuilt battlecards, demo script and objection playbook; the other eight kept selling on the old, undocumented material. Q2's pipeline gives a clean comparison, shown below.

Cohort (Q2 FY27, Jul–Sep 2026)OpportunitiesDemosPOCsClosed-wonARR (₹ crore)
Certified (6 AEs)403420124.56
Not yet certified (8 AEs)56421783.04
Total / all 14 AEs967637207.60

Every stage compounds: of the certified cohort's 40 opportunities, 34 reached a demo (85.0%); of those, 20 became POCs (58.8%); of those, 12 closed (60.0%) — a chained win rate of 12 of 40, or 30.0%. The uncertified cohort booked demos at 75.0%, converted only 40.5% to a POC, and closed 47.1% of those, landing at 8 of 56, or 14.3% overall. Blended across all fourteen reps, Zanjeer closed 20 of 96 opportunities, a blended rate of 20.8%, worth ₹7.60 crore at an average contract of ₹38 lakh — the 20.8% blended figure and the 30.0% certified-cohort figure describe the same quarter on different bases and should never be quoted interchangeably.

Now change one input: assume by Q3 FY27 all fourteen reps are certified and the pipeline grows to 110 opportunities. Recomputing from the certified cohort's actual chain, not by estimating a round number: 110 × 85.0% ≈ 94 demos, 94 × 58.8% ≈ 55 POCs, 55 × 60.0% = 33 closed — matching the cohort's 30.0% chained rate applied directly (110 × 0.30 = 33.0). At ₹38 lakh average, that is ₹12.54 crore in new ARR. The same pipeline at Q2's old 20.8% blended rate would close only 23 deals worth ₹8.74 crore. The difference — 10 deals, ₹3.80 crore — is what full certification is forecast to add: a projection, not booked business, and Amanpreet flagged it that way to the CRO.

Figures rounded to the nearest whole demo, POC or deal; the 33-deal and 23-deal rows are forecasts on a certified-cohort and blended-rate basis respectively, not counted closed business.

5. The nuances a learner must sit with

Enablement is not training, and not content marketing

Training builds general skill over weeks; content marketing aims at the buyer. Enablement sits between them, judged narrowly: did the rep say the right thing, with proof, at the right moment. A well-trained rep can still be poorly enabled if the battlecard never surfaces.

It is strictly downstream of messaging, and inherits every flaw in it

Enablement cannot repair unsettled positioning. If the company has not agreed why it wins against a rival, no battlecard produces a stable answer — only one that changes each time someone rewrites it, which reps trust until it fails them live.

A battlecard is only as good as its source, and most are written backwards

The common failure is drafting a battlecard from assumption rather than from win/loss interviews. Zanjeer's stale card listed three objections; the deals it lost that quarter all turned on a fourth, unwritten one.

Certification measures readiness on a test, not performance in a room

Scoring well on a quiz shows recall under no pressure with unlimited time. The gap between that and recalling the fact in the fourth minute of a live objection — the adoption gap — is why usage analytics matter more than exam scores.

Ownership is genuinely contested, and the contest has consequences

Enablement can sit inside product marketing, a standalone function, or sales operations; each optimises for a different failure — over-produced content, over-indexed tooling, or drift.

Attribution is genuinely hard, and Amanpreet's own numbers show why

The 30.0% versus 14.3% gap between Zanjeer's cohorts is suggestive, not conclusive: the six certified reps volunteered for the pilot, which likely selected for stronger performers first. A defensible case separates the certification effect from self-selection rather than crediting the whole gap to the programme.

It applies differently depending on how many people the buyer sends to the call

Enablement earns its keep fastest with multiple stakeholders and a real competitor in the room; a simple sale with no credible alternative leans on product knowledge far more than on battlecards.

It cannot tell you whether the deal was ever winnable

Perfect enablement only improves the odds of winning a winnable deal; it cannot rescue one where the product lacks a required capability. Treating every loss as an enablement failure, rather than a real gap, is its own mistake.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace: the same idea, different subjects

Product typeWho is "enabled"Primary artifact
ConsumerNo sales force; product self-serves the pitchApp-store copy, onboarding flow
B2B / enterpriseAccount executives, solutions engineersBattlecards, demo scripts
Marketplace — supply sideField reps signing up sellers, driversOnboarding pitch, payout scripts
Marketplace — demand sideAccount managers growing usageCategory battlecards

Consumer products mostly have no enablement function in this sense, because no human rep stands between product and buyer; the discipline collapses into marketing copy the product itself carries. B2B is where the classic version lives, because a single lost deal is large enough to justify a battlecard built for it. Marketplaces run two problems side by side: field reps recruiting supply, where objections are about payout timing, not features, and account managers growing demand-side usage, which looks more like conventional B2B enablement. Zanjeer's size can run enablement as two people inside product marketing; two hundred reps across a dozen lines needs a dedicated function.

7. Common mistakes

MistakeSymptomUnderlying errorCheapest diagnostic
Content dumpHundreds of slides nobody opensEnablement mistaken for volumePull last-accessed dates
Product-authored battlecardsObjections don't match what reps hear liveWritten from assumption, not evidenceCompare card to loss-call notes
One-time launchMessage quality decays within a quarterTreated as an event, not a systemQuiz reps six weeks later
Certification without embeddingCertified reps still miss it liveAnswer exists but isn't surfaced at needTime the rep's mid-call lookup

Each produces a distinct symptom before it produces a lost deal, which is what makes the diagnostics cheap. The costliest, and the one Zanjeer had committed without realising it, was the last: the multi-warehouse answer was written down somewhere, and the rep still froze, because nothing put it in front of her when Zila's operations director named the scenario.

8. What good looks like

Picture the same call at Zila handled well. The CRM record already flags the named competitor, surfacing the current battlecard without the rep having to remember it exists. The demo script has a two-minute branch built for the multi-warehouse transfer question, rehearsed in the last certification cycle, ending on a named reference client running that exact scenario at comparable scale. The rep does not improvise; she navigates to an answer prepared for this moment, and the confidence a buyer reads in that is itself part of the pitch. None of this required a better product — only someone who had already fought the objection once and made sure the answer reached her.

9. What Amanpreet decided, and two questions to sit with

Amanpreet did not rebuild Zanjeer's entire programme in eleven days. She rewrote the one battlecard that mattered, embedded it so it surfaced the moment a rep opened that competitor's name, and rehearsed the objection with the account executive twice. That narrower fix worked for the deal; the broader decision she took to the CRO was to extend certification to the remaining eight reps in Q3, on the strength of the pilot's gap, while flagging that some of it was likely the pilot's own selection effect rather than certification alone. What she resisted was reading the numbers as proof when they were only evidence.

The next thing worth learning is enablement for complex sales — multi-stakeholder deals with procurement committees, where one battlecard is not enough and material must be sequenced across many conversations. Two questions to sit with: when a win rate improves after a rollout, what would have to be true for the improvement to be about something other than enablement, and how would you tell the difference? Second: is there a battlecard that already exists but has never surfaced to a rep at the moment they needed it — and if so, is that a content problem or a plumbing problem?
exp20v2-pmm.pm.pmm.split:
Go-to-Market, Growth & Monetisation · Positioning, Messaging & Product Marketing

Dividing PM and PMM Responsibilities

Who owns pricing, launches and positioning between the product manager and the product marketer — and why the honest answer is "it depends which half of the sentence you're in."

1. A launch three weeks out, and two people who both think they own it

On the morning of 24 September 2026, Harikrishnan Pillai walked into a conference room at Hunar Skilling Cloud's office in Tiruchirappalli carrying two documents that did not agree. Hunar builds SkillMap, a competency-mapping and compliance-training platform used by 210 enterprise learning teams — mid-size IT services firms, bank back-office units, manufacturing skill academies — and had closed FY26 with ₹64 crore of annual recurring revenue. Hari, the VP of Product, had for six years done what most first product hires do: decided what got built, set the price, and announced it himself. In three weeks, on 14 October, Hunar would launch SkillGraph, an AI-assisted successor mapping a learner's competencies against role requirements — the most ambitious release the company had shipped.

The two documents were a pricing memo Hari had drafted, and a launch plan from Meenakshi Raghavan, hired in July as Hunar's first Head of Product Marketing. Meenakshi's plan named a target list of 800 net-new accounts and a positioning line calling SkillGraph "the AI layer for enterprise skilling," and disagreed with Hari's memo on the Enterprise tier's seat minimum. Neither document was wrong. But CEO Rukmini Balasubramanian had asked both of them that morning to jointly own the launch — and "jointly" was already doing unexamined work. The board expected meaningful new bookings this quarter; a muddled handoff could cost real revenue, or leave existing customers unsure whether SkillGraph was a bundled upgrade or a new purchase.

2. The idea: inbound work and outbound work, split on purpose

The product manager (PM) and the product marketing manager (PMM) split divides labour between the person who decides what a company builds, and the person who decides how the market learns about it and buys it. The shorthand Hari could say without sounding glib: PM works inbound, pulling signal from the market into product decisions; PMM works outbound, pushing the product's story out to the market. Pricing sits at the seam, because a price is a promise made outward about a decision made inward.

The split exists because a single "product person" — what most young companies have — cannot simultaneously listen to the market and speak persuasively to it without one job starving the other. The formal separation traces to enterprise software's growth through the 1990s, when vendors split "product management" from "product marketing management" as distinct families; the Pragmatic Institute's curriculum, running since 1993, was among the first to codify the shorthand, and April Dunford's 2019 writing on positioning later gave PMM a rigorous practice of its own. At the firms Meenakshi had worked at, the split was settled convention — Hunar's confusion was not whether it existed, but exactly where its seam ran through pricing.

3. The mechanics: a handoff, not a wall

In practice the split is a sequence of handoffs, not two departments fencing off territory, and most of the friction Hari and Meenakshi felt came from skipping steps. It runs in five moves. First, PM defines the target segment, drawing on telemetry from the 210 existing accounts and interviews with their learning heads. Second, PM proposes the pricing model — metric, tiers, seat minimums — but this is the step teams most often do alone when they shouldn't: pricing built without PMM's read on competitor rate cards tends to be internally coherent and externally naive. Third, PMM turns that model into positioning: the category SkillGraph competes in, the one differentiating claim, the words a salesperson uses in the first ninety seconds. Fourth, PMM builds the outbound machinery while PM closes gaps in documentation and support so the product can keep the promise PMM is about to make. Fifth, after launch, PM owns the roadmap response to signal from existing customers, PMM the response from prospects; win/loss analysis must be done jointly, needing both lenses at once.

Exhibit 3 — a working RACI for the SkillGraph launch
Decision areaPMPMM
Pricing model & packaging (metric, tiers, minimums)DecidesSupplies competitive input
Price communication (rate card, pricing page copy)Approves accuracyDecides
Launch readiness (docs, support, reliability)DecidesFlags external commitments
Launch narrative & sequencingReviews for accuracyDecides
Positioning statement & messagingSupplies functional truthDecides
Roadmap prioritisationDecidesSupplies market signal
Sales enablement (battlecards, demo script)Reviews for accuracyDecides
Win/loss analysisJointJoint

4. A worked example: what the split is actually worth in bookings

SkillGraph reached the market through two parallel motions, each with a different owner. The inbound, expansion motion belonged to Hari: of Hunar's 210 existing accounts, 92 crossed a usage threshold flagging them expansion-ready — 43.8% of the base — and 23 of those 92 converted to a paid pilot within the quarter, a 25.0% conversion. The outbound, new-logo motion belonged to Meenakshi: her team targeted 800 net-new accounts at IT services and BFSI-operations firms with 500-plus seats. Of those 800, 160 requested a demo (20.0%); of the demos, 64 became qualified opportunities (40.0%); of those, 16 closed won (25.0%) — an overall conversion of exactly 2.0%.

Both motions sold into the same three tiers — Starter at ₹499/learner/month with a 100-seat minimum, Growth at ₹399 with 500 seats, Enterprise at ₹299 with 2,000 seats — giving annual contract values of ₹5.99 lakh, ₹23.94 lakh and ₹71.76 lakh. Hari's 23 expansion deals landed smaller (15 Starter, 8 Growth); Meenakshi's 16 new-logo deals landed larger (6 Growth, 10 Enterprise). Summed by tier, the quarter's bookings came to ₹1,142.58 lakh — ₹11.43 crore — across 39 deals, an average contract value of about ₹29.3 lakh.

Now change one input. Meenakshi's positioning statement — tested on 40 prospects and rewritten twice — is what lifted demo-to-opportunity conversion to 40%; it is a live editorial decision, not a constant, and degrades when reps default to generic language under deadline pressure. Had that step converted at an ordinary 25%, holding the close rate at 25%, the 160 demos would have produced 40 opportunities and 10 new-logo wins instead of 16 — six fewer deals. At the blended new-logo contract value of ₹53.83 lakh, those six deals are worth roughly ₹3.23 crore, over a quarter of the quarter's bookings — more new money than either tier's price point.

5. The nuances a learner has to sit with

Pricing has one owner and two contributors

The pricing model — metric, tiers, minimums — belongs to PM. But the number on the page and the sentence that justifies it are PMM's craft. Treating pricing as wholly PM's territory, as Hari had been doing, starves the outward half of the decision.

The split is a discipline, not a headcount

A ten-person company has one person wearing both hats. The inbound/outbound distinction does not vanish for lack of a second title; it means noticing which hat is on when a question arrives.

PMM is not demand generation

The common confusion is treating product marketing as a lead-generating subset of marketing. PMM speaks to buyers about the product itself; demand generation chases volume and channel. A company can staff PMM inside marketing and keep this distinct, or inside product and lose it.

It tells you who decides, not what the answer is

Knowing PMM owns positioning does not produce a good statement; knowing PM owns pricing does not produce a defensible price. The split is an accountability map — a team can follow it and still ship a mediocre launch if the accountable person does mediocre work.

Where it stops applying

In a single-SKU consumer app with no sales team, there is often no "outbound" motion distinct from the product itself — onboarding does the job a launch narrative would do elsewhere. Forcing this split onto a team that small manufactures a coordination cost it doesn't need yet.

Questions worth asking before relying on the split

Who talks to the customer last before a deal closes, since that language is what reaches the buyer? Is anyone measured on win rate times contract value, the one number capturing both functions? When pricing changes, who hears first — engineering, sales, or the customer?

6. How the split shifts by product and by stage

The seam sits in a different place depending on what is sold and to whom. In a consumer subscription product, PM sets price off activation and retention curves, and "positioning" is folded into the product experience — there may be no PMM below a certain scale. In enterprise B2B, SkillGraph's shape, PM still sets the pricing model but leans on PMM's competitive intelligence, since the sale involves someone other than the end user. In a marketplace, pricing ripples across two sides at once — a change aimed at demand can starve supply — so pricing becomes a genuinely joint decision, and positioning must clear the supply side too. Stage matters as much as product type: at Hunar's size, the RACI in Exhibit 3 has exactly two names in it; at a five-hundred-person company, each row belongs to a specialised sub-team, and the handoff's coordination cost grows even as the underlying logic stays the same.

7. Common mistakes

The first mistake is the one Hari was mid-way through making: PM sets pricing without pulling PMM in until the memo is final. The symptom is a pricing page that reads well internally and confuses the first ten prospects; the misunderstanding is treating pricing as one decision rather than two — model and communication. The cheapest diagnostic: hand the memo to a salesperson who hasn't seen it and time how long they take to explain it back correctly; over a minute means PMM was not in the room early enough.

The second is letting PMM write positioning without a PM sign-off on accuracy. The symptom appears months later as support tickets from customers expecting a capability the launch narrative implied but the roadmap hadn't shipped. The diagnostic: read the launch copy against the feature list and mark every claim a customer could read as a promise.

The third is collapsing win/loss analysis into whichever function runs the retrospective. The symptom is a report that blames pricing for every loss (if PM runs it) or messaging (if PMM runs it). The diagnostic: check whether it cites both price sensitivity and the words the prospect used about a competitor's edge; missing either half means only one function wrote it.

8. What good looks like

A launch handled well looks, from outside, almost uneventful: the pricing page matches the sales deck, the deck matches what support was trained to answer, and no customer emails in confused about whom to complain to. Underneath, it means Hari and Meenakshi met before the pricing memo was final, not after; that the RACI in Exhibit 3 was referred to rather than re-litigated weekly. Good does not mean no disagreement — they still argued about the seat minimum for two more days — it means the disagreement happened inside a structure that told them whose call it was.

9. What Hari decided

Hari and Meenakshi left the meeting having agreed on the RACI in Exhibit 3, with one addition: Hari would finalise the pricing model, but no pricing decision would leave the room without Meenakshi's competitive read, and no positioning claim would leave without Hari's sign-off that the product could deliver on it. SkillGraph launched on 14 October 2026 with both signatures on the brief. What Hari needed to learn next was not another framework for splitting responsibility but the discipline of positioning itself, because the second pass had just shown him, in ₹3.23 crore, what a well-written sentence is worth. Two questions worth sitting with: who actually writes the words a prospect hears in the first ninety seconds — and does the person accountable for the roadmap know, this week, which funnel their next number is coming from?

ISB Product Management · Positioning, Messaging & Product Marketing

Chaupal Rasayan Exchange: The Seal and the Toll

A case on who owns pricing, launch and positioning when a compliance feature becomes a brand.

1. Sunday night, Gangapur Road

At eleven on the night of Sunday, 4 October 2026, Bhargavi Karandikar sat at the dining table of her flat off Gangapur Road in Nashik with three printouts and a slide rewritten nine times since Friday. The board of Chaupal Rasayan Exchange met at the Lower Parel office at eleven the next morning, and item four read, in Bipin Talwalkar's flat phrasing, Kasauti — launch plan, price, owner. Bhargavi, the Chief Product Officer, was to bring one of each.

She had two of each. On her left, a plan from Eknath Phadke in Mumbai treating Kasauti as a licensed quality seal that sellers would pay an annual fee to display, asking ₹350 lakh. On her right, a plan from Bageshree Nimkar in Nashik, treating Kasauti as a verification tier inside Chaupal Pro charged at ₹1,850 for every lot that cleared assay, asking ₹340 lakh. Against a board envelope of ₹4.20 crore for new monetisation in FY27, the two came to ₹690 lakh, or ₹6.90 crore — ₹2.70 crore too much.

The third printout had kept her at the table: a note from counsel, sent at 7.40 that evening, confirming that the 2023 master agreement with the excipient makers' consortium forbade "additional platform fees of any kind on listed lots" in pharmaceutical intermediates until 31 March 2028, and observing, without enthusiasm, that whether an annual brand-licence fee counted as a fee on a lot had never been tested. She had asked for it to settle an argument about pricing. It told her the argument was also about which of her two lieutenants could define what Kasauti was.

2. How Chaupal got here

Bipin Talwalkar founded Chaupal Rasayan Exchange in Nashik in 2017 after eleven years selling solvents for a Vapi trading house. His observation was mundane and correct: a paint formulator in Aurangabad buying twelve tonnes of a glycol ether a month did so over WhatsApp, at a price he could not benchmark, against a certificate of analysis often a scan of a scan. Chaupal began as a catalogue and a payments rail, matched orders by 2020, financed them by 2022, and moved hazardous goods under Petroleum and Explosives Safety Organisation rules by 2024.

In the year ended 31 March 2026 it connected some 2,400 selling entities to roughly 18,000 buying units and cleared gross merchandise value of ₹1,840 crore across six buyer industries. Net revenue, almost all commission, was ₹42.30 crore at a blended take rate of 2.30 per cent (Exhibit 1). A Series C of ₹248 crore closed in November 2024; ₹166 crore remained against a burn of ₹4.15 crore a month, or forty months of runway. The board expected Chaupal to earn from something other than commission by FY28.

One earlier decision shaped what Bhargavi could now do. In 2023, to break into pharmaceutical intermediates and excipients, Chaupal signed a five-year agreement with thirty-four excipient makers: the consortium got commission capped at 1.4 per cent and the no-additional-fees clause, Chaupal got the category. By FY26 pharma was ₹344 crore of GMV, the platform's third largest industry and the one whose buyers cared most about verified certificates. It was also the one category Chaupal could not charge a per-lot fee in.

3. The industry

Indian speciality chemicals in 2026 had more demand than documentation. Formulators — Asian Paints, Berger Paints, Kansai Nerolac, Pidilite, Godrej Consumer Products and several hundred smaller houses — were buying more grades from more suppliers under tighter specifications, largely because their own export customers demanded it. The Bureau of Indian Standards had brought a widening list of chemicals under mandatory certification through successive Quality Control Orders; the Directorate General of Foreign Trade had tightened export documentation; European consignments carried REACH obligations. The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation's expectations for excipient traceability were rising in parallel.

Competition came from three directions. Horizontal marketplaces — IndiaMART, Moglix, OfBusiness, Zetwerk — had scale, capital and no chemistry. Global distributors — Brenntag, IMCD, Azelis — had chemistry and a century of trust, but sold from their own book rather than running an exchange. Manufacturers such as Aarti Industries and Deepak Nitrite increasingly sold direct. None had made verification itself a product, and Eknath had argued since joining that the opening would close in eighteen months.

Chaupal's exposure sat in one relationship. Rukn Speciality Trading FZE, a Jebel Ali distributor re-exporting Indian resins and coatings intermediates across the Gulf and East Africa, bought ₹212 crore through the platform in FY26 — 11.5 per cent of GMV, and Chaupal's largest single buyer. In April 2026 its procurement head wrote that from 1 January 2027 his firm would order only against lots carrying a third-party-verified certificate. He did not say what he would do otherwise. He did not have to.

4. The situation in detail

Eknath Phadke joined in March 2025 as Chaupal's first Head of Product Marketing, hired out of a speciality chemicals manufacturer. Bipin's welcome email defined the boundary in a line: Eknath owns how the market hears us; Bhargavi owns what we build. Nobody noticed that price is both.

In June 2025 Eknath presented a category narrative — "trust is the missing molecule" — at India Chem, and it changed what buyers asked the sales team for. In September 2025 Bageshree's team shipped certificate-of-analysis upload, which everyone believed closed the gap; between October 2025 and March 2026 sellers uploaded 26,400 certificates. An April audit found that 18,744 of the 26,400 — 71 per cent — were seller-typed documents with no accredited laboratory signature. The feature had industrialised the problem, not solved it.

In June 2026 Bipin approved a pilot of what Eknath had already named Kasauti, after the touchstone used to test the purity of gold. The approval named a budget and a date, no owner. Bageshree's team began laboratory integrations; Eknath's began a seal, a trademark filing and a campaign. For six weeks neither told the other, because neither believed the other's work was the product.

The pilot ran from 1 August to 30 September 2026 across four laboratories accredited by the National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories. Its funnel is Exhibit 2: 1,200 sellers invited, 312 enrolled, 1,584 lots submitted, 1,338 cleared after one re-test, ₹45.22 crore of orders citing a cleared lot.

Two things were absent from Eknath's slide. Enrolment had been bought: every enrolling seller received a ₹25,000 onboarding credit against future commission, ₹78.00 lakh across the 312. And from 12 September the pilot carried a price experiment Esha Dabholkar ran at Bageshree's request, in which a randomly chosen half of the 198 submitting sellers saw a banner quoting ₹1,850 per cleared lot. Eknath learnt of it on 26 September from an Ankleshwar seller ringing to ask whether the price was real; his own willingness-to-pay survey had reported four days earlier. The two are Exhibit 4, and side by side they appear to contradict each other flatly.

What turned out wrong is not only the reading of demand. Bageshree priced per cleared lot; the laboratories bill per test. The pilot consumed 2,028 tests at ₹1,420 each, ₹28.80 lakh, against ₹24.75 lakh the per-lot fee would have billed — a loss of ₹4.05 lakh before a rupee of credits (Exhibit 3). Break-even on her own unit is about ₹2,152 per cleared lot, a figure she first saw on 29 September.
