Dividing PM and PMM Responsibilities

Inbound and outbound work, and the three decisions — pricing, launches, positioning — where the line between product manager and product marketer is drawn differently by people each of whom is, in their own terms, right.

1. Two rooms in Guwahati, one week apart

On Saturday 12 September 2026, Jyotirmoy Mahapatra spread three pages of a pricing memo across a table at Jeevanrekha Diagnostics Cloud, in the Bhangagarh quarter of Guwahati. Jeevanrekha sells laboratory information software to diagnostic chains and hospital labs: 186 customers in 19 states, 4.1 crore test reports in FY26, ₹52.8 crore of annual recurring revenue. Sixty-four of those 186 customers hold NABH accreditation, 34.4 per cent of the base, and their critical-value reporting duties suggested the next product. On 5 November, Jeevanrekha would launch Nirnay, a module that reads an incoming result set, ranks it against reference ranges and prior results, and pushes the dangerous ones to the top of a pathologist's queue.

Jyotirmoy, Jeevanrekha's first product hire and now Director of Product, had for seven years decided what got built, set the price, written the launch email and briefed the sales team himself. The memo priced Nirnay per report, in three tiers, and was on its own terms careful. The complication had joined in August: Jhumpa Bhattacharya, hired from a Delhi hospital-information-systems vendor as the company's first Head of Product Marketing, who had read the memo and replied that the tier floors made Jeevanrekha's most promising pilot impossible to sell. CEO Bhaskar Senapati wanted one document, not two.

Eleven kilometres away, Bhaswati Kanungo was arguing the same seam from the other side. Bhaswati was Head of Product Marketing at Bimba Imaging Systems, which sells an on-premises appliance — Drishti — that pre-reads chest radiographs and ranks the reporting queue. Bimba is not a SaaS company: each of its 41 live sites pays ₹14.60 lakh once for the appliance and ₹3.60 lakh a year for the software — ₹147.60 lakh of software revenue across the estate. In the twelve months to September 2026 it had shipped nine new sites — ₹131.40 lakh of hardware and ₹32.40 lakh of first-year software, ₹163.80 lakh in all. Five stopped their rollout in July over a sentence Bhaswati had written, which her PM counterpart Jishnu Behera approved without reading closely, and which five radiology heads read as a claim that Drishti would replace a human read. Her question to CEO Bandana Mohanty was not who had erred but which of them was supposed to have caught it.

2. The idea, and the three schools that disagree about it

The split allocates two kinds of work. Inbound work converts market signal into product decisions: what to build, for whom, in what order, on what pricing metric. Outbound work converts the product into something the market can understand, want and buy: its category, the words for it, the rate card, the launch, the material a salesperson carries. Convention gives inbound to the PM and outbound to the PMM. The three decisions named in every argument about this — pricing, launches, positioning — refuse to sit on one side, because each holds an inbound and an outbound half easily mistaken for one decision.

The vocabulary is older than the industry's current shape. Enterprise vendors in the 1980s and 1990s ran product management and product marketing management as separate job families, and the Pragmatic Institute's curriculum, taught since 1993, codified the inbound/outbound language most practitioners now use without attribution. The problem it solved was a staffing pathology: one owner asked both to listen to the market and to speak persuasively to it starves whichever job has no deadline. April Dunford's 2019 work gave the outbound half a method of its own, and the marketing-rooted programmes — Kellogg, NUS, Cornell Johnson's Strategic Product Marketing — teach positioning statements and messaging hierarchies as first-class artefacts, not records of a decision taken elsewhere.

Three schools disagree, and it is worth stating what each would and would not sign. The Pragmatic school signs: outbound is a distinct competence with its own inputs — win/loss interviews, rival rate cards, buyer language — and a company that leaves it to the PM gets it done badly and late. It would not sign that positioning may constrain the roadmap; the story follows the product. The product-led school signs: the PM is accountable for the business outcome, so pricing, launch readiness and the truth of every external claim are the PM's, and PMM is a specialist service executing the story. It would not sign that a product marketer may hold a decision the PM can be fired for. The marketing-rooted school signs the strongest claim: positioning precedes the product, because the chosen category fixes which features are table stakes, so its owner holds a veto over the roadmap. It would not sign that positioning is a deliverable produced after the build.

Jyotirmoy held the product-led position, Jhumpa the marketing-rooted one; nothing in their disagreement was about competence.

3. Mechanics: the six rungs and the arithmetic underneath them

Practitioners who handle this well think not in two boxes but in a ladder of six decisions descending from the market to the words a representative says, ownership changing hands once — the discipline being to locate that change precisely.

The step teams leave implicit is the return path drawn dashed in Exhibit 2. Rungs 1 to 3 are inbound and rungs 4 to 6 outbound, but rung 4 routinely finds a defect fixable only at rung 3, and unless the return path is standing rather than an escalation, the PMM either swallows the defect or is cast as obstructive. That was Jhumpa's objection: standing on rung 4, she found that Jeevanrekha's own floors priced a pilot at nearly half a full deployment.

There is a formal treatment, worth working rather than naming: new revenue decomposes as a base times a chain of compounding stage rates times a blended contract value. Jeevanrekha ran two motions through it. Expansion was Jyotirmoy's: of the 186 customers, 74 crossed the usage rule making them Nirnay-eligible — 39.8 per cent of the base — and in the first 90 days 29 of those 74 bought, a conversion of 39.2 per cent. New logos were Jhumpa's: 640 ICP-scored target labs, 160 first meetings, 56 evaluations, 14 closed-won, an end-to-end conversion of 2.2 per cent.

The formula's value is that it says which factor each role controls, and so what each competence is worth in rupees. Exhibit 5 moves each rate five percentage points, priced at the blended contract value of its own motion.

Three second-order effects follow, each a place where the split stops being administrative. The metric chosen at rung 2 decides who signs: per-seat pricing puts a lab manager in the room, per-report pricing a finance controller who needs a different first ninety seconds — a metric is a positioning decision wearing a spreadsheet. A published rate card then constrains the roadmap, because every later feature must be assigned to a tier, and tiers ossify: Jeevanrekha's three will still shape build decisions in 2029. And readiness and narrative are coupled through support load — Jhumpa's 160 meetings generated documentation questions that landed on Jyotirmoy's team, so an outbound success is an inbound cost nobody budgets.

4. When the split applies, and when it misleads

Three conditions can be stated as testable claims. First: the split pays when buyer and user differ. Jeevanrekha passes — a pathologist uses Nirnay, a chain COO buys it, and the language that persuades one repels the other. Bimba passes more sharply, because the radiology head who must consent is neither buyer nor user. Second: it pays when the story must be carried by someone other than its builders. Jeevanrekha passes: 43 deals in 90 days through eleven salespeople, none of whom can read the code. Third: it pays when outbound work has a deadline and inbound work does not. Both pass, and this is the condition that forces the hire; Jyotirmoy's roadmap had slipped four times in two years because launch weeks ate it.

It actively misleads in two situations. One is the single-SKU, self-serve product with no sales conversation, where the experience is the positioning and an outbound owner only inserts a translation layer between it and a market reading it directly. The other is less recognised: the company where the PM is the only person able to evaluate a clinical claim. Bhaswati could not have caught her own sentence, because "so your radiologist doesn't have to" is wrong only if you know how a second read works. There, a RACI assigning positioning to PMM with PM signing for accuracy divides liability rather than labour, and fails whenever the signature is procedural.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product. Jeevanrekha sells four modules on one platform. A per-module PMM optimises each launch and nobody owns the sentence describing the whole; one platform PMM owns that sentence and starves three launches. Mature companies split the artefact, not the role: module messaging sits with whoever runs the module, the platform's category claim with one named person, reconciled quarterly by a review empowered to overrule a launch.

Two-sided. A platform that also routes referrals from clinics to labs prices two sides at once: a fee cut taken from the lab is a discount offered to the clinic, and a line aimed at clinics can frighten the labs whose volume the model needs. Pricing becomes genuinely joint, because no one owner sees both sides' willingness to pay. Platforms that handle it well make a pricing committee the decision body and have every message to one side read by whoever owns the other.

Regulated. In Indian healthcare software the outbound half carries legal weight the inbound half does not. "Meets NABH critical-value requirements" is a compliance representation; "clinically validated" invites questions about the study behind it. The mature pattern gives PMM the claim and PM the evidence file, mapping every claim to a row in it: the PM signs for evidence, not wording.

Hardware plus software. Bimba's split is distorted by the cash cycle. The appliance is recognised on shipment and the software annually, so the sales incentive points at the ₹14.60 lakh rather than the ₹3.60 lakh, and the narrative the channel uses is whichever closes hardware. A PMM whose messaging the channel does not carry has authored fiction — the failure that paused five sites.

AI-native. When behaviour changes between releases, a claim decays. Nirnay's triage precision moves on each retrain, so a sentence accurate in November may be indefensible by March with nobody having edited it. Only a standing re-test holds: the claim is an artefact with an owner, a version and an expiry.

At the organisational seam, mature companies say PMM reports into marketing and partners with product. What they do is quieter: the PMM's objectives are written half by the marketing leader and half by the product leader, and the tie-break on any claim sits with whoever would be called before a regulator. Left unstated, it makes the split decorative.

6. Eight nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Pricing has one owner and two authors. The competent practitioner learns that PM owns pricing and stops. The expert sees the model and its presentation as separate decisions with separate failure modes: a model can be right while the rate card destroys the pipeline. The sign: a pricing page that survives internal review unchanged, then draws the same three questions from the first ten prospects it meets.

A pricing metric is a positioning choice. The obvious reading is that it follows the cost structure. The expert reads it back from the buyer: the metric decides whose budget line the product lands on, and so who must be persuaded. The sign: a sales cycle that lengthens by weeks after a metric change, at an unchanged price.

The handoff needs a return path, not a review. Competent teams add a review gate after the pricing memo; experts add a standing right to send a rung-3 decision back, because the defect is structural and a review catches only wording. The sign: a PMM raising structural objections in writing after the decision — a blocked return path seen from outside.

Sign-off on accuracy is worthless unless specific. "Approved" means nothing; "every claim here maps to a row in the evidence file" means something. The obvious reading is that the PM's signature transfers risk. It does not — Jishnu's sat on a document he had skimmed. The sign: a sign-off with no marked-up copy attached.

Outbound success is an inbound cost. The competent practitioner celebrates 160 first meetings; the expert budgets for them. A launch that hits pipeline while blowing the roadmap has moved a cost, not removed one. The sign: a support queue that spikes two weeks after launch and never returns to its floor.

The split is a discipline, not a headcount. A twelve-person company has one person in both hats, and the distinction does not vanish for want of a second title; it becomes a question of which hat is on. The sign: a solo owner who can say which job they are neglecting this week.

Product marketing is not demand generation. The common collapse treats PMM as a lead-volume function. PMM speaks to a buyer about the product; demand generation buys attention through channels. A company can house PMM in marketing and keep the distinction, or in product and lose it. The sign: a PMM whose only metric is lead volume.

The map says who decides, not what to decide. Knowing PMM owns positioning produces no good positioning. The expert settles the map, then argues substance inside it. The most diagnostic sign of the eight: a team that has agreed its RACI and still argues, productively, about a tier floor.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

In consumer subscription products the seam nearly vanishes: price is set off activation and retention curves, positioning lives in onboarding, and below a certain scale there is no PMM. In B2B mid-market — Jeevanrekha's shape — the seam is where this page puts it, because a sales team must carry words it did not write. In enterprise, add procurement, which reads the rate card adversarially, extending PMM's remit into the deal desk. In platforms the change is structural: a price aimed at one side reprices the other, so pricing is joint. In hardware the channel owns the last mile, and PMM's authority is only as strong as its enablement. In AI products the difference is Exhibit 6's decay loop, not a new division of labour. By stage: at ₹52.8 crore the map has two names on it; at ten times that, each row of Exhibit 1 is a sub-team, the logic unchanged and the coordination cost larger.

8. Three worked examples

Nirnay: the split working, and what it was worth

Jeevanrekha's 90 days produced 43 deals and ₹242.76 lakh of new ARR. The split's measurable contribution was at rung 4: Jhumpa's tested framing lifted meeting-to-evaluation conversion to 35 per cent, and her pilot path unblocked the Tier C accounts. Had Jyotirmoy written both halves, as in the previous three launches, the two outbound levers of Exhibit 5 are the ones that would have gone unpulled — ₹35.20 lakh, against the ₹2.91 lakh his price rise would have netted.

Drishti: the split failing, and the recovery

Bimba's nine new sites contracted ₹163.80 lakh. In July, five paused. Bimba issued six-month service credits of ₹1.80 lakh per site, ₹9.00 lakh in all; one of the five never resumed and its ₹3.60 lakh of software ARR was lost. Total impact: ₹12.60 lakh, 7.7 per cent of the nine sites' contracted value — survivable, and far smaller than the fourteen weeks of engineering and clinical-affairs time the recovery consumed. The cause was a RACI that gave Bhaswati the claim and Jishnu the accuracy check without defining what the check consisted of. The recovery defined it: the claim became "pre-read triage that ranks the reporting queue and never issues a report", Jishnu built an audit trail showing every study a radiologist had opened, and no claim now ships without a clinician's countersignature. Four sites resumed by November.

Jauhara: the seam under a different regulator

Jauhara Medical Group LLC, of Sharjah, runs 11 labs and 6 hospitals producing 46 lakh reports a year — ₹41.40 lakh at Tier C. Its CIO, Bilal Al Mazrouei, wanted a three-lab pilot covering 12 lakh reports, which the ladder prices at Tier B: ₹19.20 lakh, 46 per cent of the group's full price for a quarter of its volume. Two things had to change and only one was Jhumpa's: the ladder needed a pilot path, and the claim needed translating for a regulator that is not NABH. They settled on a 90-day evaluation at ₹4.50 lakh credited against the first annual contract — a rung-3 amendment, made by the PM, that existed only because someone on rung 4 asked for it.

9. Failure modes, with their early warnings

Pricing decided before PMM is in the room. Warning: the first draft of the rate card is the memo reformatted. Diagnostic: hand the memo to a salesperson who has not seen it and time how long they take to explain it back correctly — over a minute means the outbound owner was not there early enough. Jhumpa timed eleven reps: a median of two minutes forty seconds before the memo was revised, fifty-five after. Cost late: a repricing in quarter two, which reads as a company that does not know its worth.

Positioning shipped without an accuracy audit. Warning: sign-off arrives as a one-word reply. Diagnostic: read the launch copy against the feature list, marking every sentence a customer could read as a promise. Cost late: ₹12.60 lakh and fourteen weeks.

Win/loss owned by whoever runs the retrospective. Warning: a loss report attributing everything to price, or everything to messaging. Diagnostic: does it cite both price sensitivity and the prospect's own words about a rival? Cost late: two quarters of roadmap on the wrong half of the problem.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does positioning constrain the roadmap, or follow it? The marketing-rooted position is that a category choice fixes which capabilities are table stakes, so positioning precedes the build and its owner holds a veto; the evidence is the long list of products excellent in a category nobody was shopping in. The product-led position is that claims about future demand are unfalsifiable and the roadmap should answer to observed usage; the evidence is the equally long list of category-defining launches with no users. For the first to be wrong you would need products that, repositioned without changing, captured the market they had missed — and those exist.

Who owns price level? One camp holds price is a product decision because it encodes the value model; the other that it is a market decision because willingness to pay is observable only outbound. Both agree PM owns the metric. The argument is about the number, and it would be settled if pricing experiments were cheap in enterprise software — a price tested on ten prospects is a price leaked.

Product or marketing? Into product, because proximity to the build keeps claims true; into marketing, because a PMM inside product is captured by the roadmap's optimism. Both work when the tie-break on claims is written down and both fail when it is not — so the reporting line is not the variable that matters, a conclusion neither camp finds satisfying.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this can recite the RACI. Someone who has internalised it does three things differently. They locate the seam before the argument starts, asking which rung a disagreement lives on rather than who is in charge. They insist every claim carry an owner, a date and an evidence reference, having seen a true sentence become false unedited. And they treat the map as settled so the substance can be fought over — a healthy split is marked not by the absence of disagreement but by disagreement about the right thing.

12. What each of them decided

Jyotirmoy took the memo back. The three tiers and the per-report metric survived; the floors did not. On 30 September he added a 90-day evaluation SKU at ₹4.50 lakh, creditable in full, and wrote into the brief that no pricing decision would leave the room without Jhumpa's competitive read and no claim without his signature against a named evidence row. Nirnay launched on 5 November and closed ₹2.43 crore in 90 days. The two are still arguing about whether Tier C's floor should exist.

Bhaswati's answer to Bandana Mohanty was that neither of them had failed and the arrangement had. At Bimba the claim would stay hers, the evidence file Jishnu's, a clinician's countersignature mandatory — and the channel would be trained on the corrected sentence before any site went live, because at Bimba the message is delivered by people neither of them employs.

Discussion question 1. Jeevanrekha's outbound levers were worth roughly twelve times its price lever. At what size does that ratio invert, and what would Jyotirmoy have to measure to know it had?

Discussion question 2. Bimba's sign-off was procedural. Is "PM signs for accuracy" defensible in a regulated category, or does it place liability where the expertise is not?

Discussion question 3. If the reporting line for product marketing does not predict outcomes, what does — and what would you write down first at a company making its first PMM hire?

13. Going deeper

Working with product marketing is the prerequisite this page formalises: the split is the contract, that topic the relationship it governs. Writing a positioning statement is where rung 5 becomes a craft question — the highest-leverage skill Exhibit 5 identifies. Messaging hierarchy derives everything below one approved claim, which keeps the section 9 audit from being an argument about taste. Naming products and features matters because a name is the most durable positioning decision you make: Nirnay will outlive its rate card. Brand fundamentals for PMs explains why a claim in one module constrains another, and category design is the marketing-rooted school's sharpest test of its own veto claim. Sales enablement is rung 6, where every earlier decision either survives contact with a human being or does not.

Kalash Jal Systems: Who Signs the Nagpur Bid?

A teaching case on dividing PM and PMM responsibility for pricing, launch and positioning.

1. Tuesday morning, Vidyanagar

At a little past nine on the morning of 15 September 2026, Yashaswini Rao, Vice President of Product at Kalash Jal Systems, opened two email attachments side by side on her laptop in the company's Vidyanagar office in Hubballi. Both were draft pricing sheets for the same tender: the Nagpur Municipal Corporation's smart water-billing modernisation contract, closing on the state e-procurement portal at 5 p.m. on 22 September, a week away. One sheet came from Hitesh Shetty, the senior product manager who had built the company's newest module. The other came from Hamsa Hebbar, the company's first dedicated head of product marketing, hired four months earlier. The two sheets quoted different prices for the same feature under different names, prepared without either author knowing the other was doing the same work. Yashaswini had one week to decide which number went to Nagpur, and who got to make that call next time.

2. Company background

Kalash Jal Systems was founded in Hubballi in 2015 by Yashwant Bhat, a water-engineering graduate who had spent six years installing bulk flow meters for the Hubballi-Dharwad Municipal Corporation before deciding the harder problem was the billing software behind the meter. The company began by retrofitting ultrasonic smart meters, then built a cloud platform, AquaSetu, that turned meter readings into consumption data, generated bills, tracked collections, and gave commissioners a dashboard for non-revenue accounting. Funding cycles under the Ministry of Jal Shakti's AMRUT 2.0 scheme and the Smart Cities Mission had pushed municipal corporations to digitise metering and billing, and Kalash Jal Systems competed against metering majors such as Genus Power Infrastructures, Secure Meters and L&T Smart World, none of whom had built billing software as usable as AquaSetu's. By September 2026, AquaSetu was live in 58 municipal corporations across ten states, including the Pune Municipal Corporation and two zones of the Delhi Jal Board, billing 31,50,000 metered connections. At the standard fee of ₹40 per connection per year, this base produced a core annual recurring revenue of ₹12.60 crore (Exhibit 1). A Series B round earlier in 2026 had been raised to chase larger, RFP-driven tenders of the kind Nagpur represented, rather than the smaller direct-sale deals that had built the company.

3. The situation

The product at issue had grown out of customer requests, not a roadmap decision. Municipal engineers kept asking whether AquaSetu's meter data could also flag where treated water was being lost between the pumping station and the customer's tap — non-revenue water, a chronic problem for every Indian municipal utility. Hitesh's team built an analytics layer using existing meter readings to flag likely leakage zones, piloted for six months with seven municipal corporations covering 2,80,000 connections at a discounted fee of ₹9 per connection, producing ₹25.2 lakh of pilot revenue for that half-year (Exhibit 1). Hitesh regarded the module as a natural extension of AquaSetu's billing engine, to be priced to maximise adoption. Hamsa, brought in to sharpen how the company competed for large tenders, had run a competitive teardown showing standalone non-revenue-water analytics vendors charged ₹15–20 per connection per year for materially the same insight, and argued the module deserved its own brand, "NeerDrishti," priced at market rate rather than at Hitesh's marginal cost of delivering it. Neither had briefed Yogesh Gowda, the national sales head who now had to submit one figure, not two, by 22 September. Yogesh had also just re-read the tender document closely enough to notice what both drafts had missed: a hard ceiling of ₹52 per connection per year for the combined offering, above which a bid would be disqualified outright, with no negotiation.

4. The people

NameRole & locationWhat they want
Yashaswini RaoVP of Product, HubballiOne defensible number for Nagpur by 22 September, and a rule that stops this fight recurring every quarter.
Hitesh ShettySenior Product Manager, NRW analytics, HubballiWants the module priced to win adoption and this tender; sees pricing as a product-cost decision.
Hamsa HebbarHead of Product Marketing, PuneWants NeerDrishti positioned and priced at market rate as a distinct, premium line the company can point to in every future bid.
Yogesh GowdaNational Sales Head, MumbaiNeeds one compliant number before the portal closes; cares most about not being disqualified.

Yashwant Bhat, the founder, had told Yashaswini he trusted her to decide and would not referee it himself — a signal that whatever she chose would set precedent well beyond Nagpur.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 — Kalash Jal Systems and AquaSetu, September 2026

Core ARR = 31,50,000 × ₹40 = ₹12,60,00,000 (₹12.60 crore). Pilot revenue = 2,80,000 × ₹9 = ₹25,20,000 for the six-month pilot only; not annualised, and not part of core ARR above.

Exhibit 1 shows why the disagreement outlasted one tender: Hitesh's module already earned modest revenue at a fraction of what Hamsa's teardown said the market would bear, and the company had never decided which fact should govern pricing.

Exhibit 2 — The two Nagpur bids against the published ceiling (4,20,000 connections)

Ceiling total = 4,20,000 × ₹52 = ₹218.4 lakh. Hitesh's bid: 4,20,000 × ₹45 = ₹189.0 lakh, ₹29.4 lakh below ceiling. Hamsa's bid: 4,20,000 × ₹57 = ₹239.4 lakh, ₹21.0 lakh above ceiling. Connection-level figures are in ₹; totals in ₹ lakh throughout.

Exhibit 2 is why Yogesh escalated rather than picking one: Hamsa's bid would be disqualified on financial grounds before an evaluator read it, while Hitesh's bid was compliant but gave away, at no extra price, exactly the capability Hamsa wanted the market to see as premium.

Exhibit 3 — the decision week. Yashaswini's call has to reach Yogesh with enough time to assemble the rest of the tender package before 22 September.

6. The options

  1. Back Hitesh's bundled price, and make pricing a product-owned decision going forward. AquaSetu bids at ₹45 per connection, comfortably under the ceiling with ₹29.4 lakh of headroom (Exhibit 2), giving Yogesh a clean, compliant number and folding NRW analytics permanently into the core platform. The cost: Kalash Jal Systems gives away its most differentiated capability free to every large account from now on, and signals that product marketing's pricing judgment carries no weight against an engineer's cost model.
  2. Back Hamsa's unbundled, market-priced NeerDrishti brand, and bid it anyway. This protects Hamsa's positioning work and the company's ability to charge what dedicated NRW vendors already charge. But Exhibit 2 shows the resulting ₹57 price is ₹21.0 lakh above the ceiling; e-procurement rules disqualify bids above ceiling with no route to negotiate afterward, so this option most likely forfeits the tender entirely.
  3. Split the decision along the line the module's history already suggests, and codify it. For Nagpur, bid Hitesh's compliant ₹45 bundled price — a procurement ceiling is a fact, not a negotiating position. But direct Hamsa to keep the NeerDrishti name and go-to-market plan alive for the 31,50,000 connections already on AquaSetu, and for future tenders with no fixed ceiling. The cost is that Hamsa's Nagpur pricing is set aside this once; the gain is a standing rule — product owns pricing architecture on a constrained deal, marketing owns brand and premium upsell on the base — neither has to relitigate next time.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What, precisely, are Hitesh and Hamsa disagreeing about — the price, the module's name, or who has standing to decide either?
  2. Using Exhibit 2, which draft could Yogesh actually submit to Nagpur without risking disqualification, and does that alone settle the question for this tender?
  3. If Yashaswini sets aside Hamsa's pricing for Nagpur, what should she do in the same conversation to avoid signalling that her judgment does not count?
  4. As Kalash Jal Systems shifts to large, RFP-driven tenders, how should pricing, launch timing and positioning be divided between product and product marketing, and should that division be the same for every deal?

8. A note for the learner

This case is best read through a simple distinction. Pricing architecture — what a module costs to deliver, what floor a business can accept, and how a procurement ceiling binds a live negotiation — is inbound work, closest to the product manager who owns the module's economics. Pricing-to-market — what a segment will pay for a differentiated capability, how it is named and positioned against competitors over future deals — is outbound work, closest to product marketing. The recurring student error is to treat "who owns pricing" as one question with one owner; Exhibit 2 shows it is two questions that collided on one tender.

A well-reasoned answer does three things. First, it treats Nagpur's ₹52 ceiling as a hard constraint, not a negotiable data point — Hamsa's ₹57 bid, however well researched, is not admissible here. Second, it does not let that settle the larger question: the same week that requires Hitesh's number also shows Kalash Jal Systems has never priced NeerDrishti at what the market, per Hamsa's teardown, will bear on ceiling-free deals. Third, it recommends a structural fix, not a one-off pick: Option 3 is defensible because it resolves the deadline on the only compliant number, while preserving Hamsa's brand and premium-pricing work for the base and future ceiling-free tenders. This turns a one-time argument into a standing rule — product owns pricing architecture under deal constraints; product marketing owns positioning and premium go-to-market — so the next tender does not require Yashaswini to referee the same fight again.

Vachan Retail Systems: What the Page Should Say Before Dhanteras

Amravati, Maharashtra · Sunday, 27 September 2026

1. The night before

By nine o'clock on Sunday, 27 September 2026, the Rajkamal Chowk end of Amravati had gone quiet, and Gauri Wankhade was still in the first-floor office of Vachan Retail Systems with three printouts on the table. Each was a version of the same web page with a different sentence at the top. On Monday evening she had to tell a board call which sentence Vachan would spend the Diwali season behind; on Wednesday, 30 September, the cancellation window on its marketing retainer closed for the year.

Gauri had been product marketing lead for nineteen months, promoted out of implementation, where she had spent two years teaching counter staff to stop writing scheme instalments in a register. The first printout said what Vachan had always said about itself; the second, what its customers had been forced to care about since 2023; the third, what they talked about at the counter — and that was the one the company's own lawyer had asked her, on Friday, to take down.

2. How Vachan got here

Vachan Retail Systems was founded in Amravati in 2019 by Madhav Gawande, who had sold billing counters to Vidarbha's family jewellers for eleven years, and Mrunal Tayade, who wrote the first version in Madhav's showroom. The software priced a sale against the morning's gold rate, applied making charges and GST, recorded the six-digit HUID of every hallmarked piece sold, and valued old gold taken in exchange after deducting for purity.

By September 2026 Vachan had 940 stores, almost all single- or two-shop family firms in Maharashtra and eastern Madhya Pradesh. The base licence listed at ₹3,500 a month, or ₹42,000 a year. The scheme module — which runs the eleven-month instalment plans family jewellers have offered for generations, collecting through UPI AutoPay mandates rather than cash — was an add-on at ₹2,500 a month, or ₹30,000 a year, and 355 of 940 stores took it (37.8 per cent). Annual recurring revenue stood at ₹438.13 lakh, of which the add-on contributed ₹106.50 lakh, or 24.3 per cent.

One decision from 2023 shaped what Gauri could now do. That February, Madhav signed a three-year agreement with the Vidarbha Saraf Sangh, the region's largest jewellers' association: members got the licence at ₹2,100 a month, the Sangh listed Vachan on its Marathi member microsite, and Vachan carried the Sangh's endorsement on its home page. It brought 310 stores in eighteen months and was renewed in February 2026 to 31 March 2027; by September, 376 of the 940 stores paid the member rate (40 per cent). Clause nine also barred Vachan from offering any module to non-members below what members paid: drafted to stop undercutting, it now meant the scheme module could not be a free hook until April 2027.

3. The industry

Organised jewellery retail had been consolidating around national chains — Tanishq, Kalyan Jewellers, Malabar Gold & Diamonds — each running systems built for itself, none a plausible Vachan customer. Below them sat tens of thousands of family sarafs, whose software decade was forced on them by rules rather than ambition. BIS hallmarking with a six-digit HUID became compulsory for sales of hallmarked gold jewellery from 1 April 2023 in notified districts, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 bound every store holding a customer's KYC copy.

Instalment schemes were the delicate part. A jeweller's scheme takes money in advance against goods and lives inside a narrow exemption: schemes are kept to eleven months, and the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules and the Banning of Unregulated Deposit Schemes Act, 2019 stand behind anything that begins to look like a deposit. The trade's custom of paying the last instalment for a customer who completes ten is advertised in every shop window and described in the trade press as a discount, not a return. Vishwaas Scheme Cloud, a small Akola firm, wound down in 2024 after rewriting its marketing around "assured monthly growth" and drawing a notice.

Vachan's only real competitor was Wafadaar Gold Systems of Akola, founded 2022, scheme-first to market: its whole home page was instalment plans, its billing thin, its price below Vachan's. Accounting packages such as Tally sat on the other flank, blind to HUID. Abroad, Manoj Bhuskade, hired in 2025 to sell to diaspora jewellers, had a proposal with Vraj Jewels Group, a nine-store chain in Edison, New Jersey, which wanted billing and HUID records and no scheme feature at all.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

In February 2026 Vachan raised ₹6.20 crore from Warud Capital Partners, whose covenant requires ARR of ₹6.00 crore by 30 June 2027 — ₹1.62 crore more than it had, a rise of 37 per cent.

On Monday, 16 February 2026, Vachan engaged Wazir Media Works, an Amravati performance agency, on ₹2.80 lakh a month, and tripled paid search. The belief then was that the funnel was starved of traffic, and Exhibit 1, Wazir's dashboard for the quarter ended 30 September, supports it: 48,800 sessions and 1,356 demo requests. It lasted until Gitanjali Kubade, in Singapore, reconciled that dashboard against the customer record. Only 812 of the 1,356 (59.9 per cent) existed in the CRM as a named store with a telephone number (Exhibit 4); the missing 544 were mostly taps on the WhatsApp button, counted as requests by Wazir's tag.

The second belief was about the headline. From Monday, 2 March to Sunday, 24 May, Wazir and Falguni Dhande, Vachan's designer in Berlin, ran a twelve-week, three-arm test on paid-search and YouTube traffic: the billing-led line, a compliance-led line on HUID reconciliation, and a scheme-led line on the instalment ledger (Exhibit 2). The scheme-led line took the enquiry rate from 1.6 per cent to 3.5 per cent, a lift of 118.8 per cent, and by mid-June the office had stopped arguing. The rollout waited on the ninety-day read, and the live page went back to the incumbent line.

On Thursday, 17 September, Zoya Ingole, Vachan's data scientist in Toronto, circulated Exhibit 3, which followed those 657 enquiries for ninety days each, the last of them closing on 22 August. The ranking inverted. Arm S's enquiries became demos far less often — 170 of the 315 (54.0 per cent) against 101 of the 144 (70.1 per cent) for the control — and produced 27 paying stores against arm H's 34; only 21 of its 27 were still paying at day 90 (77.8 per cent). Yet it booked the most revenue, ₹18.54 lakh, because 24 of the 27 took the add-on (88.9 per cent) against 9 of the 34 in arm H (26.5 per cent).

Two other beliefs had failed. Paid search, the engine in April, cost ₹68,571 per store won that quarter against ₹2,500 through referrals (Exhibit 5); and the add-on sold since 2024 as minor was now a quarter of revenue.

5. The people

Gauri Wankhade — Product Marketing Lead, Amravati. Owns the page and the recommendation, and thinks it has not described the company since 2023. Not saying: she wrote the billing-led headline herself.
Madhav Gawande — Co-founder and CEO, Amravati. Wants the best Diwali in the company's history and points at the 3.5 per cent. Not saying: he signed clause nine without reading it, and the Sangh's president guarantees his showroom lease.
Mrunal Tayade — Co-founder and VP Engineering, Amravati. Neutral on copy, hostile to promises: the scheme ledger cannot take a threefold rise in migrations without rewriting the import tool. Not saying: that rewrite is four engineer-months he would rather spend on the HUID queue, the better product in his view.
Zoya Ingole — Data Scientist, Toronto. Produced Exhibit 3 and will not name a winner: the test measured an event the business is not paid for. Not saying: her own consent notice of 1 April cut measured form fills by roughly a tenth, and she is unsure all three arms were hit equally.
Falguni Dhande — Product Designer, Berlin. Designed the scheme-led page and wants it live before Dhanteras: a page converting at double the old rate cannot be wrong. Not saying: she has already rebuilt the pricing page around a scheme-first bundle that clause nine forbids, and has not read clause nine.
Gitanjali Kubade — Head of Customer Success, Singapore. Found the 544-enquiry gap; wants a page that attracts stores which can be onboarded, not counted. Not saying: her bonus rides on day-90 retention, which arm S damages.
Manoj Bhuskade — Head of International Sales, Edison, New Jersey. Opposes a scheme-led home page; his Vraj Jewels proposal covers billing and HUID across nine US stores. Not saying: it is worth less than the ₹9.40 lakh of contract implementation a scheme-led Diwali costs.
Mohini Warhade — Field Implementation Lead, Akola. Has seven engineers for the quarter and did the arithmetic in Exhibit 6. Not saying: she has quietly deferred four scheme migrations a month since July, so the plan she signed was already beyond her team.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

Falguni Dhande, team call of Thursday, 24 September, 7.00 pm in Amravati, 3.30 pm in Berlin

"We have the number everybody in this company said they wanted. Three and a half per cent. The page finally says what the customer says, and now the same people want it back to a sentence about billing software."

Zoya Ingole, same call, 9.30 am in Toronto

"I am not arguing it back to anything. I am telling you the number you like counts a tap on a WhatsApp icon. Ninety days later that arm has twenty-one stores still paying and arm H thirty-two. Pick the metric you will be judged on, then tell me which page won."

Mohini Warhade, email to Gauri Wankhade, Friday, 25 September, 8.12 am

My concern is the page around it: taken with the eleven-month framing and the word 'plan' in the navigation, it begins to read as an invitation to deposit money with a company that may not take deposits. I would not put that page up two weeks before Dhanteras."

Manoj Bhuskade, WhatsApp to Madhav Gawande, Saturday, 26 September, 11.48 pm in Amravati

"Your bill is fine, madam. Everybody's bill is fine. What I lost sleep over was the scheme register — two hundred and forty families, eleven months each, my nephew writing in it."

8. The options as Gauri sees them

A — Put the scheme-led page up everywhere before Dhanteras

Take arm S sitewide, hold paid search at the planned ₹21.00 lakh, and accept ₹9.40 lakh of contract implementers. It bets that the page's job is the enquiry, that ₹18.54 lakh booked beats stores retained, and that Mohini can be bought out of her arithmetic. It also puts up the page counsel warned against.

B — Put the HUID-led page up everywhere

Arm H won on paid conversions, 34 against 27, and on day-90 retention, 32 against 21. It is close to what the organic pages rank for, survives counsel's reading and does not flood Mohini. It also concedes the sentence customers actually say to a rival whose whole page is that sentence, and books ₹16.98 lakh.

C — Route the page by source

Scheme-led for paid search and YouTube, HUID-led for organic, the Marathi Sangh path untouched. It harvests each channel's best line, but leaves Vachan no single answer to what it is, and a sales team promising different things by link.

D — Leave the page and move the money

Cancel Wazir by Wednesday and move the retainer and most of the ₹21.00 lakh into dealer referrals, Sangh desks and Marathi WhatsApp, where a store costs ₹2,500 rather than ₹68,571. It is the best arithmetic in Exhibit 5 and the worst answer to the covenant, since those channels do not scale — and the page still says, for a fourth year, what no customer repeats back.

What unsettled Gauri was that all four treated the headline as the only variable. Nobody had tested a page that led with the scheme and sold the licence, or one that priced the module into the base; nobody had asked whether a store that enquired and never came to a demo was failed by the page or by the twelve-day wait for a visit.

9. The deadline and the constraints

The board call is at 7.30 pm IST on Monday, 28 September, timed for Toronto and New Jersey. Wazir's retainer auto-renews for twelve months on Saturday, 10 October — ₹33.60 lakh — unless cancelled in writing by Wednesday, 30 September. Dhanteras falls in the first week of November, and stores buy software in the six weeks before it or not until Akshaya Tritiya.

Clause nine runs to 31 March 2027 and blocks any offer pricing the module to non-members below the member rate. Mohini has 462 person-days and no approved headcount; Mrunal's rewrite is four engineer-months. Cash is ₹4.05 crore at ₹28 lakh a month of burn, against the covenant's ₹6.00 crore of ARR by 30 June 2027 and ₹438.13 lakh today. Counsel's note is on file, a document a regulator could one day read alongside the page.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What is the page's job at Vachan, and which figure in Exhibits 1 to 5 honestly measures it?
  2. Exhibits 1 and 4 disagree by 544 enquiries. What does each definition make visible, and which belongs on the sales room wall?
  3. Arm S wins Exhibit 2 and loses half of Exhibit 3. Is that a bad headline, a bad offer, an implementation delay or a bad metric, and what evidence would separate them?
  4. Counsel objects to the page as a whole rather than to its best line. How should a product marketer respond when the highest-converting copy carries the regulatory risk, and who decides?
  5. Vachan's cheapest channel costs ₹2,500 a store and its dearest ₹68,571. Is the landing page the wrong place for Gauri's next four weeks?
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Gauri do, what does she tell the board, and what would she have to be wrong about for it to fail?

11. Sunday, later

Gauri turned the printouts face down and put them back in order, which took a moment, because she was no longer sure what the order was. The billing line was the company's history and its search rankings. The HUID line was why 940 stores had bought anything at all, and it kept more of them. The scheme line was the only one a jeweller had ever said back to her.

She thought about Mohini's 462 person-days, the twelve days a store waited after asking for a demo, and the fact that nobody could say whether arm S's missing enquiries had lost interest or merely been kept waiting. She thought about what she would say if a board member asked, quite reasonably, what Vachan Retail Systems was. Somewhere below the window a shutter came down. The retainer would renew on Saturday whatever she decided, unless she wrote to Wazir by Wednesday, and she had not started that letter.

Go-to-Market, Growth & Monetisation · Positioning, Messaging & Product Marketing

Landing Pages and Conversion Copy

On the second Monday of August 2025, Esha Raut pulled up a dashboard she had built herself and did not like what it showed her.

Esha was the senior product marketing manager at Ekagra Learning Cloud, a Pune-based edtech company whose flagship product was a twelve-week, cohort-based Data Analytics Certificate priced at ₹45,000. Ekagra's biggest admissions window ran September through October, catching the festive-season surge in paid and social traffic every Indian edtech company chased. The page carrying that traffic had been live since January, written by a freelancer who had never spoken to an enrolled student, and it was quietly failing. Eighty thousand sessions arrived at it monthly; twelve thousand, fifteen per cent, filled in the signup form; of those, nine hundred converted to a paid enrollment — 7.5 per cent of the leads, or 1.125 per cent of every session. At ₹45,000 a seat, nine hundred enrollments were worth ₹4,05,00,000 a month, against a marketing spend of ₹32,40,000, for a cost of acquisition of ₹3,600 per student. Esha's brief, due before the September surge, was blunt: raise the conversion rate, or explain to the CFO why H2 spend should not simply be cut. She had six weeks and genuine uncertainty about which of two rewrites to ship — and getting it wrong would cost Ekagra its best students of the year.

The idea

A landing page is a single web page whose only job is to convert a visitor who has already arrived with some intent — from an ad, a search result, a referral link — into a lead or a customer, judged by exactly one number: the percentage of arrivals who complete that action. Conversion copy is the wording written to accomplish that for a specific reader arriving with a specific expectation; it is not marketing copy in general, and not the discipline of a homepage or blog post, which serve many possible readers with many possible next steps. A landing page can be beautifully written and still fail, if it answers a question the visitor was not asking.

The idea has two lineages that met on the modern web. The older one is direct-response advertising: Claude Hopkins's 1923 Scientific Advertising argued every line of copy should be judged only by whether it sold, a principle mail-order copywriters like John Caples refined for decades. The newer lineage is digital: once paid search made it possible, around 2005 to 2010, to send traffic to one isolated page and measure exactly what happened next, marketers such as Bryan and Jeffrey Eisenberg — whose 2006 book Call to Action became a reference point — formalised landing-page writing as its own craft, closer to direct-response copywriting than to general web design. The sentence Esha could say in a meeting without sounding glib: a landing page is the messaging hierarchy compressed onto one screen and pointed at one action, with no other job than raising the percentage of arrivals who take it.

How it actually works

The mechanics run in a fixed order, and practitioners who skip steps usually skip the same two. First, message match: the promise in the ad the visitor clicked must be the first sentence they read — a visitor who clicked "become a certified data analyst in 12 weeks" and lands on "unlock your career potential" has already been let down. Second, the header carries exactly one value proposition and one call to action, visible before scrolling; three ways to get started asks the visitor to do the work of choosing, and most choose to leave instead. Third, proof — outcomes, named alumni, a placement percentage — placed close enough to the claim it supports. Fourth, objection handling: the specific hesitations a real prospect raises on a sales call, not the ones a marketer imagines. Fifth, the call to action repeats after every proof block. Sixth, the form: every field is friction, and must justify its cost against the value it gives downstream. Teams usually leave implicit writing objection-handling copy from real sales-call transcripts rather than guesswork, and testing field count independently of the copy above it, since the two are usually bundled and no one can then say which change caused which result.

A worked example

Esha's team had two credible drafts. Draft A tightened the message match and added a proof block built from real alumni placement data, keeping the same admissions-counselling call after signup. Draft B removed two form fields and softened the headline into a broader promise — "master data skills for any career" instead of the certificate's specific outcome — on the theory that a lower-friction, broader promise would pull in more leads. Both were tested against the same 80,000 monthly sessions, so the only thing that could change was what happened after a visitor arrived.

Exhibit 1 — the funnel, old page and two drafts (80,000 monthly sessions throughout)
PageSignupsSignup ratePaid enrollmentsEnrollment rateSessions→paid
Old page12,00015.0%9007.5%1.125%
Draft A (tighter match)14,40018.0%1,0807.5%1.35%
Draft B (broader, lower-friction)16,00020.0%9606.0%1.2%

The first pass looks like a clean win for Draft A: eighteen per cent of sessions signed up, against fifteen per cent on the old page, and the enrollment rate downstream held at seven and a half per cent, so 14,400 signups became 1,080 paid enrollments — a sessions-to-paid rate of 1.35 per cent, up from 1.125 per cent. At ₹45,000 a seat, that is ₹4,86,00,000 a month, against ₹4,05,00,000 on the old page: a gain of ₹81,00,000 from the same spend, which lowers the cost of acquisition from ₹3,600 to ₹3,000 per student.

The second pass is the one that changes the decision. Draft B's broader promise and shorter form pulled more signups — twenty per cent of sessions, 16,000 leads, the best top-of-funnel number of the three — but the enrollment rate fell to six per cent, because a chunk of those extra leads had signed up for "any career," not for a ₹45,000 analytics certificate, and counsellors could not convert them. Sixteen thousand leads at six per cent yield 960 enrollments, a sessions-to-paid rate of 1.2 per cent — better than the old page, worse than Draft A. Those 960 enrollments are worth ₹4,32,00,000, ₹54,00,000 less than Draft A, and the same spend buying fewer paid students pushes the cost of acquisition back up to ₹3,375. Changing one input — the breadth of the promise — moved every number after it, and the metric that looked best at the top of the funnel mattered least once the money was counted.

Nuances a learner must become aware of

The conversion rate you improved may not be the one that matters

A landing page has at least two gates — visit to signup, signup to paid outcome — and a redesign can raise the first while lowering the second, exactly as Draft B did. Report the compound rate through to the outcome the business is paid for, never the first gate alone.

Signups are not revenue

A form fill is a proxy for intent, not a sale. Treating the top-of-funnel percentage as the scoreboard is the most common way a redesign is declared a win internally and a disappointment once finance closes the month.

Message match is often confused with good design

A visually striking page whose headline does not match the ad that sent the visitor will lose to a plain page that matches the promise word for word. Design can amplify a matched message; it cannot substitute for one.

What it cannot tell you

A landing page test tells you whether the argument on the page persuades the traffic already sent to it. It cannot tell you whether the product is good, whether the price is right, or whether the positioning is wrong — those questions live upstream, not on the page.

Confused with content marketing and SEO, and with statistical noise

A landing page assumes the visitor already has intent; it does not create intent the way a blog post does, so judging it by new traffic attracted, rather than what it does with traffic sent, measures the wrong stage of the funnel. And an eighteen per cent signup rate over three days on a few hundred sessions is not the same claim as the same rate over three weeks on tens of thousands — before trusting a lift, know the smallest lift worth detecting and whether the sample could have detected it.

Where the idea stops applying

In an enterprise, sales-led motion, the page is often a business card for a salesperson to follow up on, not the instrument that closes the sale — judging it purely on its own conversion rate misreads its job.

Questions worth asking before relying on it

Is this page judged at the top of the funnel or the bottom? What is the smallest reliably detectable lift given its traffic? And is the win being reported on signups, or on the metric further downstream, where the money is counted?

Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and company stage

In a consumer product like Ekagra's certificate, the page usually carries one CTA, a visible price, and urgency built around a real deadline, because traffic is high-volume and low-touch. In a B2B product, the page typically generates a qualified lead rather than closing a sale outright, so the CTA reads "book a demo," and objection handling shifts toward a buying committee's security and procurement concerns. In a marketplace, the page must speak to supply and demand separately, arriving through different channels, so the same discipline is applied twice. Company stage matters as much as product type: an early-stage company runs one flagship page tested on small samples because traffic is scarce, while a large company runs many pages, tested with properly powered experiments and constrained by a central brand team.

Common mistakes

The first mistake is optimising the headline while leaving the form untouched. The symptom is redesigns with conversion stubbornly flat; the misunderstanding is treating copy and friction as separate problems when a reader must survive both. The diagnostic is to instrument form abandonment field by field, since a rewritten headline cannot rescue a form that loses a third of its visitors at the phone-number field. The second mistake is chasing the top-of-funnel signup rate as the only KPI, exactly Draft B's trap: the symptom is a signup rate that improves while revenue does not, and the fix is to report every result as the compound rate through to the paid outcome. The third mistake is writing copy from the inside out — features rather than the reader's own problem in the reader's own words — with a page that reads like a specification sheet; the diagnostic is to hold every sentence against a real, unprompted phrase a customer used, and cut whatever has no match. The fourth mistake is calling a result significant before sample size justified it; the diagnostic is computing the required sample size before the test begins, not after.

What good looks like

Consider a subscription fitness company running the same kind of page, whose growth team had internalised the lesson Ekagra was about to learn. Before touching a word, they built the objection-handling section entirely from phrases real prospects had used on support calls, unprompted. They audited message match against every live ad, rewriting headlines that no longer matched their campaigns rather than waiting for a quarterly redesign. Before launching a test, they calculated the sample size needed to detect the smallest lift worth caring about, and refused to call an early result before that window closed. And every dashboard reported the compound rate through to paid subscriptions, never the signup rate alone, so more low-intent signups were never mistaken for a win. None of this was exotic; it was the same mechanical steps as any landing page, done in order and measured against the right number.

Closing

Esha shipped Draft A. Her reasoning for the CFO was arithmetic, not taste: Draft A raised the sessions-to-paid rate to 1.35 per cent and revenue to ₹4,86,00,000 at a lower cost of acquisition of ₹3,000 per student, while Draft B's broader promise produced a better top-of-funnel number but a worse outcome everywhere money was counted. It also matched the messaging hierarchy agreed in March — Draft B's softened headline had quietly abandoned the specific promise that hierarchy was built around. What Esha resolved to learn next was the statistics of experimentation properly, since the gap between a real eighteen per cent lift and pure noise had nearly cost her the right call.

Sit with these:

1. When your top-line conversion rate improves, do you know which gate moved, and does the improvement survive being carried through to the metric the business is actually paid on?
2. If you had to ship a page today, with no time for one more test, which version would you choose — and could you defend that choice using only the numbers you already have?

Go-to-Market, Growth & Monetisation · Positioning, Messaging & Product Marketing

Landing Pages and Conversion Copy

What the page is really being asked to do, why the dashboard number is usually the wrong one, and what practitioners who agree about the craft still dispute.

1. Two decisions, taken in the same fortnight

On 14 April 2026, Anwesha Mhatre had a slide she did not want to present. She ran product marketing at Astitva Safety Cloud, a Pune company selling safety-compliance software to mid-sized Indian factories: incident logging, statutory registers under the Factories Act, audit-finding closure, the paperwork a state factory inspectorate asks for. Deals averaged ₹6.4 lakh of annual contract value and closed in about eleven weeks through inside sales. In February a contractor had rewritten the demand-generation page on a persuasive argument — that the company sold not compliance software but early warning — and it now led with Know which line will hurt someone next month. Demo requests rose. Anwesha's slide showed closed business had fallen, and her chief financial officer, Abhijit Sathe, had read the pipeline report.

Nine days later and 840 kilometres south, Xerxes Bhesania faced a differently shaped decision. He led growth at Ankahi Stories, a Bengaluru audio-fiction subscription app publishing serialised Hindi, Marathi and Tamil drama into a category Pocket FM and Kuku FM had taught Indian listeners to want. Ankahi bought Meta and YouTube traffic to a mobile page whose only job was to send a visitor to the Play Store. A clean five-day A/B test had just closed; the broader-promise variant produced 33 per cent more installs, and the designer wanted to ship on Friday. Ankahi's data lead, Anindita Saikia, had pointed out that the number the business lives on — paid subscribers after a seven-day free trial — would not be legible for another nine weeks, by which time the losing variant would be deleted.

Neither decision turns on better copywriting. Both turn on one structural fact: a landing page is measured where the visitor is, and paid for further down.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A landing page is one page whose whole purpose is to convert a visitor arriving with pre-existing intent into a defined next action, judged by the ratio of that action to arrivals. Conversion copy is the wording chosen to do that for one reader with one expectation. Two properties separate it from web writing: the traffic is bought against a promise, so the page inherits an obligation it did not write, and it has one success metric, so every element competes for the reader's willingness to continue.

Two strands fused around 2006. From direct-response advertising came the discipline of judging copy only by response — Claude Hopkins's Scientific Advertising (1923), John Caples's mail-order tradition, headlines split-tested against coupon returns. From paid search came cheap isolation: one traffic source could now be pointed at one page and observed, which is why the Eisenberg brothers' Call to Action (2006) reads like Caples with a dashboard.

Practitioners who all write good pages divide into three camps. The direct-response school signs that any element which does not measurably increase the target action should be removed, and will not sign that a page owes anything to a brand effect it cannot measure this quarter. The positioning school, closer to the Kellogg and Cornell product-marketing tradition, signs that the page is the messaging hierarchy on a screen and must not promise what the product is not; it will not sign that a conversion lift justifies a promise sales must walk back. The experimentation school signs that nothing about a page is knowable without a powered test, and will not sign that a marketer's judgement counts as evidence. Anwesha's contractor made a positioning argument; the variant Xerxes was handed was direct-response orthodoxy; Anindita objected on experimentation grounds. Most real arguments about landing pages are these three talking past each other.

3. Mechanics: the page as a chain of gates

Experts do not model a landing page as a conversion rate. They model it as a product of gates, each with its own copy lever, written down before a word of the page. Ankahi's chain, over the quarter ending March 2026 on 12,00,000 paid sessions: 18 per cent clicked through to the Play Store, half of those installed, 40 per cent of installs started the trial, 40 per cent of trials converted to paid. The product is 0.18 × 0.50 × 0.40 × 0.40 = 0.0144 — 1.44 per cent of sessions, 17,280 subscribers — and it is the product, not any gate, that finance is paid on.

Two consequences are routinely missed. Because the chain is multiplicative, a 10 per cent relative improvement at any gate is worth the same 10 per cent at the end — 1.44 per cent becomes 1.584 per cent, 17,280 subscribers 19,008 — so the instruction is not "fix the worst gate" but "fix the gate where ten per cent is cheapest". And copy changes rarely stay in one gate: broadening a promise raises the first and lowers a later one by changing who walks through. Variant P named the thing — Forty Marathi crime serials. First episode free. Variant Q generalised: Unlimited audio stories. Seven days free.

Exhibit 1 — Ankahi Stories, two page variants against the same 12,00,000 paid sessions per quarter
StageVariant P (specific)Variant Q (broad)
Paid sessions on page12,00,00012,00,000
Store click-throughs (Avg rate of sessions)2,16,000 (18.0%)2,88,000 (24.0%)
Installs (Avg rate of clicks)1,08,000 (50.0%)1,44,000 (50.0%)
Trial starts (Avg rate of installs)43,200 (40.0%)50,400 (35.0%)
Paid subscribers (Avg rate of trials)17,280 (40.0%)15,120 (30.0%)

Monthly subscribers are valued at ₹99 × 4.0 months average tenure = ₹396. P: 12,096 × ₹899 = ₹108.74 lakh plus 5,184 × ₹396 = ₹20.53 lakh. Q: 6,048 × ₹899 = ₹54.37 lakh plus 9,072 × ₹396 = ₹35.93 lakh. Spend is ₹1.20 crore a quarter (₹10 per session) in both arms, so cost per paid subscriber is ₹694 (P) and ₹794 (Q).

Variant Q wins the gate the test was watching by a third and loses ₹38.97 lakh of first-year revenue a quarter. A generic promise recruits listeners who wanted something; they convert worse out of trial, and when they pay they choose monthly, being unsure they want a year of this. The page changed the cohort and therefore the price those people would pre-commit to. Copy as a selection mechanism on plan mix is the step most teams leave implicit.

The formal treatment that divides the schools is sample size. For a two-arm test at 80 per cent power and 5 per cent significance, n ≈ 16·p(1−p)/δ² per arm, with p the baseline rate and δ the absolute difference to detect. At Ankahi's store-click gate, p = 0.18 and a 5 per cent relative lift means δ = 0.009: about 29,200 sessions per arm, under four days of traffic. At the paid gate, p = 0.0144 and δ = 0.00072, giving about 4,38,000 per arm — ten weeks for both arms, with the trial delaying first signal another week. That is why competent teams read installs: the honest metric takes fifteen times longer, and the incentive to declare victory arrives first.

4. When it applies, as testable claims

One: the visitor already has intent the page did not create. True for Ankahi, whose traffic is interest-targeted but arrives mid-scroll; only partly true for Astitva, whose non-brand search traffic wants a free audit checklist, not software. Where intent is absent, the page's job is education and its conversion rate means little.

Two: the requested action is causally close to revenue. Strongly true for Ankahi — four gates, about two weeks from click to cash. Weakly true for Astitva, where a demo request is separated from revenue by a qualification call, a security review and eleven weeks of selling, during which things the page cannot control decide it.

Three: traffic volume can detect a lift worth having. True for Ankahi at the top gate, false at the bottom. Flatly false for Astitva: at 20,000 quarterly sessions and a 4.3 per cent demo-request rate, a 10 per cent relative lift needs about 35,600 sessions per arm — 46 weeks of traffic split two ways. Astitva cannot test its way there, and any claim that it did is noise wearing a p-value.

The idea turns actively misleading in two situations. Where the page is a qualification instrument rather than a conversion one — which Astitva's is, whatever the dashboard column is called — raising its conversion rate is harmful. And where the problem is upstream, no wording moves the number; a well-run test says so, and teams misread it as "we need better copy".

5. The seam: one page, three audiences

A page has one conversion rate only if it has one kind of visitor. Amruta Kanhere, Astitva's demand-generation lead, segmented February's page against January's by source, and the aggregate reversed.

Exhibit 2 — Astitva Safety Cloud, quarterly funnel by page version (20,000 sessions, ₹96 lakh demand-gen spend)
VersionDemo requestsAvg request rateQualified leadsAvg qualification rateClosed deals at 12.5%New ACV (₹ lakh)
A — compliance framing8604.30%40847.4%51326.40
B — category framing9084.54%35238.8%44281.60
Split by source: A on search, B on LinkedIn9204.60%41945.5%52332.80

Requests by source, A: 450 brand, 330 non-brand, 80 LinkedIn; qualified leads 252, 132, 24. B: 350, 418, 140 requests; 196, 121, 35 qualified leads. The split takes the better version per source: 450 + 330 + 140 = 920 requests, 252 + 132 + 35 = 419 qualified leads, at 12.5 per cent 52.4 deals, reported as 52. New ACV is deals × ₹6.4 lakh; cost per closed deal ₹1.88 lakh (A), ₹2.18 lakh (B), ₹1.85 lakh (split).

The contractor was right and wrong in a way only segmentation reveals. On cold LinkedIn traffic, where nobody is searching for anything, the category promise genuinely works — 35 qualified leads against 24. On brand search, where the visitor typed "safety compliance software", it fails a message-match test the visitor runs unconsciously, and Astitva lost 56 qualified leads there. Demo requests rose 5.6 per cent; closed deals fell from 51 to 44, or ₹44.80 lakh of new ACV a quarter, ₹1.79 crore annualised. The best configuration is neither page but both, routed by source.

6. Hard edge cases

Two-sided products. Ashiyana Rentals Exchange, an Ahmedabad rental marketplace competing for attention with NoBroker and MagicBricks, ran one page for owners and tenants because the brand team wanted one story. Of 60,000 monthly sessions, 42,000 arrived with tenant intent and 18,000 with owner intent; the combined page converted tenants at 6.0 per cent and owners at 1.2 per cent. Separate pages moved those to 7.5 and 3.0 per cent. With an activated listing worth ₹5,600 of annual take and a tenant signup ₹700, monthly value rose from ₹29.74 lakh (216 × ₹5,600 plus 2,520 × ₹700) to ₹52.29 lakh (540 × ₹5,600 plus 3,150 × ₹700). The single page had been optimised for the abundant side.

Organisational seams. At Astitva the page belonged to marketing, the form fields to sales operations, and post-submit routing to a revenue-operations analyst reporting to neither; nobody owned the compound rate, which is why the February regression survived ten weeks. Mature companies fix this by naming one owner of the sessions-to-cash number, with authority over the form as well as the headline.

Regulated products. Indian insurance and lending pages carry mandatory disclosure and cannot make outcome claims, which removes the direct-response school's strongest lever. What remains is specificity about process — turnaround, documents, eligibility — and pages that convert here read like an operations manual.

Hardware plus software. Abhaya Alarm Systems sells a monitored home-security kit on a ₹499 monthly subscription; its page converts to a site-survey visit, and technician availability in the visitor's pin code moves conversion more than any sentence. Copy promising "installed this week" that is not operationally true converts brilliantly and destroys the funnel two steps later.

AI-native products. Aakhyan AI Desk, a support-automation tool, meets the problem acutely: the honest promise — resolves roughly 40 per cent of tier-one tickets, depending on ticket mix — converts worse than the confident one, which produces trials that churn in week three when the figure lands at 22 per cent. AI pages also face a novel failure, a demo that works only on curated inputs; the mature handling lets visitors bring their own data onto the page, converting fewer at a far higher realisation rate.

7. Nine distinctions that separate an expert

The conversion rate is a ratio, and both terms move

A rate improves if the numerator rises or if the denominator gets better-qualified: when a channel's targeting tightens, conversion rises with no copy change. The tell is a step change on a date when nothing shipped. Experts check traffic mix before accepting any lift.

Message match is a claim about the ad, not the page

Teams audit pages in isolation and find nothing wrong. The tell is a page converting well on one campaign and badly on another with identical copy: Astitva's category page was mismatched on two sources of three. Read the page immediately after the ad, on a phone.

Friction is not uniformly bad

Form fields, pin-code checks and prepaid nudges suppress conversion and improve realisation. The tell is a team calling every removal a win without naming what the field protected. Ask what the friction filtered, and whether admitting those visitors costs more than the volume is worth.

Specificity usually beats breadth, but not at every gate

Broad promises win the first click and lose the cohort; the tell is a variant that wins on volume and is never re-examined. But on cold traffic a specific promise can be unintelligible — why Ankahi's broad page won installs and Astitva's category page won LinkedIn.

The page selects the plan, not only the purchase

Ankahi's variants sold the same product at the same prices and produced annual-plan shares of 70 and 40 per cent. The tell is revenue per new customer drifting down while conversion improves; teams rarely report both, so a page change looks free when it has repriced the business.

Most pages cannot be tested, and saying so is the expert move

Below roughly 400 conversions per arm, tests resolve nothing in useful time. The tell is a 14 per cent lift reported on 90 conversions and shipped. Astitva's 46-week requirement means the decision rests on segmentation and judgement, defended as such rather than dressed as experiment.

The read-out date decides the winner

Because early gates move first, a test called early is biased toward whichever variant wins the earliest gate. The tell is a results template whose primary metric is the first to reach significance. Xerxes's five-day read was structurally incapable of seeing the loss.

Objection copy must be quoted, not invented

The strongest sections on high-performing pages are transcriptions. The tell is copy answering objections a marketer finds interesting — integrations, roadmap — rather than those buyers voice: implementation effort, data entry, and what happens when the inspector arrives.

A page becomes a liability the day the product changes

Pages are written once and audited never. The tell is a live page promising a feature that shipped differently, or a price that has moved. A page carries a maintenance obligation tied to the release cycle; the cheapest diagnostic is reading your own live pages monthly.

8. Differences by product type and stage

In consumer products the page is the conversion instrument: volume high, chain short, testing real. In B2B it is a qualification instrument whose conversion rate should sometimes be lowered deliberately, written for a committee reading it in a forwarded link. In enterprise the page barely converts and is read after a meeting, as reassurance; judging it on conversion is a category error. Marketplaces need one page per side. Hardware pages convert to an appointment and inherit a physical constraint the copy must not overstate. AI products meet the honesty-versus-conversion tension head on, and increasingly an interactive demo replaces the argument.

What is overstated is the craft difference. Message match, one primary action, quoted objections and mobile load time apply identically everywhere; what changes is what the page converts to and how it is measured. Stage matters more than teams admit: a seed-stage company should not run A/B tests at all and should rewrite from sales-call transcripts monthly; a growth-stage company can test its top gate but rarely its bottom; a large company's binding constraint is usually a brand review forbidding the specificity the page needs.

9. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Ashiyana, above, is the clean success: two pages instead of one raised blended conversion from 4.56 to 6.15 per cent and monthly value by ₹22.55 lakh. Astitva is the ambiguous case, right on a third of traffic and wrong on the rest.

Amiya Baby Essentials is the failure. Advaita Kher's direct-to-consumer brand rebuilt its bestselling hamper page in October 2025 on impeccable direct-response principles: remove the pin-code serviceability check, remove the prepaid nudge, lead with a ₹299 trial pack instead of the ₹1,450 hamper, one-tap cash on delivery. Orders per 10,000 sessions rose from 250 to 350.

Exhibit 3 — Amiya Baby Essentials, contribution per 10,000 sessions
Page versionOrdersCOD ordersReturnsDeliveredAvg contribution per delivered order (₹)Net contribution (₹)
v1 — original2501504420643079,340
v2 — frictionless35030010224830052,980
